Workplace culture and service delivery are both candidates.

Notices that only work on good broadband are a gate. Print in the office still matters. A skipped visit may be diesel and ice, not refusal.

Open the people CI and this place CI together when both apply. Do not use rural as code for white. If the family cannot run the exception in English, the cap is the policy.
chapters.evidence: Broadband; print; phone; county hours; diesel and ice; people CI sitting next to place.
chapters.practitioner: Name the town. Open the people CI. Write a disposition. A skipped visit may be the road.
chapters.title: How it hits DHS gates — the 40%

frame: Open this brief when place is the first fact — distance, broadband, a county desk, a closed hospital. Then open the community brief that matches the household.
Name the town. A missed visit may be diesel and ice. Open the people brief and this place brief together.

Greater Minnesota is not one region. Iron Range, prairie, forest, border towns. Compass splits on people pages — Mexican nearly 4 in 10 outside the Twin Cities; Somali about 22 percent Greater Minnesota; Hmong about 94 percent Twin Cities. Date the people page. This page is place.
This copy is a living candidate.
intelligenceGuide.stand: Rural is geography and infrastructure — broadband, distance, hospital closure, county capacity — not a racial type. Farmer and miner are not the same. Do not use rural as code for white. Somali in Worthington, Mexican in a dairy county, and the eleven nations are not afterthoughts. Meet people where they are. Start with this family and this county.
intelligenceGuide.title: Rural Minnesota (place, not a race)

sections.heading: Begin here
paragraphs: This is a language door, not one people. Ethnic Russians, Soviet Jews of the 1970s–90s stream, Ukrainian households who use Russian, evangelical Baptists in some Greater Minnesota towns, last year’s arrival, and a third generation that does not need an interpreter may share a language on a form and not a Tuesday. Not Ukrainian. Looking white is not the same as needing no interpreter. Start with this household.
Russian is a language many peoples use in Minnesota. Not one community, not Ukrainian as a synonym. Always defer to this household.
Not one people from a translation list. Not Ukrainian as a synonym. Not one politics. This brief is a hypothesis you still test on this family.

sections.heading: Keep in mind
paragraphs: Open this brief when Russian may be the language. Confirm whether it is actually the home language. Ukrainian Minnesota is a different brief.

Evidence-based means dated counts, law, history, disparity — and refusing to invent a community population where Compass has no Russian cultural-community profile. Practitioner-based means Tuesday: book a qualified Russian interpreter; do not treat Ukrainian; put the patronymic on the form; do not assume English because the person is white; do not harvest Russian-speaking staff as the interpreter or the community. Employee groups may fact-check. They do not veto Ukraine-war structure, alcohol and family violence as facts, or queer people in this language because a Minimization room is uncomfortable.

There is no Compass “Russian Minnesota” people-count. Compass immigration table: about 6,483 foreign-born from Russia — date the table; that is not speakers. Compass Ukrainian cultural community is about 22,570 (ACS 2019–2023) — do not mash it into this door. Star Tribune 2025: Russian is among languages each representing about 2% of Minnesotans who speak a language other than English at home. SOS voter materials include Russian. Date the number. Do not invent the rest.
Nothing from the depth this program requires was kept at full depth. This copy is a living candidate: staff keep a stable doorway until you or an Equity Director in the administration promote.

sections.heading: A Note on This Guide — a language door, not one people
paragraphs: Russian is a CLAS five-language door, not a people. Ethnic Russian, Soviet Jewish, Ukrainian-using-Russian, Belarusian, Central Asian, Caucasian, evangelical. No Compass cultural-community profile. Date what you cite.
There is no single Russian client. Defer to this household. Do not open the Ukrainian people-page. Book a qualified interpreter. A list is not the person.

This brief is about Russian as a language door on the department’s CLAS five-language standing written list — with Hmong, Somali, Spanish, and Vietnamese — not as one people. If you invent a single “Russian community” from that list, you have already left this door. A list is not the person and not the dialect. Still book a qualified interpreter.

### Who this is

Disaggregate before you open a file. Ethnic Russians. Soviet Jews of the 1970s–90s refusenik / Jackson-Vanik stream. Ukrainian households who use Russian — not the Ukrainian people-page; Compass Ukrainian is about 22,570 (ACS 2019–2023); do not mash. Belarusian, Central Asian, and Caucasian Russian-speakers. Evangelical and Baptist Russians, including some Greater Minnesota towns. Recent arrivals versus 1990s versus a third generation that may not need you to speak Russian at all.

### Who this is not

A full mosaic is not a stereotype. A stereotype is when this page becomes the person in the lobby. Shared language is not shared origin, not shared religion, and not shared politics. The Ukraine war is current structure for some households and a trap if you assume every Russian speaker is a combatant or a Putin voter.

There is no Minnesota Compass cultural-community profile titled Russian. Compass immigration table: about 6,483 foreign-born from Russia — date the table you open; that is not a count of speakers. ACS language-at-home figures disagree across vintages. Star Tribune (31 July 2025): Russian is among languages each representing about 2% of Minnesotans who speak a language other than English at home. Minnesota Secretary of State voter materials include Russian. Date the number. Do not invent a community population.

The diversity inside this language is the point. A Jewish grandmother who left on an exit visa in 1989, an Orthodox parishioner, a Belarusian family that uses Russian at the table, a Ukrainian household that will not accept a “former Soviet” interpreter after 2022, a Baptist family in a Greater Minnesota town, a professional who does not need an interpreter and whose elder does — share a language on a form and do not share a Tuesday.

### How to read this

Always defer to the person in front of you. This page is a hypothesis you still test on this household.

sections.heading: Origins — empire, Soviet, and named streams
paragraphs: Late-imperial emigration; Soviet emigration; 1970s–90s Jewish refusenik / Jackson-Vanik stream; 1991 USSR collapse; later waves. Named streams, not one origin myth.
History is literacy for the desk. It is not a speech you give the family. Do not start with a nesting-doll tourism sentence.

There is no single founding of “Russian-speaking Minnesota.” Ethnic Russian peoplehood is older than the Soviet Union and older than this department. It is not the whole door. Other peoples used Russian as an imperial and Soviet language of school, army, and office. That history is why a language list is not a census of who counts.

### History for the meeting

Late-imperial emigration included Jews fleeing pogroms and others leaving the Russian Empire. Some of that older Jewish Minnesota is English-dominant now and is not this CLAS door. Do not mash a 1910 synagogue story onto a 1994 arrival and call it one community.

### What people brought

The Soviet period produced later streams: dissidents, Jews denied exit (refuseniks) until Jackson-Vanik and the years that followed opened a way, and then the 1991 collapse of the USSR, which moved people for work, family, and survival. Evangelical Protestants — Baptists and related churches — left in named waves as well. Central Asian and Caucasian families may carry Russian as a public language beside another home language.

What people brought is not one kit: Orthodox practice, Jewish peoplehood, evangelical church, Soviet official atheism, Cyrillic literacy, professional skill the U.S. did not always recognize, and a memory of a state that surveilled. What they met in Minnesota: an English form, a racial order that may file them as white and skip the interpreter, and often one interpreter labeled “Russian.”

sections.heading: The Geography of Russian-Speaking Worlds
paragraphs: Russian Federation; Ukraine; Belarus; Central Asia; Caucasus; Baltic; global diaspora. Minnesota is not Brighton Beach and not Moscow.
Do not assume Northeast Minneapolis. Do not assume they have been to Russia. Greater Minnesota evangelical towns are on this map.

Homeland is not one flag. The Russian Federation is a geography some families name. Ukraine is another — and a Ukrainian household that uses Russian is still not this page’s invented people. Belarus, Kazakhstan and other Central Asian states, the Caucasus, the Baltics: Russian as a Soviet-era public language still sits in some of those rooms. Do not referee borders in a waiver meeting. Listen if they name a place.

### Homeland

The diaspora is global: Israel and Germany for large Jewish streams, the United States, Canada, and Europe. Brighton Beach is not Minnesota. Brooklyn, northern New Jersey, and California sit on a different map. Secondary migration and church networks built some of what you will meet here.

### Minnesota

In Minnesota: Twin Cities households; some inner-ring suburbs; Orthodox parishes and synagogues as named places, not a blob; evangelical and Baptist congregations in some towns, including Greater Minnesota. Do not assume Northeast Minneapolis. Do not assume the person in front of you has been to Russia. Do not assume a Greater Minnesota town has no Russian-speaking church.

sections.heading: Emigration Waves — Foundational Events, Not One Flight
paragraphs: Imperial, Soviet, Jewish 1970s–90s, 1991 collapse, later family and professional streams, and 2022-onward displacement for some households. Different Tuesdays.
If you only know “Russian,” you will miss the Ukrainian household that uses Russian, the Jewish elder from the refusenik stream, and the U.S.-born adult who does not need you to lecture 1991.

If 1975 is the foundational event of Hmong Minnesota and 1991 of Somali Minnesota, Russian-speaking Minnesota does not get one year. It gets a stack, and you will misread the room if you pick the wrong one.

### Foundational events

Late-imperial flight. Soviet emigration in drips and then in named openings. The 1970s–90s Jewish stream — refuseniks, Jackson-Vanik (1974) as U.S. law tying trade to emigration, then the late-1980s and 1990s movement — built part of Twin Cities Jewish life. That stream is Jewish peoplehood meeting Minnesota synagogues and a JCC, not a nesting-doll exhibit. 1991 and the collapse of the USSR moved others: ethnic Russians, mixed families, professionals, people from republics that were suddenly different countries.

### Who you meet

Evangelical and Baptist Russians arrived in church-sponsored patterns that sometimes landed in Greater Minnesota, not only in Minneapolis. Later family and employment streams are ordinary immigration, not a refugee poster.

2022 and the war on Ukraine is current structure for some households in this language: relatives under fire, mixed families, people who will not accept a Russian-language flyer that looks like Moscow. It is a trap if you treat every Russian speaker as a combatant or a Putin voter. It is also a trap if you pretend the war is not in the room when they name it. Literacy for the desk. Not a speech you give the family.

sections.heading: Family
paragraphs: Nuclear and multi-generation both live here. Patronymic names the father in the person. Elders in some households; adult children as the English door in others.
Ask who should be in the room. A nuclear English form already has a who. Do not use a child as the interpreter. Do not drop the patronymic.

Family is not one size. Some households look nuclear on an English form and still carry obligation to a parent who does not drive and does not read the form. Some are three generations in one week. Some are a single elder whose children live in another metro. Elder isolation is a named harm in this language door. It is not a cultural virtue.

### Who is in the household

The patronymic — a name built from the father — is how a person is fully named in Russian. A form that keeps only first and last has already dropped a who. Ask how to file. Ask who should be in the room.

### Who speaks

Adult children may speak for an elder in English. That is a hypothesis, not permission to skip the interpreter or to use a child. CLAS still stands. A sixteen-year-old in the lobby is not the qualified interpreter.

Women’s labor and professional second generation sit next to older gender patterns in some rooms. Both can be true. Minnesota law still stands on violence, neglect, and who may consent. Do not skip mandated reporting and call it culture.

sections.heading: Minnesota and Russian-Speaking History
paragraphs: Pattern: synagogues and JCC for some Jewish streams; Orthodox parishes; evangelical / Baptist churches in some towns. No single “Russian community center” as the whole. CECLC is a door.
Pay partners you actually have. Staff are colleagues, not the curriculum. Do not treat  Russian-speaking staff. A parish visit is not consultation. Guest.

Minnesota put Russian on the CLAS five because the building already knew it would meet this language on notices, health care, cash, food, aging, and voting — not because Compass drew a people-blob titled Russian. That is the honest origin of this spine. A language list is operations. It is not a census.

### Places

Places, not a blob: Twin Cities; inner-ring suburbs; some Greater Minnesota towns with evangelical churches. Do not write “the Russian neighborhood” onto a map you do not have. Pattern now. Date a geography when a controlling source exists.

### Partners

Partners: synagogues and Jewish Community Centers for some of the Jewish stream; Russian Orthodox parishes some families name; evangelical and Baptist churches in some towns; no single “Russian community center” as the whole. CECLC is a department door — not the community. Pay the partner this household actually uses.

Do not extract Russian-speaking staff as the interpreter or as “the community.” They may be Jewish, Ukrainian, Belarusian, or a third generation that does not want to be your culture desk. A liturgy or a JCC visit is optional professional development. You are a guest. It does not make you the expert.

sections.heading: A Language Door — not a people you invented
paragraphs: The object is a language and named variation inside it. Ethnic Russian peoplehood exists. It is not this whole door. Jewish peoplehood is not “Russian culture.”
Do not invent a people from a translation list. Do not copy a Ukrainian, Somali, or “white Minnesota” sentence onto this page.

The heart of this intelligence is a refusal. Russian on the five is a door onto many peoples. Ethnic Russian peoplehood is real — language, literature, Orthodox memory for some, a state that did harm and a state some people still defend. It is not permission to file a Ukrainian, a Tajik, or a Soviet Jew under one folk costume.

### In this state

Jewish peoplehood in the 1970s–90s stream is not “Russian culture with a menorah.” Ukrainian households that use Russian are not a round-up for this page. Evangelical Russians may organize life around a church in a town that has never heard the word CLAS.

In Minnesota another fact sits on the same desk: many of these households are read as white. The building’s unmarked default will skip the interpreter, skip the Cyrillic notice, and call that fairness. That skip is the gate. White appearance is not English proficiency and not the absence of a people.

This guide is a working orientation. Individual variation always supersedes group generalization. Always defer to the person in front of you.

sections.heading: Core Concepts
paragraphs: Disaggregation; formality and titles; patronymic as personhood; hospitality; Soviet-state memory for some; church or synagogue as a channel, not the community; Minnesota Nice is not this grammar.
You work with these. You do not perform them. Follow this room. Do not make a priest, rabbi, or pastor the case plan unless this family asked.

Disaggregation. The first grammar. If you cannot name the stream, you do not have a household yet.

### Patronymic

Given name, father’s name as a middle element, family name. Dropping it invents a person. Filing it wrong invents a person. Ask.

### Formality and titles

First name plus patronymic is respectful address in Russian. First name only can be too familiar with an elder. English “hi guys” is not a translation.

### Hospitality

Tea, food, time in some rooms. Refusing everything can read as cold. You still keep medical and legal clocks.

### State memory

For some, a Soviet past means you do not volunteer extra facts to a government desk. For some, the Russian Federation is still the frame. For some, 2022 ended that sentence. You do not interrogate loyalty. You do the form.

### Church, synagogue, none

A parish, a shul, or a Baptist church may be the actual information channel. It is not “the community.” Do not make clergy the case plan unless this family asked.

### Directness

Some Russian-speaking rooms will say the hard sentence without Minnesota Nice. That is not hostility. Follow this room. Do not punish candor and do not invent a Slavic personality.

sections.heading: Religion — Orthodox, Jewish, evangelical, none
paragraphs: Russian Orthodox, Jewish, evangelical Protestant, none — ask. Streams do not share a sanctuary. An ancestor of Soviet official atheism sits in some rooms.
Do not make a priest, rabbi, or pastor the case plan unless this family asked. Do not assume Orthodox because the language is Russian.

Ask. Do not assume Russian Orthodox because the language is Russian. Russian Orthodox, Jewish, evangelical Protestant, and none all live in this door. Soviet official atheism left a mark in some families that still keep a holiday table.

### Streams

The parish is a center of liturgy, memorial, and sometimes mutual aid. It is not the community. Do not BCC one priest and call it consultation. Icons in a home are not a case plan and not a museum.

### Practice

Jewish households in the 1970s–90s stream may be secular in the Soviet sense and still Jewish in peoplehood — synagogue, JCC, kosher as a maybe, Hebrew school as a maybe. Do not give them an Orthodox Christian flyer and call it language access. Do not give them a “Russian culture night” and call it Jewish.

Evangelical and Baptist congregations — some in Greater Minnesota — can be the whole public life of a household. Church English and home Russian may sit together. Do not make the pastor the case plan unless they asked.

Do not rank piety. A person who left the church or the synagogue is still this language door if that is the language they need.

sections.heading: Greetings
paragraphs: Handshake common in many rooms. Titles. First name plus patronymic is respectful address in Russian. Follow this room.
Do not force a hug. Do not import Somali right-hand rules or the Black nod. Say the name. Ask how to address an elder.

Handshake is common in many rooms — men, and often women in professional space. Follow this room. Some older Orthodox or observant Jewish settings will change the rule. You nod if a hand is not offered. You do not make a scene in the lobby.

### Titles

Titles matter. First name plus patronymic is the respectful Russian address for an adult you do not know well. English Mr./Ms. plus family name is a decent substitute if you cannot produce the patronymic. Do not use a first name with an elder because the form printed it.

### This room

Zdravstvuyte is the formal hello. English “hello” is ordinary, especially with the second generation. Say the name. Ask how to say it.

Do not import Somali right-hand rules or the Black nod onto this page. This is not those grammars. Physical contact: follow this person. A hug from staff is not warmth if the household did not offer it.

sections.heading: Naming — given name, patronymic, family name
paragraphs: Given name + patronymic + family name. Databases that drop the patronymic invent a person. Women may have a gendered family-name ending.
Ask how to file. Ask how to say it. Do not invent a middle name because the screen wants one. The invented name becomes a gate.

A common Russian pattern is given name, patronymic, family name: a person is Ivan Petrovich Sokolov because his father is Petr. Maria Ivanovna Sokolova because her father is Ivan. The patronymic is not a middle name you may drop for convenience. Databases that drop it invent a person. That invented person then fails a match in MHCP, child welfare, and school.

### How to file

Family names may take a gendered ending. Sokolov / Sokolova is the same family. The form that flags the difference as fraud has already chosen a household type. Ask how to file. Ask how this person wants the English record to read.

Jewish, Ukrainian, Belarusian, Central Asian, and Caucasian names in this language door will not all look like Ivan and Maria. Do not “correct” a name toward a Russian textbook. Pronounce it. Ask.

The form that demands first-middle-last and a hyphen will invent a person. Do not invent a last name, and do not invent a middle initial from a patronymic without asking. Three people in one household may not share a “last name” the way a Swedish Minnesota form expects. That is not fraud until you have a reason.

sections.heading: Dates of Significance
paragraphs: Orthodox Nativity and Pascha on the Julian calendar for some; Jewish calendar for some; 9 May Victory Day memory for some; 1991 literacy; 2022 as current structure for some.
A calendar click is literacy. It is not community engagement. Do not put a Ukraine-war slogan on a case note.

Orthodox Nativity and Pascha follow the Julian calendar for many Russian Orthodox households — often later than Western Christmas and Easter. Schedule around them when you can. They are not a day off the work. They are literacy.

### Calendar

Jewish High Holidays, Passover, and other calendar days matter in the Jewish stream. They are not “Russian holidays.” Open the Jewish calendar if that is the household.

9 May — Victory Day in Soviet and Russian memory of 1945 — is real for some elders and a political fight for others after 2022. Listen. Do not put a victory parade on a case note. Do not lecture.

1991 is literacy, not a holiday. 24 February 2022 is current structure for some families. Do not put “Fall of Saigon party” energy — or a Ukraine-war slogan — on a case note.

New Year’s Eve (Novy God) was the large Soviet winter holiday and still is for some secular families. A calendar click on this program is literacy for scheduling. It is not community engagement.

sections.heading: Education
paragraphs: Soviet-era credentials were often high and not always recognized here. Elders may be LEP; professionals may not be. No Compass education profile for “Russian speakers.” Pattern now.
A parent who reads Cyrillic and limited English is not illiterate. The English-only packet is the gate. Do not skip the interpreter because the person looks professional.

There is no Compass education table for “Russian speakers.” Pattern now — date the number when a controlling source exists. Do not invent a rate.

### School and language

Soviet and post-Soviet credentials were often high — engineering, medicine, teaching — and not always recognized here. A person who was a professional in 1994 and a warehouse worker in 1996 is not a personality. Children of that stream may be in English-dominant schools with a parent who still cannot run an IEP in English.

Elders may be LEP and fully literate in Cyrillic. Professionals and the U.S.-born may not need an interpreter and may still have a parent who does. Do not skip the interpreter because the adult in the lobby is white, employed, or accent-light.

A parent who speaks fluent Russian and limited English is not illiterate. The English-only form is the gate. Put Russian on the line. Confirm it is Russian, not Ukrainian.

sections.heading: Etiquette
paragraphs: Shoes in some homes. Hospitality. Formality with elders. Flowers and food as ordinary courtesy in some rooms.
Accept a little tea. Keep medical and legal time. Do not photograph icons or a home altar. Follow this household.

Shoes off in some homes. Follow the household. Accept a little tea or food if offered. Hospitality is a virtue. You still keep medical and legal time.

### In the home

Elders first. Formal address until invited. Flowers in odd numbers for some living-room visits is a pattern you do not need to perform; you do need to not mock it.

### Time

Do not walk into a living room and photograph an icon corner, a Sabbath table, or a family photograph wall. Do not touch ritual objects.

On-time for appointments. Traffic and multi-household logistics are real. Courtesy-yes then no-show happens when the plan was never agreed. Ask whether they agree. Confirm in the language they use.

Do not enter a parish, synagogue, or church as a researcher. Guest, if invited.

sections.heading: Language and Communication
paragraphs: Russian on the five. Not Ukrainian. Not “former Soviet” interpreter. Cyrillic vs Latin literacy. Elders may be LEP; U.S.-born may not be.
Confirm the language. Still book a qualified interpreter. A list is not the person and not the dialect. Staff are colleagues, not the curriculum. Do not treat  staff. Do not take a smile as consent.

Russian is on the five. It is not Ukrainian. It is not Belarusian. It is not “former Soviet.” An interpreter labeled Russian who is the wrong language for this household is still a closed door — and after 2022, a political door. Confirm. CLAS: still book a qualified interpreter. A list is not the person and not the dialect.

### Language

Cyrillic literacy and Latin literacy are not the same. Many elders read Russian in Cyrillic and do not read the English PDF. Some U.S.-born adults do not read Cyrillic. A “Russian notice” in Latin transliteration can still be a closed door. Put the language they read on the line.

Elders may be LEP. Professionals may not be. White appearance is not English. Do not take a light accent as “no interpreter needed” without asking.

A direct answer may be the point, not rudeness. A short English yes may be exhaustion or courtesy. Do not take a smile as consent. Ask whether they agree with the plan.

Do not make a Russian-speaking coworker the interpreter.

sections.heading: Other Considerations — unvarnished, not Minnesota Nice
paragraphs: Alcohol and family violence exist and are not “the culture.” Elder isolation. RF anti-LGBTQ climate vs Minnesota Human Rights Act. Status fear for some. Ukraine-war politics in the room.
Follow law. Still see a household. Do not out anyone. Do not skip mandated reporting and call it humility. Do not collect status you do not need.

Unvarnished, because Minnesota Nice is how a room that treats everyone the same deletes facts.

### Named harms

Alcohol harm and family violence exist in some households in this language door. They are not “the culture.” They are not a Slavic joke. You follow the law. You still see a household, not a crime scene walking in. Do not skip mandated reporting and call it humility.

Elder isolation is real for some post-Soviet elders: thin English, adult children at work, winter, no single community center that holds everyone. A missed appointment can be a bus and a language, not noncompliance.

The Russian Federation’s anti-LGBTQ legal climate is current structure for some families. Queer and trans Russian-speakers exist in Minnesota. Minnesota’s Human Rights Act still applies. You use the name. You do not out someone to kin and call it culture.

Immigration status fear is real for some recent arrivals. Do not collect status you do not need. Do not treat fear as noncompliance.

Do not treat every Russian speaker as one origin or one politics. Staff who share this community may add facts. They do not get to delete a fact because it is hard to say.

sections.heading: Health
paragraphs: No Compass health profile for this language door. Pattern now — date a rate when a controlling source exists. Elder isolation, trauma in some streams, mental-health stigma, biomedicine as default for many.
Believe reported pain. Do not invent a Slavic stoicism. Offer the interpreter even if the person is white. Gender match if they ask.

There is no Compass health profile for this language door. Pattern now — date a rate when a controlling source exists. Do not invent one to fill the spine.

### Access

Elder isolation, depression, and alcohol harm sit in some rooms. War and displacement sit in others. Soviet-era medical culture was biomedical and hierarchical for many; “traditional Slavic medicine” as a staff story is often tourism. Ask what this person uses. Co-create. Do not mock. Do not skip the waiver because a home remedy is in the story.

Mental-health stigma exists in some families. Naming a counselor is not the same as a family accepting one. A smile is not a PHQ-9.

Believe reported pain. Do not invent a Slavic or “European stoicism” slide. Do not fold this into Tuskegee or into an Asian mash.

Gender match may be requested in maternal and intimate care. Offer it. Book the interpreter even if the person is white. Confirm Russian, not a “former Soviet” default.

sections.heading: LGBTQ
paragraphs: Queer and trans Russian-speakers exist in Minnesota. The Russian Federation’s anti-LGBTQ legal climate is current structure for some families. Minnesota Human Rights Act still applies.
Use the name. Do not out someone to family as culture. Do not treat RF law as this household’s law.

Queer and trans Russian-speakers exist in Minnesota. Conservative Orthodox, evangelical, and some family climates can mean silence or exile. The Russian Federation’s laws targeting LGBTQ people are current structure for some households and irrelevant in others. You do not assume either.

### This person

Staff duty is the same as on the other spines: use the name they use; do not out them to an elder as cultural humility; Minnesota Human Rights Act still applies.

Do not use this chapter to raid a household. Do not pretend the tension is not there. Do not treat RF propaganda law as Minnesota practice.

sections.heading: Hair, Dress, and Body
paragraphs: No daily “costume.” Head covering in church, synagogue, or evangelical rooms for some. Second generation looks like Minnesota. White appearance is not a closed CI.
Do not touch. Do not ask if they “still dress Russian.” Do not skip language access because of skin.

There is no daily Russian costume in the lobby. Second generation looks like Minnesota. Do not ask whether they “still dress Russian.” Head covering happens in some Orthodox churches, some Jewish settings, some evangelical rooms. It is not a security threat and not a consent problem.

### Dress

White appearance is not the absence of a language gate and not the absence of a body that staff may still other. Do not touch. Do not comment on gold, a cross, a magen david, or a headscarf as a case note.

Winter dress is Minnesota. It is not ethnography.

sections.heading: Music
paragraphs: Orthodox chant; Jewish music in some streams; bard and popular song; church music in evangelical rooms. Named variation.
A playlist is not engagement. A liturgy is not staff entertainment.

Orthodox chant is liturgy, not a playlist. Jewish music — liturgical and popular — belongs to the Jewish stream, not to a “Russian mix.” Bard song, Soviet-era popular music, and contemporary pop exist. Evangelical rooms have their own hymn and chorus life.

### Variation

A playlist is not engagement. A funeral or a liturgy is not staff entertainment. Knowing that music splits along stream will stop you from putting one YouTube mix on a Heritage Month table and calling it this door.

Named variation is the point. An Orthodox memorial, a Jewish wedding, and a Baptist hymn night are not one “Russian culture night” you can BCC.

sections.heading: Sports
paragraphs: Hockey, soccer, figure skating, chess as prestige in some post-Soviet families. Ordinary school sport in the second generation.
Do not assume the kid plays. Sport clubs are not language access.

Hockey, soccer, figure skating, and chess carry prestige in some post-Soviet families. Ordinary school sport is ordinary for the second generation. Do not assume the kid plays. Do not make sport the only excellence you can see.

### Not the whole person

Sport clubs are social infrastructure for some. They are not language access and not a case plan. A hockey sticker on a minivan is not proof the elder reads English.

Greater Minnesota and Twin Cities both play. A club flyer in English is still a closed door for the parent who needs Russian on the line.

sections.heading: Literature
paragraphs: A vast written literature in Russian. Cyrillic literacy for many elders. U.S.-born may not read it. Jewish, Ukrainian, and other literatures sit in some of the same households.
You do not need to quote Tolstoy. You need to know this is not a people without letters — and not one people.

Russian is a major written language with a long literature. That fact is literacy: this is not a people without letters. It is not a prompt to quote Tolstoy in the lobby. Jewish, Ukrainian, and other literatures sit in some of the same households. Do not mash them.

### Literacy in the lobby

Cyrillic literacy for many elders is the actual operations fact. A notice that exists only in English, or only in Latin letters, is a closed door. U.S.-born adults may not read Cyrillic and may still be the person who has to explain the form.

You do not need a novel. You need the language this person reads.

sections.heading: Art
paragraphs: Icons, Soviet visual culture, contemporary work, Jewish and other arts in named streams. Pattern now. No single museum as the whole.
Guest, not researcher. An icon is not a case plan. A festival is not consultation.

Icons are liturgical art in Orthodox homes and parishes — not décor for a unit bulletin board. Soviet visual culture, contemporary work, and Jewish arts in the 1970s–90s stream are not one exhibit.

### Guest

There is no single Minnesota museum that is this whole door. Guest. An icon is not a case plan. A festival is not consultation. Do not photograph a sanctuary as professional development without being asked.

chapters.body:
This brief is about Russian as a language door on the department’s CLAS five-language standing written list — with Hmong, Somali, Spanish, and Vietnamese — not as one people. If you invent a single “Russian community” from that list, you have already left this door. A list is not the person and not the dialect. Still book a qualified interpreter.

### Who this is

Disaggregate before you open a file. Ethnic Russians. Soviet Jews of the 1970s–90s refusenik / Jackson-Vanik stream. Ukrainian households who use Russian — not the Ukrainian people-page; Compass Ukrainian is about 22,570 (ACS 2019–2023); do not mash. Belarusian, Central Asian, and Caucasian Russian-speakers. Evangelical and Baptist Russians, including some Greater Minnesota towns. Recent arrivals versus 1990s versus a third generation that may not need you to speak Russian at all.

### Who this is not

A full mosaic is not a stereotype. A stereotype is when this page becomes the person in the lobby. Shared language is not shared origin, not shared religion, and not shared politics. The Ukraine war is current structure for some households and a trap if you assume every Russian speaker is a combatant or a Putin voter.

There is no Minnesota Compass cultural-community profile titled Russian. Compass immigration table: about 6,483 foreign-born from Russia — date the table you open; that is not a count of speakers. ACS language-at-home figures disagree across vintages. Star Tribune (31 July 2025): Russian is among languages each representing about 2% of Minnesotans who speak a language other than English at home. Minnesota Secretary of State voter materials include Russian. Date the number. Do not invent a community population.

The diversity inside this language is the point. A Jewish grandmother who left on an exit visa in 1989, an Orthodox parishioner, a Belarusian family that uses Russian at the table, a Ukrainian household that will not accept a “former Soviet” interpreter after 2022, a Baptist family in a Greater Minnesota town, a professional who does not need an interpreter and whose elder does — share a language on a form and do not share a Tuesday.

### How to read this

Always defer to the person in front of you. This page is a hypothesis you still test on this household.

chapters.title: A Note on This Guide — a language door, not one people

chapters.body:
There is no single founding of “Russian-speaking Minnesota.” Ethnic Russian peoplehood is older than the Soviet Union and older than this department. It is not the whole door. Other peoples used Russian as an imperial and Soviet language of school, army, and office. That history is why a language list is not a census of who counts.

### History for the meeting

Late-imperial emigration included Jews fleeing pogroms and others leaving the Russian Empire. Some of that older Jewish Minnesota is English-dominant now and is not this CLAS door. Do not mash a 1910 synagogue story onto a 1994 arrival and call it one community.

### What people brought

The Soviet period produced later streams: dissidents, Jews denied exit (refuseniks) until Jackson-Vanik and the years that followed opened a way, and then the 1991 collapse of the USSR, which moved people for work, family, and survival. Evangelical Protestants — Baptists and related churches — left in named waves as well. Central Asian and Caucasian families may carry Russian as a public language beside another home language.

What people brought is not one kit: Orthodox practice, Jewish peoplehood, evangelical church, Soviet official atheism, Cyrillic literacy, professional skill the U.S. did not always recognize, and a memory of a state that surveilled. What they met in Minnesota: an English form, a racial order that may file them as white and skip the interpreter, and often one interpreter labeled “Russian.”
chapters.evidence: Late-imperial emigration; Soviet emigration; 1970s–90s Jewish refusenik / Jackson-Vanik stream; 1991 USSR collapse; later waves. Named streams, not one origin myth.
chapters.practitioner: History is literacy for the desk. It is not a speech you give the family. Do not start with a nesting-doll tourism sentence.
chapters.title: Origins — empire, Soviet, and named streams

chapters.body:
Homeland is not one flag. The Russian Federation is a geography some families name. Ukraine is another — and a Ukrainian household that uses Russian is still not this page’s invented people. Belarus, Kazakhstan and other Central Asian states, the Caucasus, the Baltics: Russian as a Soviet-era public language still sits in some of those rooms. Do not referee borders in a waiver meeting. Listen if they name a place.

### Homeland

The diaspora is global: Israel and Germany for large Jewish streams, the United States, Canada, and Europe. Brighton Beach is not Minnesota. Brooklyn, northern New Jersey, and California sit on a different map. Secondary migration and church networks built some of what you will meet here.

### Minnesota

In Minnesota: Twin Cities households; some inner-ring suburbs; Orthodox parishes and synagogues as named places, not a blob; evangelical and Baptist congregations in some towns, including Greater Minnesota. Do not assume Northeast Minneapolis. Do not assume the person in front of you has been to Russia. Do not assume a Greater Minnesota town has no Russian-speaking church.
chapters.evidence: Russian Federation; Ukraine; Belarus; Central Asia; Caucasus; Baltic; global diaspora. Minnesota is not Brighton Beach and not Moscow.
chapters.practitioner: Do not assume Northeast Minneapolis. Do not assume they have been to Russia. Greater Minnesota evangelical towns are on this map.
chapters.title: The Geography of Russian-Speaking Worlds

chapters.body:
If 1975 is the foundational event of Hmong Minnesota and 1991 of Somali Minnesota, Russian-speaking Minnesota does not get one year. It gets a stack, and you will misread the room if you pick the wrong one.

### Foundational events

Late-imperial flight. Soviet emigration in drips and then in named openings. The 1970s–90s Jewish stream — refuseniks, Jackson-Vanik (1974) as U.S. law tying trade to emigration, then the late-1980s and 1990s movement — built part of Twin Cities Jewish life. That stream is Jewish peoplehood meeting Minnesota synagogues and a JCC, not a nesting-doll exhibit. 1991 and the collapse of the USSR moved others: ethnic Russians, mixed families, professionals, people from republics that were suddenly different countries.

### Who you meet

Evangelical and Baptist Russians arrived in church-sponsored patterns that sometimes landed in Greater Minnesota, not only in Minneapolis. Later family and employment streams are ordinary immigration, not a refugee poster.

2022 and the war on Ukraine is current structure for some households in this language: relatives under fire, mixed families, people who will not accept a Russian-language flyer that looks like Moscow. It is a trap if you treat every Russian speaker as a combatant or a Putin voter. It is also a trap if you pretend the war is not in the room when they name it. Literacy for the desk. Not a speech you give the family.
chapters.evidence: Imperial, Soviet, Jewish 1970s–90s, 1991 collapse, later family and professional streams, and 2022-onward displacement for some households. Different Tuesdays.
chapters.practitioner: If you only know “Russian,” you will miss the Ukrainian household that uses Russian, the Jewish elder from the refusenik stream, and the U.S.-born adult who does not need you to lecture 1991.
chapters.title: Emigration Waves — Foundational Events, Not One Flight

chapters.body:
Family is not one size. Some households look nuclear on an English form and still carry obligation to a parent who does not drive and does not read the form. Some are three generations in one week. Some are a single elder whose children live in another metro. Elder isolation is a named harm in this language door. It is not a cultural virtue.

### Who is in the household

The patronymic — a name built from the father — is how a person is fully named in Russian. A form that keeps only first and last has already dropped a who. Ask how to file. Ask who should be in the room.

### Who speaks

Adult children may speak for an elder in English. That is a hypothesis, not permission to skip the interpreter or to use a child. CLAS still stands. A sixteen-year-old in the lobby is not the qualified interpreter.

Women’s labor and professional second generation sit next to older gender patterns in some rooms. Both can be true. Minnesota law still stands on violence, neglect, and who may consent. Do not skip mandated reporting and call it culture.
chapters.evidence: Nuclear and multi-generation both live here. Patronymic names the father in the person. Elders in some households; adult children as the English door in others.
chapters.practitioner: Ask who should be in the room. A nuclear English form already has a who. Do not use a child as the interpreter. Do not drop the patronymic.
chapters.title: Family

chapters.body:
Minnesota put Russian on the CLAS five because the building already knew it would meet this language on notices, health care, cash, food, aging, and voting — not because Compass drew a people-blob titled Russian. That is the honest origin of this spine. A language list is operations. It is not a census.

### Places

Places, not a blob: Twin Cities; inner-ring suburbs; some Greater Minnesota towns with evangelical churches. Do not write “the Russian neighborhood” onto a map you do not have. Pattern now. Date a geography when a controlling source exists.

### Partners

Partners: synagogues and Jewish Community Centers for some of the Jewish stream; Russian Orthodox parishes some families name; evangelical and Baptist churches in some towns; no single “Russian community center” as the whole. CECLC is a department door — not the community. Pay the partner this household actually uses.

Do not extract Russian-speaking staff as the interpreter or as “the community.” They may be Jewish, Ukrainian, Belarusian, or a third generation that does not want to be your culture desk. A liturgy or a JCC visit is optional professional development. You are a guest. It does not make you the expert.

chapters.title: Minnesota and Russian-Speaking History

chapters.body:
The heart of this intelligence is a refusal. Russian on the five is a door onto many peoples. Ethnic Russian peoplehood is real — language, literature, Orthodox memory for some, a state that did harm and a state some people still defend. It is not permission to file a Ukrainian, a Tajik, or a Soviet Jew under one folk costume.

### In this state

Jewish peoplehood in the 1970s–90s stream is not “Russian culture with a menorah.” Ukrainian households that use Russian are not a round-up for this page. Evangelical Russians may organize life around a church in a town that has never heard the word CLAS.

In Minnesota another fact sits on the same desk: many of these households are read as white. The building’s unmarked default will skip the interpreter, skip the Cyrillic notice, and call that fairness. That skip is the gate. White appearance is not English proficiency and not the absence of a people.

This guide is a working orientation. Individual variation always supersedes group generalization. Always defer to the person in front of you.
chapters.evidence: The object is a language and named variation inside it. Ethnic Russian peoplehood exists. It is not this whole door. Jewish peoplehood is not “Russian culture.”
chapters.practitioner: Do not invent a people from a translation list. Do not copy a Ukrainian, Somali, or “white Minnesota” sentence onto this page.
chapters.title: A Language Door — not a people you invented

chapters.body:
Disaggregation. The first grammar. If you cannot name the stream, you do not have a household yet.

### Patronymic

Given name, father’s name as a middle element, family name. Dropping it invents a person. Filing it wrong invents a person. Ask.

### Formality and titles

First name plus patronymic is respectful address in Russian. First name only can be too familiar with an elder. English “hi guys” is not a translation.

### Hospitality

Tea, food, time in some rooms. Refusing everything can read as cold. You still keep medical and legal clocks.

### State memory

For some, a Soviet past means you do not volunteer extra facts to a government desk. For some, the Russian Federation is still the frame. For some, 2022 ended that sentence. You do not interrogate loyalty. You do the form.

### Church, synagogue, none

A parish, a shul, or a Baptist church may be the actual information channel. It is not “the community.” Do not make clergy the case plan unless this family asked.

### Directness

Some Russian-speaking rooms will say the hard sentence without Minnesota Nice. That is not hostility. Follow this room. Do not punish candor and do not invent a Slavic personality.

chapters.title: Core Concepts

chapters.body:
Ask. Do not assume Russian Orthodox because the language is Russian. Russian Orthodox, Jewish, evangelical Protestant, and none all live in this door. Soviet official atheism left a mark in some families that still keep a holiday table.

### Streams

The parish is a center of liturgy, memorial, and sometimes mutual aid. It is not the community. Do not BCC one priest and call it consultation. Icons in a home are not a case plan and not a museum.

### Practice

Jewish households in the 1970s–90s stream may be secular in the Soviet sense and still Jewish in peoplehood — synagogue, JCC, kosher as a maybe, Hebrew school as a maybe. Do not give them an Orthodox Christian flyer and call it language access. Do not give them a “Russian culture night” and call it Jewish.

Evangelical and Baptist congregations — some in Greater Minnesota — can be the whole public life of a household. Church English and home Russian may sit together. Do not make the pastor the case plan unless they asked.

Do not rank piety. A person who left the church or the synagogue is still this language door if that is the language they need.
chapters.evidence: Russian Orthodox, Jewish, evangelical Protestant, none — ask. Streams do not share a sanctuary. An ancestor of Soviet official atheism sits in some rooms.
chapters.practitioner: Do not make a priest, rabbi, or pastor the case plan unless this family asked. Do not assume Orthodox because the language is Russian.
chapters.title: Religion — Orthodox, Jewish, evangelical, none

chapters.body:
Handshake is common in many rooms — men, and often women in professional space. Follow this room. Some older Orthodox or observant Jewish settings will change the rule. You nod if a hand is not offered. You do not make a scene in the lobby.

### Titles

Titles matter. First name plus patronymic is the respectful Russian address for an adult you do not know well. English Mr./Ms. plus family name is a decent substitute if you cannot produce the patronymic. Do not use a first name with an elder because the form printed it.

### This room

Zdravstvuyte is the formal hello. English “hello” is ordinary, especially with the second generation. Say the name. Ask how to say it.

Do not import Somali right-hand rules or the Black nod onto this page. This is not those grammars. Physical contact: follow this person. A hug from staff is not warmth if the household did not offer it.
chapters.evidence: Handshake common in many rooms. Titles. First name plus patronymic is respectful address in Russian. Follow this room.
chapters.practitioner: Do not force a hug. Do not import Somali right-hand rules or the Black nod. Say the name. Ask how to address an elder.
chapters.title: Greetings

chapters.body:
A common Russian pattern is given name, patronymic, family name: a person is Ivan Petrovich Sokolov because his father is Petr. Maria Ivanovna Sokolova because her father is Ivan. The patronymic is not a middle name you may drop for convenience. Databases that drop it invent a person. That invented person then fails a match in MHCP, child welfare, and school.

### How to file

Family names may take a gendered ending. Sokolov / Sokolova is the same family. The form that flags the difference as fraud has already chosen a household type. Ask how to file. Ask how this person wants the English record to read.

Jewish, Ukrainian, Belarusian, Central Asian, and Caucasian names in this language door will not all look like Ivan and Maria. Do not “correct” a name toward a Russian textbook. Pronounce it. Ask.

The form that demands first-middle-last and a hyphen will invent a person. Do not invent a last name, and do not invent a middle initial from a patronymic without asking. Three people in one household may not share a “last name” the way a Swedish Minnesota form expects. That is not fraud until you have a reason.
chapters.evidence: Given name + patronymic + family name. Databases that drop the patronymic invent a person. Women may have a gendered family-name ending.
chapters.practitioner: Ask how to file. Ask how to say it. Do not invent a middle name because the screen wants one. The invented name becomes a gate.
chapters.title: Naming — given name, patronymic, family name

chapters.body:
Orthodox Nativity and Pascha follow the Julian calendar for many Russian Orthodox households — often later than Western Christmas and Easter. Schedule around them when you can. They are not a day off the work. They are literacy.

### Calendar

Jewish High Holidays, Passover, and other calendar days matter in the Jewish stream. They are not “Russian holidays.” Open the Jewish calendar if that is the household.

9 May — Victory Day in Soviet and Russian memory of 1945 — is real for some elders and a political fight for others after 2022. Listen. Do not put a victory parade on a case note. Do not lecture.

1991 is literacy, not a holiday. 24 February 2022 is current structure for some families. Do not put “Fall of Saigon party” energy — or a Ukraine-war slogan — on a case note.

New Year’s Eve (Novy God) was the large Soviet winter holiday and still is for some secular families. A calendar click on this program is literacy for scheduling. It is not community engagement.
chapters.evidence: Orthodox Nativity and Pascha on the Julian calendar for some; Jewish calendar for some; 9 May Victory Day memory for some; 1991 literacy; 2022 as current structure for some.
chapters.practitioner: A calendar click is literacy. It is not community engagement. Do not put a Ukraine-war slogan on a case note.
chapters.title: Dates of Significance

chapters.body:
There is no Compass education table for “Russian speakers.” Pattern now — date the number when a controlling source exists. Do not invent a rate.

### School and language

Soviet and post-Soviet credentials were often high — engineering, medicine, teaching — and not always recognized here. A person who was a professional in 1994 and a warehouse worker in 1996 is not a personality. Children of that stream may be in English-dominant schools with a parent who still cannot run an IEP in English.

Elders may be LEP and fully literate in Cyrillic. Professionals and the U.S.-born may not need an interpreter and may still have a parent who does. Do not skip the interpreter because the adult in the lobby is white, employed, or accent-light.

A parent who speaks fluent Russian and limited English is not illiterate. The English-only form is the gate. Put Russian on the line. Confirm it is Russian, not Ukrainian.
chapters.evidence: Soviet-era credentials were often high and not always recognized here. Elders may be LEP; professionals may not be. No Compass education profile for “Russian speakers.” Pattern now.
chapters.practitioner: A parent who reads Cyrillic and limited English is not illiterate. The English-only packet is the gate. Do not skip the interpreter because the person looks professional.
chapters.title: Education

chapters.body:
Shoes off in some homes. Follow the household. Accept a little tea or food if offered. Hospitality is a virtue. You still keep medical and legal time.

### In the home

Elders first. Formal address until invited. Flowers in odd numbers for some living-room visits is a pattern you do not need to perform; you do need to not mock it.

### Time

Do not walk into a living room and photograph an icon corner, a Sabbath table, or a family photograph wall. Do not touch ritual objects.

On-time for appointments. Traffic and multi-household logistics are real. Courtesy-yes then no-show happens when the plan was never agreed. Ask whether they agree. Confirm in the language they use.

Do not enter a parish, synagogue, or church as a researcher. Guest, if invited.
chapters.evidence: Shoes in some homes. Hospitality. Formality with elders. Flowers and food as ordinary courtesy in some rooms.
chapters.practitioner: Accept a little tea. Keep medical and legal time. Do not photograph icons or a home altar. Follow this household.
chapters.title: Etiquette

chapters.body:
Russian is on the five. It is not Ukrainian. It is not Belarusian. It is not “former Soviet.” An interpreter labeled Russian who is the wrong language for this household is still a closed door — and after 2022, a political door. Confirm. CLAS: still book a qualified interpreter. A list is not the person and not the dialect.

### Language

Cyrillic literacy and Latin literacy are not the same. Many elders read Russian in Cyrillic and do not read the English PDF. Some U.S.-born adults do not read Cyrillic. A “Russian notice” in Latin transliteration can still be a closed door. Put the language they read on the line.

Elders may be LEP. Professionals may not be. White appearance is not English. Do not take a light accent as “no interpreter needed” without asking.

A direct answer may be the point, not rudeness. A short English yes may be exhaustion or courtesy. Do not take a smile as consent. Ask whether they agree with the plan.

Do not make a Russian-speaking coworker the interpreter.
chapters.evidence: Russian on the five. Not Ukrainian. Not “former Soviet” interpreter. Cyrillic vs Latin literacy. Elders may be LEP; U.S.-born may not be.
chapters.practitioner: Confirm the language. Still book a qualified interpreter. A list is not the person and not the dialect. Staff are colleagues, not the curriculum. Do not treat  staff. Do not take a smile as consent.

chapters.body:
Unvarnished, because Minnesota Nice is how a room that treats everyone the same deletes facts.

### Named harms

Alcohol harm and family violence exist in some households in this language door. They are not “the culture.” They are not a Slavic joke. You follow the law. You still see a household, not a crime scene walking in. Do not skip mandated reporting and call it humility.

Elder isolation is real for some post-Soviet elders: thin English, adult children at work, winter, no single community center that holds everyone. A missed appointment can be a bus and a language, not noncompliance.

The Russian Federation’s anti-LGBTQ legal climate is current structure for some families. Queer and trans Russian-speakers exist in Minnesota. Minnesota’s Human Rights Act still applies. You use the name. You do not out someone to kin and call it culture.

Immigration status fear is real for some recent arrivals. Do not collect status you do not need. Do not treat fear as noncompliance.

Do not treat every Russian speaker as one origin or one politics. Staff who share this community may add facts. They do not get to delete a fact because it is hard to say.
chapters.evidence: Alcohol and family violence exist and are not “the culture.” Elder isolation. RF anti-LGBTQ climate vs Minnesota Human Rights Act. Status fear for some. Ukraine-war politics in the room.
chapters.practitioner: Follow law. Still see a household. Do not out anyone. Do not skip mandated reporting and call it humility. Do not collect status you do not need.
chapters.title: Other Considerations — unvarnished, not Minnesota Nice

chapters.body:
There is no Compass health profile for this language door. Pattern now — date a rate when a controlling source exists. Do not invent one to fill the spine.

### Access

Elder isolation, depression, and alcohol harm sit in some rooms. War and displacement sit in others. Soviet-era medical culture was biomedical and hierarchical for many; “traditional Slavic medicine” as a staff story is often tourism. Ask what this person uses. Co-create. Do not mock. Do not skip the waiver because a home remedy is in the story.

Mental-health stigma exists in some families. Naming a counselor is not the same as a family accepting one. A smile is not a PHQ-9.

Believe reported pain. Do not invent a Slavic or “European stoicism” slide. Do not fold this into Tuskegee or into an Asian mash.

Gender match may be requested in maternal and intimate care. Offer it. Book the interpreter even if the person is white. Confirm Russian, not a “former Soviet” default.

chapters.practitioner: Believe reported pain. Do not invent a Slavic stoicism. Offer the interpreter even if the person is white. Gender match if they ask.

Queer and trans Russian-speakers exist in Minnesota. Conservative Orthodox, evangelical, and some family climates can mean silence or exile. The Russian Federation’s laws targeting LGBTQ people are current structure for some households and irrelevant in others. You do not assume either.

### This person

Staff duty is the same as on the other spines: use the name they use; do not out them to an elder as cultural humility; Minnesota Human Rights Act still applies.

Do not use this chapter to raid a household. Do not pretend the tension is not there. Do not treat RF propaganda law as Minnesota practice.

There is no daily Russian costume in the lobby. Second generation looks like Minnesota. Do not ask whether they “still dress Russian.” Head covering happens in some Orthodox churches, some Jewish settings, some evangelical rooms. It is not a security threat and not a consent problem.

### Dress

White appearance is not the absence of a language gate and not the absence of a body that staff may still other. Do not touch. Do not comment on gold, a cross, a magen david, or a headscarf as a case note.

Winter dress is Minnesota. It is not ethnography.
chapters.evidence: No daily “costume.” Head covering in church, synagogue, or evangelical rooms for some. Second generation looks like Minnesota. White appearance is not a closed CI.

Orthodox chant is liturgy, not a playlist. Jewish music — liturgical and popular — belongs to the Jewish stream, not to a “Russian mix.” Bard song, Soviet-era popular music, and contemporary pop exist. Evangelical rooms have their own hymn and chorus life.

### Variation

A playlist is not engagement. A funeral or a liturgy is not staff entertainment. Knowing that music splits along stream will stop you from putting one YouTube mix on a Heritage Month table and calling it this door.

Named variation is the point. An Orthodox memorial, a Jewish wedding, and a Baptist hymn night are not one “Russian culture night” you can BCC.

Hockey, soccer, figure skating, and chess carry prestige in some post-Soviet families. Ordinary school sport is ordinary for the second generation. Do not assume the kid plays. Do not make sport the only excellence you can see.

### Not the whole person

Sport clubs are social infrastructure for some. They are not language access and not a case plan. A hockey sticker on a minivan is not proof the elder reads English.

Greater Minnesota and Twin Cities both play. A club flyer in English is still a closed door for the parent who needs Russian on the line.

Russian is a major written language with a long literature. That fact is literacy: this is not a people without letters. It is not a prompt to quote Tolstoy in the lobby. Jewish, Ukrainian, and other literatures sit in some of the same households. Do not mash them.

### Literacy in the lobby

Cyrillic literacy for many elders is the actual operations fact. A notice that exists only in English, or only in Latin letters, is a closed door. U.S.-born adults may not read Cyrillic and may still be the person who has to explain the form.

You do not need a novel. You need the language this person reads.
chapters.evidence: A vast written literature in Russian. Cyrillic literacy for many elders. U.S.-born may not read it. Jewish, Ukrainian, and other literatures sit in some of the same households.

Icons are liturgical art in Orthodox homes and parishes — not décor for a unit bulletin board. Soviet visual culture, contemporary work, and Jewish arts in the 1970s–90s stream are not one exhibit.

### Guest

There is no single Minnesota museum that is this whole door. Guest. An icon is not a case plan. A festival is not consultation. Do not photograph a sanctuary as professional development without being asked.

Heritage Month tables that mash matryoshka, a menorah, and a Ukrainian vyshyvanka into one “Eastern European” booth have already mashed what this brief asks you to keep apart.

chapters.body:
Empire, Soviet surveillance, collapse, Jewish emigration under Jackson-Vanik, and later enforcement climate for some arrivals — that is the political stack. A DHS badge is not automatically help. For some people, a government form is a thing you survive. That is not “paranoia.” It is pattern.

### The badge

The war on Ukraine is current structure for some households in this language: family under fire, mixed marriages, people who left Russia, people who did not, people who will not speak politics in a lobby. It is a trap if you assume every Russian speaker is a combatant or a Putin voter. It is also a trap if you punish someone for not performing the politics you prefer.

Do not use 1991 or 2022 as a personality. Do not ask a person to narrate a war for your professional development. Do not collect status you do not need.

chapters.practitioner: A DHS badge is not automatically help. Do not use 1991 or 2022 as a personality. Do not assume every Russian speaker is a combatant or a Putin voter.

Professional work, trades, small business, public employment, and under-recognized Soviet credentials all live here. A small-business owner and a waiver recipient may be the same extended family.

### Work

Russian-speaking staff exist inside DHS and counties. They are not unpaid interpreters and not “the community.” Identity is not a staffing plan.

### Staff

Relationship and hospitality may precede a signature. That is not permission to skip a notice. It is a reason the first visit may not be the decision. The notice still has to exist in Russian, in a script they can read.

An English eList comment period is not how this language door was reached.

### Adjacent doors

Not Belarusian mash. Not a “former Soviet” interpreter for a Kazakh or Georgian household that needs another language. Not Somali. Not the African American CI. Not “white = no cultural intelligence.”

chapters.body:
There is no Minnesota Compass cultural-community profile for Russian. Do not invent one to make this spine look like Hmong or Somali.

### Counts

Minnesota Compass immigration table: about 6,483 foreign-born from Russia. Date the table you open. That is not a count of Russian speakers. It is not Jewish. It is not Ukrainian. It is not the third generation born here.

### What the count is not

Star Tribune, 31 July 2025, on languages spoken at home: German, French, Chinese, Russian, and Arabic each represent about 2% of Minnesotans who speak a language other than English at home. The same reporting said Vietnamese, Chinese, and Russian home-speaker populations had stayed about the same. Date that article. ACS vintages disagree. Date the vintage.

Minnesota Secretary of State voter materials include Russian. That is operations evidence that the state already treats this language as a public-contact fact. It is not a population.

Compass Ukrainian: about 22,570 (ACS 2019–2023). Do not add it to 6,483 and call the sum “Russian-speaking Minnesota.” A rate is not the person. Pattern now — date the number when a controlling source exists.

DHS Equal Opportunity and Access LEP resources — five primary written languages: Hmong, Russian, Somali, Spanish, Vietnamese. The ten-language block and the fifteen interpreter cards also include Russian. A list is not the notice and not the interpreter.

### Public doors

Minnesota Compass immigration table (Russian immigrants ~6,483 — date it). Minnesota Compass Ukrainian cultural community profile — adjacent, not this page. Star Tribune, 31 July 2025, languages at home. Minnesota Secretary of State multilingual voter materials.

### Learn on your own time

Synagogues and Jewish Community Centers some Jewish households name. Orthodox parishes some families name. Evangelical and Baptist churches in some towns. CECLC is a door, not the community.

Learn on your own time. Do not make a Russian-speaking colleague your unpaid tutor. Do not BCC one priest or one rabbi and call it consultation. Pay partners you actually have. Report back.

Workplace culture and service delivery are both candidates.

Language: Russian is on the five. An interpreter labeled “former Soviet” is a closed door. Ukrainian is a different language and a different brief. Still book a qualified interpreter. A list is not the person and not the dialect. Cyrillic is not optional decoration on a notice that actually has to be read.

Names: given name, patronymic, family name. The database that drops the patronymic or flags Sokolov / Sokolova as unmatched fraud is a gate that follows the person.

Assuming English because the person is white is a CLAS failure wearing Minnesota Nice.

Hour caps, exception processes, and life-sharing matches without language are not culturally neutral.

Enforcement climate: some recent arrivals skip clinic, school, and waiver meetings. That is not noncompliance. Do not collect status you do not need.

Notices and comment: an eList and an English PDF is not how this language door was reached. Empty follow-up cells are theater. SOS already prints Russian for voters. The packet can too.

Workforce: Russian-speaking staff are not the interpreter pool and not the community. Staff are colleagues, not the curriculum. Do not treat  them.

Legislation, funding, rule: you cannot advocate for a channel you will not study. This cultural intelligence exists so the 40% has a household in it — not a paternalistic program designed in a building that treated a white face as no CI and a language list as a people.
