sections.heading: A Note on This Guide
paragraphs: Bosniak / Bosnian Minnesota. CLAS ten labels the language Serbo-Croatian (Bosnian) — operations, not the people-name. Croatian and Serbian households are adjacent. No Compass cultural-community count. Date any number you cite. Do not invent 40,000.
There is no single Bosnian client. Defer to this family. Do not open a Somali, Russian, Albanian, or generic Balkan case with this page. Book the language they ask for.

This brief is about Bosniak / Bosnian Minnesota as a people-page. The CLAS ten language block says Serbo-Croatian (Bosnian). That is operations. It is how the building batches a notice. It is not the name of the household in the lobby.

### Who this is

Bosniak names the Muslim peoplehood of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Bosnian can also mean a citizen of a state that Dayton wrote as three constituent peoples — Bosniak, Croat, Serb. Croatian and Serbian households in Minnesota are adjacent. They may share a mutually intelligible language. They do not share this war story by default. Ask. Do not file them here because the interpreter catalog used a hyphen.

### Who this is not

This is not a Census “white” mash and not a Balkan blob. It is not Somali Islam with a different flag. It is not Russian, not Albanian, not Kosovar, not Ukrainian. Shared continent is not shared culture. Shared Islam is not shared culture. A full mosaic is not a stereotype. A stereotype is when this page becomes the person in the lobby.

### How to read this

There is no Minnesota Compass cultural-community count for Bosnian. That absence is a finding, not a reason to invent 40,000. Between 1993 and 2003 more than 2,300 primary Bosnian refugees resettled in Minnesota; they were part of about 140,000 Bosnian and Herzegovinian refugees who came to the United States (MSP Magazine, looking back at Minnesota’s refugee history). Primary placement is not the community. Secondary migration happened. Date the number you use. A rate is not the person.

The diversity inside this people is the point. A Srebrenica widow, a man who will not name the camp, a Catholic Croat neighbor who speaks the same language and not the same memory, a less-observant Bosniak who drinks coffee and does not keep Ramadan, a woman who covers, a woman who does not, a U.S.-born nurse who uses English with friends and Bosnian with an elder — share a language family and do not share a Tuesday.

Always defer to the person in front of you. This page is a hypothesis you still test on this family.

sections.heading: Origins and the Founding of a People
paragraphs: South Slavic people of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Ottoman centuries; Austro-Hungarian; Yugoslavia; 1992 independence. Bosniak names the Muslim peoplehood. Bosnian can also mean citizenship of a three-people state.
History is literacy for the desk. It is not a speech you give the family. Do not start with a war anecdote.

Bosniak peoplehood is older than 1992 and older than the refugee file. South Slavic speakers in the Dinaric and Bosnian lands lived under medieval kingdoms, Ottoman centuries (from the 15th century), Austro-Hungarian rule after 1878, royal and then socialist Yugoslavia, and the 1992 independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Islam in this land is Ottoman-era and European. That sentence is literacy. It is not a piety rank.

### History for the meeting

Bosniak, Croat, and Serb in Bosnia are not three languages you can hear from across a lobby. They are political names on a mutually intelligible South Slavic speech. The 1990s war made the names lethal. The desk that treats them as flavor has already failed the household.

### What people brought

What people brought: family, coffee, a language with a literature, Islam as heritage for most Bosniaks (sometimes as daily order, sometimes as a name without a public mark), Catholic and Orthodox streams in adjacent households, and a memory of neighbors who became a front. What they met in Minnesota: an English form, a language block that says Serbo-Croatian (Bosnian), and often one interpreter labeled “former Yugoslav.”

There is no Bosniak nation-state in the simple sense the checkbox wants. Dayton wrote a state with two entities and three constituent peoples. Do not referee that constitution in a waiver meeting. Listen if they name home.

sections.heading: The Geography of the Bosnian World
paragraphs: Bosnia and Herzegovina: Sarajevo, Tuzla, Banja Luka, Mostar, eastern enclaves including Srebrenica. Diaspora in Germany, Austria, Scandinavia, St. Louis, Chicago, New York. Minnesota received a notable 1990s resettlement — not the U.S. map.
Do not assume Minneapolis. Do not assume they have been back. St. Louis is a larger U.S. hub; Minnesota is still this desk.

Homeland is Bosnia and Herzegovina — Sarajevo, Tuzla, Zenica, Banja Luka, Mostar, Bihać, the Drina towns, the eastern enclaves. Srebrenica is a place-name and a crime. Do not put it on a small-talk map.

### Homeland

The 1992–1995 war produced camps and exile in Croatia, Serbia, Montenegro, Germany, Austria, Scandinavia, and then the United States. St. Louis became a large U.S. Bosnian hub. Chicago, New York, and other cities hold communities. Minnesota received a notable resettlement in the mid and late 1990s. Minnesota is not St. Louis. Do not copy a Missouri story onto this desk and call it local.

### Minnesota

In Minnesota: Twin Cities pattern. Islamic Community of Bosniaks in Minnesota has been a named Minneapolis door. Greater Minnesota households exist because work and kin exist. Do not assume one neighborhood. Do not assume the person in front of you has been back. Do not assume they want to go.

sections.heading: 1992–1995, Srebrenica, Dayton — Foundational Event
paragraphs: 1992–1995 war; Srebrenica July 1995 genocide of Bosniak men and boys; Dayton December 1995; camps; U.S. resettlement mid/late 1990s; MN primary refugees 1993–2003 more than 2,300. Secondary migration after that. Date it.
If you only know “refugee,” you will miss the 25-year-old who has never lived in Bosnia and still cannot get the right language for an elder. Do not ask a survivor to narrate the pit.

If the Great Migration is the foundational demographic event of modern Black America, and 1991 of Somali Minnesota, 1992–1995 is the foundational event of Bosnian Minnesota.

### Foundational events

Yugoslavia broke. Bosnia and Herzegovina declared independence. War followed: siege of Sarajevo, ethnic cleansing, camps, mass rape as a method of war, and on 11 July 1995 the genocide at Srebrenica — more than 8,000 Bosniak men and boys killed after a UN “safe area” failed. That is public record (ICTY, International Court of Justice). It is literacy for the desk. It is not a speech you give the family. Do not ask a survivor to narrate the pit.

### Who you meet

Dayton, December 1995, stopped the shooting and froze a political map. Camps and temporary protection in Europe came first for many. U.S. resettlement followed in the mid and late 1990s. Minnesota’s primary-refugee arrivals between 1993 and 2003 were more than 2,300. Secondary migration after that is real and not a Compass cell.

The desk in 2026 does not only meet that first wave. It meets their children — U.S.-born, English-dominant with peers, still translating for a parent who will not tell the war to a stranger and still cannot get the right language in the lobby. If you only know “refugee,” you will miss them.

sections.heading: Family
paragraphs: South Slavic extended household; kumovi (godparent) ties; elders; who cares for the child may not match a nuclear English form.
Ask who should be in the room. A nuclear English form already has a who. Do not use the war as a family icebreaker.

Family is larger than a nuclear English form. Elders often speak. Kumovi — godparent ties — can be as binding as blood in some households. Who cares for a child, an elder, or a disabled adult may be a network the waiver checkbox does not have a box for.

### Who is in the household

War and exile also broke families. Missing men. Split siblings. A neighbor who is now the household. Camp years and then a U.S. apartment. Ask who should be in the room. Do not reconstruct a family tree as icebreaker.

### Who speaks

Women’s labor — factory, care work, professional second generation — sits next to a household in which an elder man may still be named as head. Both can be true in the same room.

Do not use 1995 as a family personality. Do not skip mandated reporting and call it culture. Minnesota law still stands.

sections.heading: Minnesota and Bosnian History
paragraphs: Notable 1990s resettlement. Twin Cities pattern. Islamic Community of Bosniaks in Minnesota (Minneapolis) is a named door some families use — not the whole. No Compass profile. Primary-refugee count is not the community.
Partners, not a harvest list. Staff are colleagues, not the curriculum. Do not treat  Bosnian staff. A Bajram visit does not make you the expert. Pay the partner this household names.

Minnesota received a notable Bosnian resettlement in the mid and late 1990s. That is why this page has to be as complete as the Hmong and Somali intelligences — because this department will meet this community on waivers, child welfare, health care, cash, food, aging, and employment, including the elder who still needs the language and the adult child who does not think of themselves as a refugee.

### Places

Places, not a blob: Twin Cities; a Minneapolis Bosniak civic and religious life some families name; Greater Minnesota when work pulled people. Do not invent a Little Sarajevo on a case note. Ask this family where they live.

### Partners

Partners: Islamic Community of Bosniaks in Minnesota; mosques and churches families actually name; resettlement-era voluntary agencies as history, not a current partner list; CECLC as a department door — not the whole community.

Bosnian staff are not unpaid interpreters and not the community. Identity is not a staffing plan. A Bajram greeting is optional professional courtesy. It does not make you the expert.

sections.heading: Bosniak / Bosnian — the heart of a people
paragraphs: Bosniak peoplehood; European Muslims whose public mark is often quieter than Somali Minnesota; war memory without a personality; U.S.-born second generation.
Do not copy the Somali page onto this one because both are Muslim. Do not fold this household into “white immigrant” and delete 1995.

To be Bosniak in Minnesota is to be a European Muslim people whose public mark is often quieter than Somali Minnesota, carrying a war the United States watched on television and then filed under the 1990s. In this building it sits inside another fact: many Bosnian Minnesotans are white in a U.S. racial order that will delete 1995 and call them assimilated, or Muslim in a room that treats everyone the same that will copy the Somali page and get the covering, the mosque, and the language wrong.

### In this state

Bosnian can mean the language, the passport, or the people-name. Bosniak is the ethnic name for the Muslim peoplehood. Use what this family uses. Do not lecture them on the difference as a greeting.

This guide is a working orientation. Individual variation always supersedes group generalization.

sections.heading: Core Concepts
paragraphs: Language as a political name; Islam as heritage for most Bosniaks, not always as public mark; family; coffee; memory; face.
You work with these. You do not perform them. Do not make a mosque the case plan unless they asked. Do not assume hijab.

Language as a political name. Bosnian, Croatian, Serbian — mutually intelligible, not interchangeable as identity. Book what they ask. “Former Yugoslav” is a closed door with a polite label.

### Islam as heritage for most Bosniaks

Often less publicly marked than Somali Minnesota. Do not assume hijab. Do not assume five daily prayers in the lobby. Do not assume the absence of a mark means the absence of faith — or of trauma.

### Family and kumovi

Who is in the room. Who signs.

### Coffee

Hospitality is a virtue. You still keep medical and legal time.

### Memory

Srebrenica and the siege are in the room for some people whether they speak them or not. You do not extract the memory. You do not deny it. You do not platform denial.

### Face

Direct refusal may be costly, or it may be blunt. Ask whether they agree. Do not take a smile as consent.

sections.heading: Religion and Healing
paragraphs: Islam for most Bosniaks — often less publicly marked than Somali Minnesota. Catholic Croat and Orthodox Serb streams exist in the broader language. Ask.
Do not assume hijab. Do not assume mosque is the case plan. Do not mash with Somali Islam. Church or mosque is information channel only if they name it.

Islam for most Bosniaks — Sunni, Ottoman heritage, a European Muslim history. Practice in Minnesota ranges from daily order to a name on a form. Hijab is not the default public mark. Do not copy the Somali religion chapter onto this page. Do not assume mosque is the case plan. Do not assume Friday prayer sets the appointment grid the way it might for another household. Ask.

### Streams

Catholic Croat and Orthodox Serb streams exist in the broader language. Christmas dates differ. A “Bosnian” interpreter for a household that names itself Croatian or Serbian may still be the wrong political door even when the words are understood. Ask.

### Practice

Do not make an imam, a priest, or a pastor the case plan unless this family asked. Church or mosque can be the information channel. It is not “the community.”

Illness meaning after war may not be the DSM sentence. PTSD, unexplained pain, sleep, and alcohol sit in the same clinic as ordinary Minnesota chronic disease. You can hold both. You do not interrogate the pit to complete a field.

sections.heading: Greetings
paragraphs: Handshake is common in many rooms. Elders first. Some observant Muslim Bosniaks will not shake across gender — ask the room.
Do not copy Somali handshake rules blindly. Do not force a hand. Do not import the Black nod. Follow this room.

Elders first. A handshake is common in many Bosnian Minnesota rooms — European-style, not a Somali right-hand rule you import. Some observant Muslim Bosniaks will not shake hands across gender. Follow this room. Nod if a hand is not offered. Do not force one. Do not make a lesson of it.

### Titles

Merhaba, dobro jutro, zdravo, selam — follow what they offer. English “hello” is ordinary in the second generation. Say the name. Ask how to say the -ić.

### This room

Do not open with the war. Do not open with “I have a friend from Bosnia.” Do not import the Black nod or Somali As-salāmu ʿalaykum as the default here. This is not those grammars unless this person uses them.

sections.heading: Naming Conventions
paragraphs: South Slavic given name + family name. -ić / -vić endings are common. Ask pronunciation. Women’s forms vary in U.S. records.
Ask how to say it. Do not joke about the ć. Do not treat a spelling variant as fraud by default.

South Slavic: given name, then family name. -ić and -vić endings are common (Hodžić, Begović, Hadžić, Petrović — examples of a pattern, not a roll call). The ć is not optional decoration. Ask how to say it. Do not joke. Do not anglicize it on the file without being asked.

### How to file

Women may or may not take a husband’s family name in U.S. records. Ask how to file. Do not “correct” a mother and child who do not share a last name as a fraud signal until you have a reason.

Given names may be Bosnian, South Slavic Christian, Arabic-origin, or English in the second generation. The form that demands first-middle-last and a hyphen will invent a person if you force it.

Pronounce it. Ask. Write what they say.

sections.heading: Dates of Significance
paragraphs: Ramadan and Bajram (Eid) for many Bosniaks. Catholic Christmas; Orthodox Christmas (January 7) in adjacent streams. Srebrenica 11 July is literacy, not a holiday on the packet.
A calendar click is literacy. It is not community engagement. Do not put “Balkan holiday” on a case note.

Ramadan and Bajram (Eid al-Fitr, Eid al-Adha) for many Bosniak households. Lunar. Date them each year. They are operations for fasting, appointments, and an elder who will not drink water in your lobby. They are not a festival you attend as consultation.

### Calendar

Catholic Christmas (December 25) and Orthodox Christmas (January 7) in adjacent Croat and Serb streams — and in mixed families. Ask. Do not put “Balkan holiday” on a case note.

11 July — Srebrenica Genocide Memorial Day. Literacy for the desk. Not a day off the work. Not a prompt to ask who they lost.

1 March is Independence Day for some. Dayton’s anniversary is not a greeting. A calendar click is literacy. It is not community engagement.

sections.heading: Education
paragraphs: No Compass education rate for this page — do not invent one. Interrupted schooling from war and camps is structure for some elders. Second generation is in English-dominant schools.
A parent who speaks fluent Bosnian and limited English is not illiterate. The English-only IEP is the gate. Put the language they ask for on the line.

There is no Compass education rate on this page. Do not invent one. Interrupted schooling from siege, flight, and camps is structure for some first-wave adults — not a personality and not illiteracy in Bosnian.

### School and language

A parent who speaks fluent Bosnian and limited English is not illiterate. The English-only IEP is the gate. Put the language they ask for on the interpreter line. Latin script is not the same as English literacy. Cyrillic in a Serbian-identifying household is a different written door.

Second-generation educational mobility is real. So is an elder who still cannot run an exception form in English. Date a Minnesota figure when a controlling source exists. Until then: pattern, not a fake percent.

sections.heading: Etiquette
paragraphs: Coffee is hospitality. Elders. Shoes in some homes. Directness can sit next to courtesy.
Accept a little coffee. Keep medical and legal time. Do not photograph a home as a war exhibit.

Coffee is hospitality. Bosnian coffee is not a delay tactic. Accept a little if offered. You still keep medical and legal time. Name the conflict instead of punishing the cup.

### In the home

Shoes off in some homes. Elders first. Direct speech is not always rudeness here; courtesy-yes is not always agreement either. Ask whether they agree with the plan. Confirm in the language they use.

### Time

Do not walk into a living room and hunt for war photographs as professional development. Do not comment on pork, alcohol, or covering as a piety audit.

On-time for appointments. Traffic and multi-household logistics are real. So is a no-show when the plan was never agreed. Ask. Confirm.

sections.heading: Language and Communication
paragraphs: Bosnian, Croatian, and Serbian are mutually intelligible with political names. Latin for Bosnian/Croatian; Cyrillic for much Serbian. CLAS ten: Serbo-Croatian (Bosnian).
Book what the household asks. A “former Yugoslav” interpreter is a closed door with a polite label. Do not take a smile as consent.

Bosnian, Croatian, and Serbian are mutually intelligible with political names. The differences that matter on Tuesday are the name the household claims, the script, and whether the interpreter will walk in as “former Yugoslav.” That label is a closed door with a polite hyphen.

### Language

Script: Latin for Bosnian and Croatian; Cyrillic for much Serbian. Book what the household asks. CLAS ten writes Serbo-Croatian (Bosnian) on the language block. That is notice. It is not the interpreter. Staff who answer the number must be ready; the interpreter request must still name the variety.

Second-generation English is common. Elders may not have it. A long answer may be story. A short English yes may be exhaustion or courtesy. Do not take a smile as consent.

Do not make a Bosnian coworker the interpreter.

sections.heading: Other Considerations
paragraphs: Genocide denial in the region is current politics. PTSD and unexplained pain. Alcohol. LGBTQ Bosnians exist. Second generation is American and may still need language for an elder.
Do not platform denial in a lobby. Follow law. Still see a family. Do not out anyone. Do not skip mandated reporting and call it humility.

Unvarnished, because Minnesota Nice is how a room that treats everyone the same deletes facts.

### Named harms

Genocide denial in Bosnia and in diaspora politics is current, not archival. Do not platform it in a lobby. Do not “both-sides” Srebrenica to keep a meeting calm. Literacy is not a debate club.

PTSD, unexplained pain, sleep, and alcohol use sit in this diaspora’s clinical literature. Alcohol is not a joke and not a Muslim impossibility. Islam and drinking can exist in the same extended family. You follow law. You still see a person, not a bottle with an ethnicity. LGBTQ Bosnians exist. Conservative family, mosque, and church climates can mean silence. You use the name. You do not out someone to kin and call it culture.

Do not mash this page with Somali Islam, FGC, or Maay. Those are other intelligences. Second generation is American. They may still need language for an elder. An English IEP that never reached the parent is still a gate.

Staff who share this community may add facts. They do not get to delete a fact because it is hard to say.

sections.heading: Health
paragraphs: War trauma, PTSD, unexplained pain, and alcohol use are patterns named in Bosnian diaspora clinical literacy — not a rate this page invents. Date a Minnesota figure when a controlling source exists.
Believe reported pain. Do not ask them to narrate the pit for your chart. Gender match if they want it. Do not mash with Somali FGC or autism pages.

War trauma is structure for some first-wave adults and for some children who grew up inside someone else’s silence. PTSD, depression, unexplained pain, and somatic complaint are patterns named in Bosnian diaspora clinical literacy. This page does not invent a Minnesota rate. Date a figure when a controlling source exists. Do not skip screening because “they don’t talk about that.”

### Access

Alcohol use is part of the unvarnished picture for some households — men more often in the stereotype, not a rule. Do not treat a Bosniak Muslim as impossible for a substance-use screen. Do not treat a screen as a nationality.

Believe reported pain. Do not ask them to narrate the pit to make the pain credible. Gender match may be requested in maternal and intimate care. Offer it.

Do not fold this history into Tuskegee, into Somali FGC, or into a generic “refugee trauma” slide that erases Srebrenica as a specific crime.

sections.heading: LGBTQ
paragraphs: Queer and trans Bosnian Minnesotans exist. Conservative family and mosque climates can mean silence. So can Catholic or Orthodox streams.
Use the name. Do not out someone to family as culture.

Queer and trans Bosnian Minnesotans exist. Conservative family, mosque, and church climates can mean silence or exile. Some people live a public English life and a private Bosnian life.

### This person

You use the name they use. You do not out them to an elder as cultural humility. Minnesota’s Human Rights Act still applies.

So does the duty not to treat a whole people as a family-values exhibit or as automatically secular because they are European Muslims.

sections.heading: Hair, Dress, and Body
paragraphs: Do not assume hijab. Many Bosniak women in Minnesota dress like other European-origin Minnesotans. Traditional dress is public at weddings, not a daily uniform.
Do not ask if they “still cover.” Do not touch. Do not rank covering as piety or assimilation.

Do not assume hijab. Many Bosniak women in Minnesota dress like other European-origin Minnesotans. Some cover. Ask the woman, with gender match if she wants it.

### Dress

chapters.body:
This brief is about Bosniak / Bosnian Minnesota as a people-page. The CLAS ten language block says Serbo-Croatian (Bosnian). That is operations. It is how the building batches a notice. It is not the name of the household in the lobby.

### Who this is

Bosniak names the Muslim peoplehood of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Bosnian can also mean a citizen of a state that Dayton wrote as three constituent peoples — Bosniak, Croat, Serb. Croatian and Serbian households in Minnesota are adjacent. They may share a mutually intelligible language. They do not share this war story by default. Ask. Do not file them here because the interpreter catalog used a hyphen.

### Who this is not

This is not a Census “white” mash and not a Balkan blob. It is not Somali Islam with a different flag. It is not Russian, not Albanian, not Kosovar, not Ukrainian. Shared continent is not shared culture. Shared Islam is not shared culture. A full mosaic is not a stereotype. A stereotype is when this page becomes the person in the lobby.

### How to read this

There is no Minnesota Compass cultural-community count for Bosnian. That absence is a finding, not a reason to invent 40,000. Between 1993 and 2003 more than 2,300 primary Bosnian refugees resettled in Minnesota; they were part of about 140,000 Bosnian and Herzegovinian refugees who came to the United States (MSP Magazine, looking back at Minnesota’s refugee history). Primary placement is not the community. Secondary migration happened. Date the number you use. A rate is not the person.

The diversity inside this people is the point. A Srebrenica widow, a man who will not name the camp, a Catholic Croat neighbor who speaks the same language and not the same memory, a less-observant Bosniak who drinks coffee and does not keep Ramadan, a woman who covers, a woman who does not, a U.S.-born nurse who uses English with friends and Bosnian with an elder — share a language family and do not share a Tuesday.

Always defer to the person in front of you. This page is a hypothesis you still test on this family.
chapters.evidence: Bosniak / Bosnian Minnesota. CLAS ten labels the language Serbo-Croatian (Bosnian) — operations, not the people-name. Croatian and Serbian households are adjacent. No Compass cultural-community count. Date any number you cite. Do not invent 40,000.
chapters.practitioner: There is no single Bosnian client. Defer to this family. Do not open a Somali, Russian, Albanian, or generic Balkan case with this page. Book the language they ask for.
chapters.title: A Note on This Guide

chapters.body:
Bosniak peoplehood is older than 1992 and older than the refugee file. South Slavic speakers in the Dinaric and Bosnian lands lived under medieval kingdoms, Ottoman centuries (from the 15th century), Austro-Hungarian rule after 1878, royal and then socialist Yugoslavia, and the 1992 independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Islam in this land is Ottoman-era and European. That sentence is literacy. It is not a piety rank.

### History for the meeting

Bosniak, Croat, and Serb in Bosnia are not three languages you can hear from across a lobby. They are political names on a mutually intelligible South Slavic speech. The 1990s war made the names lethal. The desk that treats them as flavor has already failed the household.

### What people brought

What people brought: family, coffee, a language with a literature, Islam as heritage for most Bosniaks (sometimes as daily order, sometimes as a name without a public mark), Catholic and Orthodox streams in adjacent households, and a memory of neighbors who became a front. What they met in Minnesota: an English form, a language block that says Serbo-Croatian (Bosnian), and often one interpreter labeled “former Yugoslav.”

There is no Bosniak nation-state in the simple sense the checkbox wants. Dayton wrote a state with two entities and three constituent peoples. Do not referee that constitution in a waiver meeting. Listen if they name home.
chapters.evidence: South Slavic people of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Ottoman centuries; Austro-Hungarian; Yugoslavia; 1992 independence. Bosniak names the Muslim peoplehood. Bosnian can also mean citizenship of a three-people state.
chapters.practitioner: History is literacy for the desk. It is not a speech you give the family. Do not start with a war anecdote.
chapters.title: Origins and the Founding of a People

chapters.body:
Homeland is Bosnia and Herzegovina — Sarajevo, Tuzla, Zenica, Banja Luka, Mostar, Bihać, the Drina towns, the eastern enclaves. Srebrenica is a place-name and a crime. Do not put it on a small-talk map.

### Homeland

The 1992–1995 war produced camps and exile in Croatia, Serbia, Montenegro, Germany, Austria, Scandinavia, and then the United States. St. Louis became a large U.S. Bosnian hub. Chicago, New York, and other cities hold communities. Minnesota received a notable resettlement in the mid and late 1990s. Minnesota is not St. Louis. Do not copy a Missouri story onto this desk and call it local.

### Minnesota

In Minnesota: Twin Cities pattern. Islamic Community of Bosniaks in Minnesota has been a named Minneapolis door. Greater Minnesota households exist because work and kin exist. Do not assume one neighborhood. Do not assume the person in front of you has been back. Do not assume they want to go.
chapters.evidence: Bosnia and Herzegovina: Sarajevo, Tuzla, Banja Luka, Mostar, eastern enclaves including Srebrenica. Diaspora in Germany, Austria, Scandinavia, St. Louis, Chicago, New York. Minnesota received a notable 1990s resettlement — not the U.S. map.
chapters.practitioner: Do not assume Minneapolis. Do not assume they have been back. St. Louis is a larger U.S. hub; Minnesota is still this desk.
chapters.title: The Geography of the Bosnian World

chapters.body:
If the Great Migration is the foundational demographic event of modern Black America, and 1991 of Somali Minnesota, 1992–1995 is the foundational event of Bosnian Minnesota.

### Foundational events

Yugoslavia broke. Bosnia and Herzegovina declared independence. War followed: siege of Sarajevo, ethnic cleansing, camps, mass rape as a method of war, and on 11 July 1995 the genocide at Srebrenica — more than 8,000 Bosniak men and boys killed after a UN “safe area” failed. That is public record (ICTY, International Court of Justice). It is literacy for the desk. It is not a speech you give the family. Do not ask a survivor to narrate the pit.

### Who you meet

Dayton, December 1995, stopped the shooting and froze a political map. Camps and temporary protection in Europe came first for many. U.S. resettlement followed in the mid and late 1990s. Minnesota’s primary-refugee arrivals between 1993 and 2003 were more than 2,300. Secondary migration after that is real and not a Compass cell.

The desk in 2026 does not only meet that first wave. It meets their children — U.S.-born, English-dominant with peers, still translating for a parent who will not tell the war to a stranger and still cannot get the right language in the lobby. If you only know “refugee,” you will miss them.
chapters.evidence: 1992–1995 war; Srebrenica July 1995 genocide of Bosniak men and boys; Dayton December 1995; camps; U.S. resettlement mid/late 1990s; MN primary refugees 1993–2003 more than 2,300. Secondary migration after that. Date it.
chapters.practitioner: If you only know “refugee,” you will miss the 25-year-old who has never lived in Bosnia and still cannot get the right language for an elder. Do not ask a survivor to narrate the pit.
chapters.title: 1992–1995, Srebrenica, Dayton — Foundational Event

chapters.body:
Family is larger than a nuclear English form. Elders often speak. Kumovi — godparent ties — can be as binding as blood in some households. Who cares for a child, an elder, or a disabled adult may be a network the waiver checkbox does not have a box for.

### Who is in the household

War and exile also broke families. Missing men. Split siblings. A neighbor who is now the household. Camp years and then a U.S. apartment. Ask who should be in the room. Do not reconstruct a family tree as icebreaker.

### Who speaks

Women’s labor — factory, care work, professional second generation — sits next to a household in which an elder man may still be named as head. Both can be true in the same room.

Do not use 1995 as a family personality. Do not skip mandated reporting and call it culture. Minnesota law still stands.
chapters.evidence: South Slavic extended household; kumovi (godparent) ties; elders; who cares for the child may not match a nuclear English form.
chapters.practitioner: Ask who should be in the room. A nuclear English form already has a who. Do not use the war as a family icebreaker.
chapters.title: Family

chapters.body:
Minnesota received a notable Bosnian resettlement in the mid and late 1990s. That is why this page has to be as complete as the Hmong and Somali intelligences — because this department will meet this community on waivers, child welfare, health care, cash, food, aging, and employment, including the elder who still needs the language and the adult child who does not think of themselves as a refugee.

### Places

Places, not a blob: Twin Cities; a Minneapolis Bosniak civic and religious life some families name; Greater Minnesota when work pulled people. Do not invent a Little Sarajevo on a case note. Ask this family where they live.

### Partners

Partners: Islamic Community of Bosniaks in Minnesota; mosques and churches families actually name; resettlement-era voluntary agencies as history, not a current partner list; CECLC as a department door — not the whole community.

Bosnian staff are not unpaid interpreters and not the community. Identity is not a staffing plan. A Bajram greeting is optional professional courtesy. It does not make you the expert.
chapters.evidence: Notable 1990s resettlement. Twin Cities pattern. Islamic Community of Bosniaks in Minnesota (Minneapolis) is a named door some families use — not the whole. No Compass profile. Primary-refugee count is not the community.
chapters.practitioner: Partners, not a harvest list. Staff are colleagues, not the curriculum. Do not treat  Bosnian staff. A Bajram visit does not make you the expert. Pay the partner this household names.
chapters.title: Minnesota and Bosnian History

chapters.body:
To be Bosniak in Minnesota is to be a European Muslim people whose public mark is often quieter than Somali Minnesota, carrying a war the United States watched on television and then filed under the 1990s. In this building it sits inside another fact: many Bosnian Minnesotans are white in a U.S. racial order that will delete 1995 and call them assimilated, or Muslim in a room that treats everyone the same that will copy the Somali page and get the covering, the mosque, and the language wrong.

### In this state

Bosnian can mean the language, the passport, or the people-name. Bosniak is the ethnic name for the Muslim peoplehood. Use what this family uses. Do not lecture them on the difference as a greeting.

This guide is a working orientation. Individual variation always supersedes group generalization.
chapters.evidence: Bosniak peoplehood; European Muslims whose public mark is often quieter than Somali Minnesota; war memory without a personality; U.S.-born second generation.
chapters.practitioner: Do not copy the Somali page onto this one because both are Muslim. Do not fold this household into “white immigrant” and delete 1995.
chapters.title: Bosniak / Bosnian — the heart of a people

chapters.body:
Language as a political name. Bosnian, Croatian, Serbian — mutually intelligible, not interchangeable as identity. Book what they ask. “Former Yugoslav” is a closed door with a polite label.

### Islam as heritage for most Bosniaks

Often less publicly marked than Somali Minnesota. Do not assume hijab. Do not assume five daily prayers in the lobby. Do not assume the absence of a mark means the absence of faith — or of trauma.

### Family and kumovi

Who is in the room. Who signs.

### Coffee

Hospitality is a virtue. You still keep medical and legal time.

### Memory

Srebrenica and the siege are in the room for some people whether they speak them or not. You do not extract the memory. You do not deny it. You do not platform denial.

### Face

Direct refusal may be costly, or it may be blunt. Ask whether they agree. Do not take a smile as consent.
chapters.evidence: Language as a political name; Islam as heritage for most Bosniaks, not always as public mark; family; coffee; memory; face.
chapters.practitioner: You work with these. You do not perform them. Do not make a mosque the case plan unless they asked. Do not assume hijab.
chapters.title: Core Concepts

chapters.body:
Islam for most Bosniaks — Sunni, Ottoman heritage, a European Muslim history. Practice in Minnesota ranges from daily order to a name on a form. Hijab is not the default public mark. Do not copy the Somali religion chapter onto this page. Do not assume mosque is the case plan. Do not assume Friday prayer sets the appointment grid the way it might for another household. Ask.

### Streams

Catholic Croat and Orthodox Serb streams exist in the broader language. Christmas dates differ. A “Bosnian” interpreter for a household that names itself Croatian or Serbian may still be the wrong political door even when the words are understood. Ask.

### Practice

Do not make an imam, a priest, or a pastor the case plan unless this family asked. Church or mosque can be the information channel. It is not “the community.”

Illness meaning after war may not be the DSM sentence. PTSD, unexplained pain, sleep, and alcohol sit in the same clinic as ordinary Minnesota chronic disease. You can hold both. You do not interrogate the pit to complete a field.
chapters.evidence: Islam for most Bosniaks — often less publicly marked than Somali Minnesota. Catholic Croat and Orthodox Serb streams exist in the broader language. Ask.
chapters.practitioner: Do not assume hijab. Do not assume mosque is the case plan. Do not mash with Somali Islam. Church or mosque is information channel only if they name it.
chapters.title: Religion and Healing

chapters.body:
Elders first. A handshake is common in many Bosnian Minnesota rooms — European-style, not a Somali right-hand rule you import. Some observant Muslim Bosniaks will not shake hands across gender. Follow this room. Nod if a hand is not offered. Do not force one. Do not make a lesson of it.

### Titles

Merhaba, dobro jutro, zdravo, selam — follow what they offer. English “hello” is ordinary in the second generation. Say the name. Ask how to say the -ić.

### This room

Do not open with the war. Do not open with “I have a friend from Bosnia.” Do not import the Black nod or Somali As-salāmu ʿalaykum as the default here. This is not those grammars unless this person uses them.
chapters.evidence: Handshake is common in many rooms. Elders first. Some observant Muslim Bosniaks will not shake across gender — ask the room.
chapters.practitioner: Do not copy Somali handshake rules blindly. Do not force a hand. Do not import the Black nod. Follow this room.
chapters.title: Greetings

chapters.body:
South Slavic: given name, then family name. -ić and -vić endings are common (Hodžić, Begović, Hadžić, Petrović — examples of a pattern, not a roll call). The ć is not optional decoration. Ask how to say it. Do not joke. Do not anglicize it on the file without being asked.

### How to file

Women may or may not take a husband’s family name in U.S. records. Ask how to file. Do not “correct” a mother and child who do not share a last name as a fraud signal until you have a reason.

Given names may be Bosnian, South Slavic Christian, Arabic-origin, or English in the second generation. The form that demands first-middle-last and a hyphen will invent a person if you force it.

Pronounce it. Ask. Write what they say.
chapters.evidence: South Slavic given name + family name. -ić / -vić endings are common. Ask pronunciation. Women’s forms vary in U.S. records.
chapters.practitioner: Ask how to say it. Do not joke about the ć. Do not treat a spelling variant as fraud by default.
chapters.title: Naming Conventions

chapters.body:
Ramadan and Bajram (Eid al-Fitr, Eid al-Adha) for many Bosniak households. Lunar. Date them each year. They are operations for fasting, appointments, and an elder who will not drink water in your lobby. They are not a festival you attend as consultation.

### Calendar

Catholic Christmas (December 25) and Orthodox Christmas (January 7) in adjacent Croat and Serb streams — and in mixed families. Ask. Do not put “Balkan holiday” on a case note.

11 July — Srebrenica Genocide Memorial Day. Literacy for the desk. Not a day off the work. Not a prompt to ask who they lost.

1 March is Independence Day for some. Dayton’s anniversary is not a greeting. A calendar click is literacy. It is not community engagement.
chapters.evidence: Ramadan and Bajram (Eid) for many Bosniaks. Catholic Christmas; Orthodox Christmas (January 7) in adjacent streams. Srebrenica 11 July is literacy, not a holiday on the packet.
chapters.practitioner: A calendar click is literacy. It is not community engagement. Do not put “Balkan holiday” on a case note.
chapters.title: Dates of Significance

chapters.body:
There is no Compass education rate on this page. Do not invent one. Interrupted schooling from siege, flight, and camps is structure for some first-wave adults — not a personality and not illiteracy in Bosnian.

### School and language

A parent who speaks fluent Bosnian and limited English is not illiterate. The English-only IEP is the gate. Put the language they ask for on the interpreter line. Latin script is not the same as English literacy. Cyrillic in a Serbian-identifying household is a different written door.

Second-generation educational mobility is real. So is an elder who still cannot run an exception form in English. Date a Minnesota figure when a controlling source exists. Until then: pattern, not a fake percent.
chapters.evidence: No Compass education rate for this page — do not invent one. Interrupted schooling from war and camps is structure for some elders. Second generation is in English-dominant schools.
chapters.practitioner: A parent who speaks fluent Bosnian and limited English is not illiterate. The English-only IEP is the gate. Put the language they ask for on the line.
chapters.title: Education

chapters.body:
Coffee is hospitality. Bosnian coffee is not a delay tactic. Accept a little if offered. You still keep medical and legal time. Name the conflict instead of punishing the cup.

### In the home

Shoes off in some homes. Elders first. Direct speech is not always rudeness here; courtesy-yes is not always agreement either. Ask whether they agree with the plan. Confirm in the language they use.

### Time

Do not walk into a living room and hunt for war photographs as professional development. Do not comment on pork, alcohol, or covering as a piety audit.

On-time for appointments. Traffic and multi-household logistics are real. So is a no-show when the plan was never agreed. Ask. Confirm.
chapters.evidence: Coffee is hospitality. Elders. Shoes in some homes. Directness can sit next to courtesy.
chapters.practitioner: Accept a little coffee. Keep medical and legal time. Do not photograph a home as a war exhibit.
chapters.title: Etiquette

chapters.body:
Bosnian, Croatian, and Serbian are mutually intelligible with political names. The differences that matter on Tuesday are the name the household claims, the script, and whether the interpreter will walk in as “former Yugoslav.” That label is a closed door with a polite hyphen.

### Language

paragraphs: Amharic-speaking Minnesota: Amhara and other Amharic speakers. Amharic is a federal working language — many non-Amhara Ethiopians speak it as a second language. Compass Ethiopian 40,324 (ACS 2019–2023) is an umbrella, not an Amharic count. Not Oromo. Not Somali. Not Tigrinya.

This brief is about Amharic-speaking Minnesota — Amhara households and other households that use Amharic as a first or working language — as a people-page. Amharic is on the CLAS fifteen interpreter cards. That is operations. It is not a census of who is Ethiopian, and it is not permission to treat Ethiopia as one people.

### Who this is

Amharic is not Oromo. Amharic is not Somali. Amharic is not Tigrinya. Amharic is a federal working language of Ethiopia. Many non-Amhara Ethiopians speak it as a second language of school, army, and office. If the household is Oromo, open Oromo and book Afaan Oromoo. If Tigrayan, book Tigrinya. If Somali — including people born in Ethiopia who name Somali ancestry — open Somali Minnesota. Compass counts those last households as Somali, not Ethiopian. Shared Horn is not shared culture. Shared Orthodox calendar is not shared politics.

### Who this is not

Minnesota Compass Ethiopian (ACS 2019–2023) is 40,324. About 89.4 percent Twin Cities, 10.6 percent Greater Minnesota. About 43.5 percent age 17 or younger. Foreign-born 61.7 percent. Language other than English (age 5+) 74.9 percent; English less than “very well” 30.4 percent. Median household income about $57,106 (2022 dollars, averaged). Poverty 13.0 percent. Renter 65.3 percent. Date the number. It is an umbrella. Census recodes some people who write Oromo into Ethiopian. It is not an Amharic speaker count. Minnesota Secretary of State voter materials include Amharic. Do not invent a population.

The diversity inside this door is the point. An Amhara Orthodox grandmother who fasts more days than the clinic has slots, a Protestant professional, a Muslim Ethiopian household, a person who uses Amharic at work and Oromo at home, a U.S.-born student who uses English with friends and Amharic with an elder, a Tigrayan family who should not have been booked here — share a language door and do not share a Tuesday.

### How to read this

Always defer to the person in front of you. This page is a hypothesis you still test on this family.

sections.heading: Origins and the Founding of a People
paragraphs: Ethiopian imperial history; Amhara highland peoplehood; Amharic as court and federal language. 1974 revolution; Red Terror; Derg; 1980s famine; 1991; 2020–2022 Tigray war as current structure for some.
History is literacy for the desk. It is not a speech you give the family. Do not referee empire in a waiver meeting.

Amhara peoplehood and Amharic as a written language are older than the refugee file and older than 1974. Highland agricultural life, Ethiopian imperial history, the Orthodox Tewahedo Church, and Ge’ez as liturgical language organized a state that was not a European colony in the way the Somali and Karen files were. That fact is literacy. It is not a rank you give the family, and it is not a reason to skip language access.

### History for the meeting

Amharic became the court and then the federal working language. That is why a non-Amhara Ethiopian may speak it and still not be this people-page as a first identity. Empire’s second language in a Minnesota home is a Tuesday question: which language does this elder actually use for a legal notice?

### What people brought

1974 ended the empire. The Derg, the Red Terror, the 1980s famine, and 1991 are the foundational political events of much of the Minnesota first wave. The 2020–2022 war in Tigray is current structure for some households — Tigrayan, Amhara, Eritrean-adjacent, and others. Do not referee it in a waiver meeting.

What people brought: Amharic and fidel, Orthodox fasting and Protestant and Muslim streams, kin obligation, injera as ordinary food, honorifics, a memory of state violence. What they met in Minnesota: an English form, one “Ethiopian” checkbox, and often one interpreter who was Somali or Oromo because the building mashed the Horn.

The diaspora is global: Washington D.C. as a large U.S. hub, Los Angeles, Dallas, Toronto, the Gulf, Italy. Minnesota is a real community, not the U.S. capital of it. Secondary migration and church networks pulled people here.

If 1991 is Somali Minnesota’s foundational political event, 1974 and what followed is the foundational event of much of Amharic-speaking Minnesota’s first wave.

### Foundational events

The revolution overthrew Haile Selassie. The Derg and the Red Terror killed and scattered people. The 1980s famine and resettlement brought some of the first African refugees Minnesota named as Ethiopian — MSP Magazine: Minnesota admitted 17 refugees from Ethiopia in 1982, the first African refugees in the state’s telling of that file. Others came through Sudan, Kenya, Europe. 1991 ended the Derg and opened another politics. Family reunification and later diversity streams followed.

### Who you meet

2020–2022 war in Tigray is current structure. Some Minnesota households are living it through kin, remittance, silence, or politics in the parish parking lot. Do not referee. Do not pick a side. Do not make a waiver meeting a map of the front.

To speak Amharic in Minnesota is sometimes to be Amhara, and sometimes to be a person the empire taught a second language. Both sit in this door. ### In this state

In this building another fact sits on top: many of these households are Black in a U.S. racial order that will file them under Somali or under historic African American and get the language, the church, and the name wrong. Shared race is not shared culture.

Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo is central for many Amhara households — one of the oldest Christian churches, Ge’ez liturgy, icons, fasting, Timkat, Meskel, Gena (January 7). Debtera and priest are church roles. They are not the case plan unless this family asked. Do not book a liturgy as DHS programming.

### Streams

Protestant and evangelical Ethiopian streams are large in the diaspora. Muslim Ethiopian streams exist — ask; book the language; do not copy Somali Islam onto this page; lunar Islamic dates if this family is Muslim.

### Practice

Fasting calendars are operations. A missed morning appointment during a fast, a medication labeled “with food,” a blood draw — ask. Noncompliance may be the calendar you never learned.

Illness meaning may sit next to holy water, vow, and parish counsel. You can hold that next to a waiver. You do not mock it. You do not skip the clinic.

sections.heading: Greetings
paragraphs: Elders first. Shoulder bumps and cheek kisses in some rooms. Church titles. Ato / Weizero / Weizerit.
Do not copy Somali handshake rules blindly. Do not force a hand. Follow this room. Use the honorific until invited not to.

Elders first. Ato, Weizero, Weizerit plus the given name until invited otherwise. Church titles for a priest. Say the name. Ask how to say it.

### Titles

Shoulder bumps and cheek kisses (often two or three) happen in some rooms among people who already know each other. A hard American handshake is not universal. Some people will shake in English-language offices. Follow this room. Do not force a hand. Do not copy Somali right-hand-across-gender rules blindly — and do not assume they do not apply. Ask the room.

### This room

Selam, tenastëllïn, English hello — follow what they offer. Do not import the Black nod as default. This is not that grammar unless this person uses it.

sections.heading: Naming Conventions
paragraphs: Often given name + father’s name; no family surname as the database wants. Same trap as Somali, different grammar. Honorifics Ato / Weizero.
Ask how to say it. Do not invent a last name because the screen requires one. That invented name becomes a gate. Same three-name problem, not the same people.

Often given name plus father’s given name. The second name is not a family surname as the database wants it. Children take the father’s given name as their second name. The grandfather’s name may appear as a third. Same trap as Somali, different grammar, different people. Do not invent a last name because the screen requires one. That invented name becomes a gate that follows the person to Medicaid, school, and a background check.

### How to file

Women do not automatically take a husband’s name. Ask how to file. Do not “correct” a mother and child who do not share a last name as fraud until you have a reason.

Honorifics: Ato, Weizero, Weizerit. Use them. Pronounce the name. Ask. The form that demands first-middle-last and a hyphen will invent a person.

### Calendar

Timkat (Epiphany, 19 January). Meskel (Finding of the True Cross, late September). Gena — Orthodox Christmas, 7 January. Fasika — Easter, on the Orthodox calculation. Fasting seasons before these, and weekly fasts for some. Operations.

Lunar Islamic dates if this family is Muslim. Do not assume they are not.

An Oromo interpreter is the wrong door. A Somali interpreter is the wrong door. A Tigrinya interpreter is the wrong door unless they asked for Tigrinya. Confirm whether Amharic is first language or the empire’s second language in this home. Book what they name.

chapters.body:
This brief is about Amharic-speaking Minnesota — Amhara households and other households that use Amharic as a first or working language — as a people-page. Amharic is on the CLAS fifteen interpreter cards. That is operations. It is not a census of who is Ethiopian, and it is not permission to treat Ethiopia as one people.

### Who this is

Amharic is not Oromo. Amharic is not Somali. Amharic is not Tigrinya. Amharic is a federal working language of Ethiopia. Many non-Amhara Ethiopians speak it as a second language of school, army, and office. If the household is Oromo, open Oromo and book Afaan Oromoo. If Tigrayan, book Tigrinya. If Somali — including people born in Ethiopia who name Somali ancestry — open Somali Minnesota. Compass counts those last households as Somali, not Ethiopian. Shared Horn is not shared culture. Shared Orthodox calendar is not shared politics.

### Who this is not

Minnesota Compass Ethiopian (ACS 2019–2023) is 40,324. About 89.4 percent Twin Cities, 10.6 percent Greater Minnesota. About 43.5 percent age 17 or younger. Foreign-born 61.7 percent. Language other than English (age 5+) 74.9 percent; English less than “very well” 30.4 percent. Median household income about $57,106 (2022 dollars, averaged). Poverty 13.0 percent. Renter 65.3 percent. Date the number. It is an umbrella. Census recodes some people who write Oromo into Ethiopian. It is not an Amharic speaker count. Minnesota Secretary of State voter materials include Amharic. Do not invent a population.

The diversity inside this door is the point. An Amhara Orthodox grandmother who fasts more days than the clinic has slots, a Protestant professional, a Muslim Ethiopian household, a person who uses Amharic at work and Oromo at home, a U.S.-born student who uses English with friends and Amharic with an elder, a Tigrayan family who should not have been booked here — share a language door and do not share a Tuesday.

### How to read this

Always defer to the person in front of you. This page is a hypothesis you still test on this family.

chapters.title: A Note on This Guide

chapters.body:
Amhara peoplehood and Amharic as a written language are older than the refugee file and older than 1974. Highland agricultural life, Ethiopian imperial history, the Orthodox Tewahedo Church, and Ge’ez as liturgical language organized a state that was not a European colony in the way the Somali and Karen files were. That fact is literacy. It is not a rank you give the family, and it is not a reason to skip language access.

### History for the meeting

Amharic became the court and then the federal working language. That is why a non-Amhara Ethiopian may speak it and still not be this people-page as a first identity. Empire’s second language in a Minnesota home is a Tuesday question: which language does this elder actually use for a legal notice?

### What people brought

1974 ended the empire. The Derg, the Red Terror, the 1980s famine, and 1991 are the foundational political events of much of the Minnesota first wave. The 2020–2022 war in Tigray is current structure for some households — Tigrayan, Amhara, Eritrean-adjacent, and others. Do not referee it in a waiver meeting.

What people brought: Amharic and fidel, Orthodox fasting and Protestant and Muslim streams, kin obligation, injera as ordinary food, honorifics, a memory of state violence. What they met in Minnesota: an English form, one “Ethiopian” checkbox, and often one interpreter who was Somali or Oromo because the building mashed the Horn.
chapters.evidence: Ethiopian imperial history; Amhara highland peoplehood; Amharic as court and federal language. 1974 revolution; Red Terror; Derg; 1980s famine; 1991; 2020–2022 Tigray war as current structure for some.
chapters.practitioner: History is literacy for the desk. It is not a speech you give the family. Do not referee empire in a waiver meeting.
chapters.title: Origins and the Founding of a People

chapters.body:
Homeland is not one ethnic map. Amhara region, Addis Ababa, and a country where Amharic is heard in offices far from Amhara land. Tigray, Oromia, the south, and Eritrea are adjacent geographies with different languages. Do not draw one Ethiopia on a case note.

### Homeland

The diaspora is global: Washington D.C. as a large U.S. hub, Los Angeles, Dallas, Toronto, the Gulf, Italy. Minnesota is a real community, not the U.S. capital of it. Secondary migration and church networks pulled people here.

### Minnesota

In Minnesota: Compass Ethiopian is 89.4 percent Twin Cities. Minneapolis parishes (Debre Selam Medhanealem Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church among them, Seward / Minnehaha). Inner-ring suburbs. Greater Minnesota — including Worthington, where Ethiopian Orthodox life is public — is 10.6 percent of the Compass Ethiopian umbrella. Do not assume Cedar-Riverside. That hub is Somali. Do not assume the person in front of you has been to Addis.
chapters.evidence: Ethiopian highlands; Addis Ababa; Amhara region; Amharic used far beyond it. Diaspora in D.C., L.A., Dallas, Toronto. Compass Ethiopian: 89.4% Twin Cities, 10.6% Greater Minnesota — umbrella, dated.
chapters.practitioner: Do not assume Minneapolis. Worthington and other towns have Ethiopian Orthodox life. Do not assume Cedar-Riverside — that is a Somali hub.
chapters.title: The Geography of the Amharic-speaking World

chapters.body:
If 1991 is Somali Minnesota’s foundational political event, 1974 and what followed is the foundational event of much of Amharic-speaking Minnesota’s first wave.

### Foundational events

The revolution overthrew Haile Selassie. The Derg and the Red Terror killed and scattered people. The 1980s famine and resettlement brought some of the first African refugees Minnesota named as Ethiopian — MSP Magazine: Minnesota admitted 17 refugees from Ethiopia in 1982, the first African refugees in the state’s telling of that file. Others came through Sudan, Kenya, Europe. 1991 ended the Derg and opened another politics. Family reunification and later diversity streams followed.

### Who you meet

2020–2022 war in Tigray is current structure. Some Minnesota households are living it through kin, remittance, silence, or politics in the parish parking lot. Do not referee. Do not pick a side. Do not make a waiver meeting a map of the front.

The desk in 2026 also meets U.S.-born children — English with peers, still translating, still unable to get Amharic (or the actual home language) in the lobby. If you only know “Ethiopian,” you will miss the Oromo mother and the Tigrayan elder you booked wrong.

Compass Ethiopian average household size 3.09 — umbrella, dated, smaller than some other Compass communities, still not Mary Jones.

### Who is in the household

Who cares for the child may not match the checkbox. Hour caps and “natural supports” can dump unpaid work onto women in that network and call it culture.

### Who speaks

Naming is already a who: given name plus father’s name, often no surname. The database that invents a last name invents a kinship the family did not file.

Ask who should be in the room. Do not skip mandated reporting and call it respect for elders. Minnesota law still stands.

chapters.title: Family

chapters.body:
Amharic-speaking Minnesota is why this page has to be as complete as Somali and Hmong — because this department will meet this community on waivers, child welfare, health care, cash, food, aging, and employment, and because the building has a long habit of hearing “East African” and booking Somali.

### Places

Places, not a blob: Minneapolis parishes; inner-ring suburbs; Worthington and other Greater Minnesota towns where Orthodox liturgy is public; not Cedar-Riverside as the default. Compass Ethiopian: about nine in ten in the Twin Cities.

### Partners

chapters.body:
To speak Amharic in Minnesota is sometimes to be Amhara, and sometimes to be a person the empire taught a second language. Both sit in this door. Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo is central for many Amhara. Protestant and Muslim Ethiopian streams are real. Intra-Ethiopian politics — Amhara, Oromo, Tigrayan — live in Minnesota parking lots. You do not pick a side.

### In this state

In this building another fact sits on top: many of these households are Black in a U.S. racial order that will file them under Somali or under historic African American and get the language, the church, and the name wrong. Shared race is not shared culture.

This guide is a working orientation. Individual variation always supersedes group generalization.

### Orthodox fasting and calendar

Many fast days — weekly Wednesday and Friday for some, long Lenten and Advent fasts, other seasons. This is operations for appointments, blood draws, and medication with food. It is not a piety rank.

### Honorifics

Ato (Mr.), Weizero (Mrs.), Weizerit (Miss). Church titles. Elders.

### Three names

Given name, father’s name, often grandfather’s. No family surname as the database wants. Same trap as Somali. Different grammar. Do not invent a last name.

### Elders and face

Direct refusal may be costly. Ask whether they agree. Do not take a smile as consent.

### Injera, coffee ceremony, parish

Ordinary life, not a festival you attend as consultation.

Debtera and priest are church roles. They are not the case plan unless this family asked. Do not book a liturgy as DHS programming.

### Streams

Protestant and evangelical Ethiopian streams are large in the diaspora. Muslim Ethiopian streams exist — ask; book the language; do not copy Somali Islam onto this page; lunar Islamic dates if this family is Muslim.

### Practice

Fasting calendars are operations. A missed morning appointment during a fast, a medication labeled “with food,” a blood draw — ask. Noncompliance may be the calendar you never learned.

Illness meaning may sit next to holy water, vow, and parish counsel. You can hold that next to a waiver. You do not mock it. You do not skip the clinic.

Shoulder bumps and cheek kisses (often two or three) happen in some rooms among people who already know each other. A hard American handshake is not universal.
