sections.heading: A Note on This Guide
paragraphs: French-speaking Minnesota is a language door, not a people. Haiti / Kreyòl; West and Central Africa; France / Belgium / Quebec; a few Horn households with French from Djibouti or camps. Star Tribune 2025: French ~2% of the non-English-at-home group. Date it. Do not invent a Francophone census.
Ask which French, and whether another language is actually home. Book Kreyòl if that is the home language. Do not open African American or Somali with this page unless that is the household.

This brief is a language door, not a people. “French-speaking Minnesota” names a CLAS fifteen line and a set of households who may use French at school, at the clinic, or with the state — and who often use another language at home. Ask which French, and whether another language is actually the home language.

### Who this is

Streams that are not interchangeable: Haiti, where Kreyòl (Haitian Creole) is often the home language and French the school or official language; West and Central Africa, where Wolof, Bambara, Lingala, Kinyarwanda, and many others may be home and French the colonial/school language; France, Belgium, Quebec, and other European or North American streams — smaller in Minnesota services, real; some Somali and other Horn households with French from Djibouti or camps — not the default.

### Who this is not

This is not historic African American CI with a different flag. It is not Somali. It is not one Africa. It is not France. Do not assume Africa. Do not assume France. Do not assume Haiti. A full mosaic is not a stereotype. A stereotype is when this page becomes the person in the lobby.

### How to read this

There is no Minnesota Compass cultural-community row for “French” or “Francophone.” Do not invent a census. Star Tribune (July 31, 2025): among people in Minnesota who speak a language other than English at home, French is among the languages — with German, Chinese, Russian, and Arabic — each representing about 2 percent of that group. Date it. That is a language share. It is not a Haitian count, not a Senegalese count, not a Québécois count.

The diversity inside the door is the point. A Kreyòl-speaking mother, a Lingala-speaking father from Kinshasa who uses French with the school, a Dakar household that wants Wolof, a Quebecois professional, a French national on a campus, a Djiboutian elder who has French from a camp — do not share a Tuesday.

Always defer to the person in front of you. This page is a hypothesis you still test on this family.

sections.heading: Origins — several peoples, one colonial language
paragraphs: Haitian peoplehood is 1804 and a Caribbean history, not an African checkbox. West and Central African nations are many peoples under a colonial school language. France / Belgium / Quebec are European and North American streams.
History is literacy for the desk. It is not a speech you give the family. Do not assume Africa. Do not assume France. Do not assume Haiti.

Haitian peoplehood is not an African checkbox and not a French checkbox. The Haitian Revolution reached independence on January 1, 1804 — the first Black republic in the hemisphere. U.S. occupation (1915–1934), dictatorships, the 2010 earthquake, and later TPS designations are Haitian history. Kreyòl is the home language of the people. French was the colonial and school language. Book Kreyòl if that is the home language.

### History for the meeting

West and Central Africa are many nations and many peoples under a French school language left by colonization: Senegal, Mali, Guinea, Côte d’Ivoire, Cameroon, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Congo-Brazzaville, francophone Rwanda and Burundi, and others. Wolof, Bambara, Lingala, Kinyarwanda, Fulani, and more may be what the grandmother actually speaks. An “African French” interpreter can still be the wrong door.

### What people brought

France, Belgium, Switzerland, and Quebec are European and North American streams. They are smaller in Minnesota human services. They are real. Do not assume Africa when the household is Paris. Do not assume Paris when the household is Port-au-Prince or Yaoundé.

Some Somali and other Horn households have French from Djibouti, from camps, or from a third country. That is not the default for Somali Minnesota. Open Somali for Somali. Ask about French if they name it.

sections.heading: The Geography of French as a Door
paragraphs: Haiti; Senegal, Mali, Guinea, Côte d’Ivoire, Cameroon, DRC, Congo-Brazzaville, francophone Rwanda/Burundi, and others; France, Belgium, Quebec. Minnesota is a present. No Compass map for this umbrella.
Do not assume Minneapolis. Do not assume they have been to Paris. Name the country they name.

Haiti is Caribbean. Dakar, Bamako, Abidjan, Yaoundé, Kinshasa, Brazzaville, Kigali, Bujumbura are African cities with different languages under the French door. Paris, Brussels, Montreal are not those cities.

### Homeland

Minnesota is a present. Twin Cities and Greater Minnesota both. Do not assume Minneapolis. Plant towns, student neighborhoods, and inner-ring suburbs can all hold a household on this door.

### Minnesota

There is no Compass map for this umbrella. Date any town-level school-language count when a professional has it. Pattern now: people are here. Do not invent a county number.

sections.heading: 1804, Occupation, Earthquake, Colonies, and TPS — Foundational Events
paragraphs: Haiti: revolution 1804, U.S. occupation 1915–1934, 2010 earthquake, TPS. West and Central Africa: colonial school language plus later displacement and skilled migration. Euro-French and Quebec streams are smaller in MN services, real.
If you only know “French,” you will book the wrong interpreter and the wrong CI. TPS climate is current structure. Do not collect status you do not need.

Haiti: 1804 is peoplehood. The U.S. occupied Haiti from 1915 to 1934. The January 12, 2010 earthquake killed on a scale this building should not turn into a speech. Temporary Protected Status for Haiti was first designated after that earthquake and has been extended, terminated, and redesignated in later years — including after the 2021 assassination of President Jovenel Moïse and another earthquake. Date the designation you mean. Do not invent this person’s status. Do not collect status you do not need.

### Foundational events

West and Central African migration into Minnesota includes students, skilled workers, family, and people displaced by conflict. French is often the language a school left them, not the language of the kitchen. Colonial borders and later wars are literacy. They are not a news-clip briefing you give the family.

### Who you meet

Euro-French, Belgian, and Quebec streams arrive as professionals, students, and family. Smaller in the service lobby, real. Do not run a refugee script on a Lyon household. Do not run a Paris script on a Cap-Haïtien household.

If you only know “French,” you will miss Kreyòl, miss Lingala, and mash a people.

sections.heading: Family
paragraphs: Extended households in many Haitian and West/Central African streams. Godparent and church or mosque kin. Euro-French nuclear forms are not the default for this door.
Ask who should be in the room. A nuclear English form already has a who. Do not assume a Paris family grammar in a Port-au-Prince or Dakar household.

Extended household is common in many Haitian and West/Central African streams. Godparents, church sisters, mosque kin, and cousins who are “auntie” on Tuesday may not match the waiver checkbox. Ask who should be in the room.

### Who is in the household

Euro-French nuclear grammar is not the default for this door. Do not import it.

### Who speaks

Who cares for the child, who holds the lease, and who can sign may not be the same adult. Mixed-status households exist in Haitian and some African streams. Do not collect status you do not need.

Minnesota law still stands. Do not skip mandated reporting and call it culture. Do not turn a family argument into a national personality.

sections.heading: Minnesota and This Language Door
paragraphs: Twin Cities and Greater Minnesota both. Churches, mosques, and community associations are often the information channel. Alliance Française is a Euro-French civic door — not the service door for a Haitian or Senegalese household unless they name it.
Pay the door this person names. Staff are colleagues, not the curriculum. Do not treat  Haitian or African staff. A festival is not consultation.

This department will meet these households on waivers, child welfare, health care, cash, food, aging, TPS-adjacent fear, and employment. Twin Cities and Greater Minnesota. Rural is not an afterthought when the plant or the college is the draw.

### Places

Churches (Catholic and Protestant) and mosques are often the actual information channel. Parish and mosque are not “the community.” They are a door if this family names them.

### Partners

Alliance Française and campus French clubs are Euro-French civic and student doors. They are not the service partner for a Haitian or Senegalese household unless that household names them. Do not BCC a conversation group and call it consultation.

Do not make Haitian, Senegalese, Congolese, or Cameroonian staff the interpreter pool or “the African voice.”

sections.heading: A language door, not a people mash
paragraphs: A shared colonial language is not a people. Anti-Blackness in Minnesota hits Haitian and African francophone people and is not the same file as historic African American CI.
Open African American for a Great Migration household. Open this for a Haitian or Senegalese household. Open Somali for Somali. Never one Black module.

To be filed under French in Minnesota is often to be asked whether you are from France, or from Africa, as if those were two rooms and Haiti were in one of them.

### In this state

Anti-Blackness in this state hits Haitian and African francophone people in the lobby, the clinic, and the traffic stop. That is not a reason to open historic African American CI and stop. Open African American for a Great Migration household. Open this for a Haitian or Senegalese household. Open Somali for Somali. Shared race in the United States is not shared culture. Shared French class in a colonial school is not shared culture.

Colorism sits inside some Haitian and West African families and inside Minnesota’s racial order. You do not lecture it. You do not pretend it is absent.

This guide is a working orientation. Individual variation always supersedes group generalization.

sections.heading: Core Concepts
paragraphs: Which language is home. Kreyòl vs French. Lingala, Wolof, Bambara, Kinyarwanda vs French. Colorism. Church or mosque as channel. TPS and enforcement as climate.
You work with these. You do not perform them. Book the home language. Do not use “Francophone Africa” as a personality.

Home language is the first grammar. French may be school. Kreyòl, Lingala, Wolof, Bambara, or Kinyarwanda may be home. Book home.

### One Francophone client is a mash

Haiti is not Senegal. DRC is not Cameroon. Quebec is not Port-au-Prince.

### Colorism and anti-Blackness

Both can be in the room. Neither is a personality.

### Church or mosque as channel

Not the case plan unless they asked.

### TPS and enforcement climate

People skip clinic and waiver meetings when a relative can be moved. That is not noncompliance.

### Respect and titles in many streams

Do not force first-name familiarity on an elder.

sections.heading: Religion
paragraphs: Catholic, Muslim (West Africa, some Haiti), Protestant, Vodou in some Haitian households (do not sensationalize), none.
Do not make a priest, an imam, or a Vodou priest the case plan unless this family asked. Do not treat Vodou as horror-film content.

Catholic Christianity is large in Haiti and in parts of West and Central Africa and in Euro-French streams. Protestant and evangelical churches are ordinary too. Islam is ordinary in much of West Africa and present in some Haitian households. None is real.

### Streams

Vodou is a Haitian religious fact in some households. Do not sensationalize it. Do not treat it as horror-film content, as witchcraft for the file, or as the “real” Haiti. Do not make a Vodou priest the case plan unless this family asked. The same rule for a Catholic priest or an imam.

### Practice

Do not assume a mosque because the passport is West African. Do not assume a cathedral because the language is French.

sections.heading: Greetings
paragraphs: French vous/tu, Kreyòl greetings, Wolof and Lingala greetings — not one script. Elders and titles in many streams. Handshake in many professional rooms.
Follow this room. Do not force familiarity. Do not import a Paris rule onto a Haitian elder or a Bamako mother.

French vous vs tu is a formality system some Euro-French and African school-French speakers use. Kreyòl greetings are not that system. Wolof and Lingala greetings are not that system. Follow this room.

### Titles

Elders and titles in many Haitian and African streams. Handshake in many professional rooms. Do not force a hug.

### This room

Do not import a Paris rule onto a Haitian elder. Do not import a Port-au-Prince manner onto a Lille professional. Do not import the Black nod or Somali right-hand rules unless this person is on those pages.

Physical contact: ask the room. Cross-gender touch with elders is not a default.

sections.heading: Naming Conventions
paragraphs: French-style given name plus family name in some streams; Haitian and West African naming that does not match first-middle-last; Muslim names in some West African and some Haitian households.
Ask how to say it and how to file it. Do not invent a last name. Do not “correct” spelling to Paris French.

French-style given name plus family name appears in some streams. Haitian naming may not match first-middle-last. West African naming may include a day name, a Muslim name, a family name, or a French school name that is not what the grandmother uses. Ask how to say it. Ask how to file it.

### How to file

Do not invent a last name. Do not “correct” Kreyòl or Wolof spelling to Paris French. Do not treat unmatched last names in a household as fraud by default.

A child may have a different school name than the name on the birth record. Ask. Do not humiliate.

sections.heading: Dates of Significance
paragraphs: Haitian Independence Day January 1, 1804. 2010 earthquake. West African independence dates vary by country. Catholic and Muslim calendars. Bastille Day is not this household’s day unless they say so.
A calendar click is literacy. It is not community engagement. Do not put Bastille Day on a Haitian case note.

January 1 — Haitian Independence Day, 1804. Literacy. Not a day off the work unless this family names it. Not Bastille Day.

### Calendar

January 12, 2010 — Haiti earthquake. TPS history starts here for many families. Literacy. Not a speech.

West African independence dates vary by country (1960 is a cluster, not a single day). Catholic calendars, Ramadan and Eid in Muslim households, and national days this family names — ask. Do not put Bastille Day (July 14) on a Haitian or Senegalese case note.

A calendar click is not community engagement.

sections.heading: Education
paragraphs: French as school/official language does not mean French is home, and does not mean the parent can run an English IEP. Literacy in the form language is not guaranteed.
A parent who speaks fluent Kreyòl or Wolof and limited English is not illiterate. Book the home language. The English-only packet is the gate.

French as a school or official language does not mean French is the home language, and does not mean the parent can run an English IEP. Literacy in any language of the form is not guaranteed. Interrupted schooling in Haiti after 2010, or in a conflict region, is structure.

### School and language

A parent who speaks fluent Kreyòl, Wolof, or Lingala and limited English is not illiterate. The English-only form is the gate. So is a French form when the home language is Kreyòl.

Second-generation English is common. CLAS still says do not use minors as interpreters. Book the home language.

Do not invent a Minnesota Francophone attainment rate. Compass has no such row.

sections.heading: Etiquette
paragraphs: Titles, elders, hospitality, church and mosque time. Variation across Haiti, West Africa, Central Africa, and Europe is the point.
Accept a little food. Keep medical and legal time. Do not assume a French-restaurant manner is the rule in this living room.

Titles and elders in many Haitian and African streams. Hospitality is a virtue in many rooms. You still keep medical and legal time.

### In the home

Do not assume a French-restaurant manner — wine, first names after one meeting, cheek kisses — is the rule in this living room. Do not assume the absence of that manner is “less educated.”

### Time

Shoes, food, and Sunday church or Friday mosque will vary. Ask. On-time for appointments is a professional default for some and a bus-and-shift problem for others.

Courtesy-yes then no-show happens when the plan was never agreed. Ask whether they agree. Confirm in the language they use.

sections.heading: Language and Communication
paragraphs: Ask which language is actually home. Kreyòl vs French. Lingala vs French. Wolof, Bambara, Kinyarwanda. An “African French” interpreter can still be the wrong door. Star Tribune 2025: French ~2% of non-English-at-home.
Put the home language on the line. Do not take a smile as consent. Staff are colleagues, not the curriculum. Do not treat  a Francophone coworker.

Ask which language is actually home. Book that language.

### Language

Kreyòl is not French. A French interpreter for a Kreyòl household is a closed door. Lingala is not French. Wolof is not French. Bambara is not French. Kinyarwanda is not French. An interpreter billed as “African French” can still be the wrong country, the wrong register, and the wrong language.

French itself is not one French. Haitian school French, Dakar French, Kinshasa French, and Paris French differ in accent and vocabulary. Mutual understanding is often possible and not guaranteed. Ask.

Star Tribune (July 31, 2025): French is about 2 percent of the non-English-at-home group in Minnesota, listed with German, Chinese, Russian, and Arabic. Date it. That share does not tell you which French, or whether French is home.

A short English yes may be exhaustion or courtesy. Do not take a smile as consent. Do not make a Francophone coworker the interpreter.

sections.heading: Other Considerations
paragraphs: Anti-Blackness in Minnesota; do not fold into historic African American CI; colorism; LGBTQ exist; enforcement and TPS climate; one Francophone client is a mash.
Do not collect status you do not need. Do not skip mandated reporting and call it humility. Do not out anyone. Open the right CI.

Unvarnished, because Minnesota Nice is how a room that treats everyone the same deletes facts.

### Named harms

Anti-Blackness in Minnesota hits Haitian and African francophone people. Traffic stops, clinic dismissal, and “where are you really from” are structure. Do not fold this household into historic African American CI because both are Black — and do not pretend anti-Blackness is absent because the passport is Haitian or Senegalese.

Colorism inside families and in the U.S. racial order is real. You do not lecture it. You do not skip it when it is the harm in the room.

LGBTQ Haitian and African francophone Minnesotans exist. Enforcement and TPS climate is current structure. People skip clinic, school, and waiver meetings. That is not noncompliance. Do not collect status you do not need.

One Francophone client is how treating everyone the same hides difference. Haiti is not Africa. Africa is not France. France is not Haiti.

Staff who share this community may add facts. They do not get to delete a fact because it is hard to say.

sections.heading: Health
paragraphs: Language is the first health gate. Trauma and displacement in some Haitian and African streams. Do not invent a Minnesota Francophone rate.
Book the home language. Offer gender match. Believe reported pain. Do not mash Tuskegee onto a Port-au-Prince or Dakar history.

Language is the first health gate. A French consent form for a Kreyòl speaker is not consent. A smile is not consent.

### Access

Trauma and displacement in some Haitian and African streams are real. Do not invent a Minnesota Francophone PTSD rate. Do not skip screening. Do not make earthquake or war a personality.

Believe reported pain. Anti-Blackness in U.S. medicine is documented. Do not mash Tuskegee onto a Port-au-Prince or Dakar history; do not pretend the clinic is neutral.

Gender match may be requested in maternal and intimate care. Offer it. If they name a healer, a priest, or an imam, listen. Do not make that person the case plan unless they asked.

sections.heading: LGBTQ
paragraphs: Queer and trans Haitian, African francophone, and Euro-French Minnesotans exist. Conservative church, mosque, and family climates can mean silence.
Use the name. Do not out someone to family as culture.

Queer and trans Haitian, African francophone, and Euro-French Minnesotans exist. Conservative church, mosque, and family climates can mean silence or exile. Some people live a public English life and a private home-language life. You use the name they use. You do not out them to an elder as cultural humility.

### This person

Minnesota’s Human Rights Act still applies. So does the duty not to treat Haiti or “Africa” as a family-values exhibit.

Do not assume a Paris household is affirming. Do not assume a Port-au-Prince household is not. Ask this person.

sections.heading: Hair, Dress, and Body
paragraphs: Hair is political for many Black francophone people in Minnesota. Natural hair, braids, wraps, wigs — follow this person. CROWN Act still applies.
Do not touch. Do not ask to “see it out.” Do not treat a headwrap as a costume.

Hair is political for many Black francophone people in this state. Natural hair, braids, locs, wraps, wigs — follow this person. Minnesota’s CROWN Act still applies. Do not touch. Do not ask to “see it out.” Do not treat a headwrap as a costume.

### Dress

Euro-French dress codes are not the rule on this door. Do not police “professional” hair on Haitian or African staff.

Festival dress is public on some dates and not a daily uniform. Do not ask if they “still wear traditional clothes.”

sections.heading: Music
paragraphs: Kompa, rara, mbalax, Congolese rumba, church music, French pop — not one soundtrack. Not a festival booth.
A playlist is not engagement. Do not ask someone to perform.

Kompa and rara in Haitian public life; mbalax in Senegalese streams; Congolese rumba and ndombolo; church music; French pop. Not one soundtrack. Not a festival booth.

### Variation

A playlist is not engagement. Do not ask a client or a staff person to perform.

Sunday choir is operations for some Baptist and Catholic households. It is not consultation.

sections.heading: Sports
paragraphs: Soccer is public in many Haitian and African streams. Ordinary school sport in the second generation. Not language access.
Sport clubs are not a case plan.

Soccer is public in many Haitian and African francophone communities. Ordinary school sport is ordinary for the second generation. Neither is language access.

### Not the whole person

Do not use a national-team jersey as a case plan. Sport clubs are not a substitute for an interpreter or a notice.

A Saturday league in a southern town is not consultation. Book the home language for the parent who is in the stands and cannot run the IEP.

sections.heading: Literature
paragraphs: Haitian, Senegalese, Congolese, and French literary traditions exist. Kreyòl literature is literature. Oral and written both.
You do not need to quote Césaire. You need to know this is not a people without letters, and not one people.

Haitian literature in Kreyòl and French, Senegalese and Congolese and Cameroonian writing, and the French canon are not one shelf. Kreyòl literature is literature. Oral tradition is not the absence of letters.

### Literacy in the lobby

You do not need to quote Césaire, Chauvet, or a Paris syllabus. You need to know this door is not a people without letters, and not one people.

Do not put a proverb on a brochure and call it CLAS.

sections.heading: Art
paragraphs: Haitian painting, West and Central African cloth and mask traditions, Euro-French museum culture — not interchangeable, not a lobby display.
Guest. Do not mash into a generic “African art” table.

Haitian painting, sequined flags, West and Central African cloth and carving, Euro-French museum culture — not interchangeable. Do not mash them onto a generic “African art” Heritage Month table.

### Guest

Guest. Public festivals are not consultation. Do not extract a staff person’s child as entertainment.

Alliance Française gallery nights are a Euro-French civic door. They are not the service partner for a Haitian or Senegalese household unless that household names them.

sections.heading: Conflict, the State, and This Climate
paragraphs: Haitian Revolution 1804; U.S. occupation; 2010 earthquake; TPS. Colonial borders and wars in West and Central Africa. Enforcement climate now. A DHS badge is not automatically help.
Do not invent a briefing from a news clip. Do not collect status you do not need. Do not use 1804 or 2010 as a personality.

1804 is Haitian peoplehood. U.S. occupation, dictatorship, 2010, and TPS are U.S. and Haitian state history in the same file. Colonial borders and wars in West and Central Africa produced displacement and a school language. You do not invent a briefing from a news clip.

### The badge

Enforcement climate now — TPS uncertainty, raids in the news, a relative who can be moved — changes who opens the door. A DHS badge is not automatically help. Do not collect status you do not need. Do not treat fear as noncompliance.

Do not use 1804 or 2010 as a personality. Do not ask a person to narrate an earthquake or a war for your professional development.

sections.heading: Work, Business, and Government
paragraphs: Service, care work, professional class, students, small business — do not invent a Minnesota Francophone occupational census. Public employment exists.
Haitian and African staff are not unpaid interpreters. Identity is not a staffing plan.

Service, care work, plants in Greater Minnesota, professional class, students, small business. Do not invent a Minnesota Francophone occupational census. Compass has no such row. Pattern: people work here.

### Work

Haitian, Senegalese, Congolese, Cameroonian, and other African staff inside the department are not unpaid interpreters and not “the African community.” Identity is not a staffing plan.

### Staff

Relationship may precede a signature. That is not permission to skip a notice.

sections.heading: Health-care and Human-service Encounters
paragraphs: Home language vs school French; Kreyòl; who is in the room; TPS climate; anti-Blackness in the clinic; Vodou or church in the story.
Confirm the home language. Offer gender match. Believe reported pain. Do not collect status. Mandated reporting still exists.

Home language vs school French. Kreyòl. Lingala. Wolof. Who is in the room. Gender. TPS climate. Anti-Blackness in the clinic. A priest, an imam, or Vodou in the story.

### Language

Confirm the home language. Offer gender match. Believe reported pain. Do not collect status. Do not make staff the interpreter. Mandated reporting still exists.

### The meeting

A French consent form for a Kreyòl speaker is not consent. A smile is not consent. Name who the form was built for.

sections.heading: Adjacent Peoples — Do Not Mash
paragraphs: Not historic African American. Not Somali. Not one Africa. Not France as default. Haitian, Senegalese, Congolese, Cameroonian, Rwandan, Québécois are not interchangeable.
Never one Black module. Never one Francophone client. Ask this household.

Not historic African American. Not Somali. Not Oromo. Not Liberian. Not Nigerian. Not one Africa. Not France as default. Open those CIs for those households.

### Adjacent doors

Haitian, Senegalese, Malian, Guinean, Ivorian, Cameroonian, Congolese, Rwandan, Burundian, and Québécois households are not interchangeable. Some Somali households have French from Djibouti or camps — not the default. Ask this household.

Never one Black module. Never one Francophone client.

sections.heading: Counts, Dated — and what you may not invent
paragraphs: No Compass Francophone row. Do not invent a census. Star Tribune July 31, 2025: French ~2% of Minnesotans who speak a language other than English at home (with German, Chinese, Russian, Arabic). Date that language share.
A language share is not a people. A rate you do not have is not a rate you may invent.

There is no Minnesota Compass cultural-community row for French, Haitian, Senegalese, or “Francophone.” Do not invent a census. Do not borrow Compass African American, Somali, or Kenyan counts and file them here.

### Counts

Star Tribune, July 31, 2025, on languages spoken at home in Minnesota: among people who speak a language other than English at home, German, French, Chinese, Russian, and Arabic each represent about 2 percent of that group. Date it. That is a language share. It does not tell you home language vs school language. It does not disaggregate Kreyòl. Kreyòl may be coded elsewhere or missed. Name the gap.

### What the count is not

School-language and interpreter-request data in a county are a pattern when you have them. Date them. A rate you do not have is not a rate you may put on this page.

sections.heading: Doors and Sources
paragraphs: Star Tribune July 31, 2025 languages-at-home. CLAS fifteen: French. Book Kreyòl, Lingala, Wolof, or the language they name when that is home. Haitian and African community associations this person names. CECLC is a door, not the whole.
Learn on your own time. Do not make a Haitian or Senegalese colleague your unpaid tutor. Pay partners. Book the home language.

Star Tribune, July 31, 2025, languages spoken at home. CLAS fifteen: French. Book Kreyòl when Kreyòl is home. Book Lingala, Wolof, Bambara, or Kinyarwanda when that is home. A French interpreter can still be the wrong door.

### Public doors

Haitian, West African, and Central African associations this person names. Churches and mosques this person names. Alliance Française is a Euro-French civic door — use it if they name it, not as the default partner.

### Learn on your own time

CECLC is a door, not the whole. Learn on your own time. Do not make a Haitian or Senegalese colleague your unpaid tutor. Pay partners. Report back.

sections.heading: How it hits DHS gates — the 40%
paragraphs: Which language is actually home; Kreyòl vs French; Lingala vs French; assuming France; assuming Africa; assuming Haiti; one Francophone client; harvesting staff; TPS/enforcement climate; eList comment periods.

Ask which language is home. Put that language on the line. Toolkit disposition on the packet. If the family cannot run the exception in the language they use, the cap is the policy. Statute may still stand. Name who the packet was built for.

Workplace culture and service delivery are both candidates.

Language: a French interpreter for a Kreyòl household is a closed door. A French interpreter for a Lingala or Wolof household can be a closed door. “African French” is not a dialect you may invent. Gender match may be requested in maternal and intimate care.

Names: the database that invents a last name or “corrects” Kreyòl spelling to Paris French is a gate.

Hour caps, exception processes, and life-sharing matches without the home language are not culturally neutral. An English IEP is a gate. A French packet when home is Kreyòl is a gate.

One Francophone client: Haiti is not Africa. Africa is not France. France is not Haiti. Folding a Haitian household into historic African American CI because both are Black is a closed gate with a polite label. Open the right page.

Enforcement and TPS climate: people skip clinic, school, and waiver meetings when a relative can be moved. That is not noncompliance. Do not collect status you do not need.

Notices and comment: an eList and an English PDF is not how these households were reached. Empty follow-up cells are theater.

Workforce: Haitian and African francophone staff are not the interpreter pool and not the community.

Legislation, funding, rule: you cannot advocate for a channel you will not study. This cultural intelligence exists so the 40% has a household in it — not a paternalistic program designed in a building that never asked which French, or whether French was home at all.

chapters.body:
This brief is a language door, not a people. “French-speaking Minnesota” names a CLAS fifteen line and a set of households who may use French at school, at the clinic, or with the state — and who often use another language at home. Ask which French, and whether another language is actually the home language.

### Who this is

Streams that are not interchangeable: Haiti, where Kreyòl (Haitian Creole) is often the home language and French the school or official language; West and Central Africa, where Wolof, Bambara, Lingala, Kinyarwanda, and many others may be home and French the colonial/school language; France, Belgium, Quebec, and other European or North American streams — smaller in Minnesota services, real; some Somali and other Horn households with French from Djibouti or camps — not the default.

### Who this is not

This is not historic African American CI with a different flag. It is not Somali. It is not one Africa. It is not France. Do not assume Africa. Do not assume France. Do not assume Haiti. A full mosaic is not a stereotype. A stereotype is when this page becomes the person in the lobby.

### How to read this

There is no Minnesota Compass cultural-community row for “French” or “Francophone.” Do not invent a census. Star Tribune (July 31, 2025): among people in Minnesota who speak a language other than English at home, French is among the languages — with German, Chinese, Russian, and Arabic — each representing about 2 percent of that group. Date it. That is a language share. It is not a Haitian count, not a Senegalese count, not a Québécois count.

The diversity inside the door is the point. A Kreyòl-speaking mother, a Lingala-speaking father from Kinshasa who uses French with the school, a Dakar household that wants Wolof, a Quebecois professional, a French national on a campus, a Djiboutian elder who has French from a camp — do not share a Tuesday.

Always defer to the person in front of you. This page is a hypothesis you still test on this family.
chapters.evidence: French-speaking Minnesota is a language door, not a people. Haiti / Kreyòl; West and Central Africa; France / Belgium / Quebec; a few Horn households with French from Djibouti or camps. Star Tribune 2025: French ~2% of the non-English-at-home group. Date it. Do not invent a Francophone census.
chapters.practitioner: Ask which French, and whether another language is actually home. Book Kreyòl if that is the home language. Do not open African American or Somali with this page unless that is the household.
chapters.title: A Note on This Guide

chapters.body:
Haitian peoplehood is not an African checkbox and not a French checkbox. The Haitian Revolution reached independence on January 1, 1804 — the first Black republic in the hemisphere. U.S. occupation (1915–1934), dictatorships, the 2010 earthquake, and later TPS designations are Haitian history. Kreyòl is the home language of the people. French was the colonial and school language. Book Kreyòl if that is the home language.

### History for the meeting

West and Central Africa are many nations and many peoples under a French school language left by colonization: Senegal, Mali, Guinea, Côte d’Ivoire, Cameroon, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Congo-Brazzaville, francophone Rwanda and Burundi, and others. Wolof, Bambara, Lingala, Kinyarwanda, Fulani, and more may be what the grandmother actually speaks. An “African French” interpreter can still be the wrong door.

### What people brought

France, Belgium, Switzerland, and Quebec are European and North American streams. They are smaller in Minnesota human services. They are real. Do not assume Africa when the household is Paris. Do not assume Paris when the household is Port-au-Prince or Yaoundé.

Some Somali and other Horn households have French from Djibouti, from camps, or from a third country. That is not the default for Somali Minnesota. Open Somali for Somali. Ask about French if they name it.
chapters.evidence: Haitian peoplehood is 1804 and a Caribbean history, not an African checkbox. West and Central African nations are many peoples under a colonial school language. France / Belgium / Quebec are European and North American streams.
chapters.practitioner: History is literacy for the desk. It is not a speech you give the family. Do not assume Africa. Do not assume France. Do not assume Haiti.
chapters.title: Origins — several peoples, one colonial language

chapters.body:
Haiti is Caribbean. Dakar, Bamako, Abidjan, Yaoundé, Kinshasa, Brazzaville, Kigali, Bujumbura are African cities with different languages under the French door. Paris, Brussels, Montreal are not those cities.

### Homeland

Minnesota is a present. Twin Cities and Greater Minnesota both. Do not assume Minneapolis. Plant towns, student neighborhoods, and inner-ring suburbs can all hold a household on this door.

### Minnesota

There is no Compass map for this umbrella. Date any town-level school-language count when a professional has it. Pattern now: people are here. Do not invent a county number.
chapters.evidence: Haiti; Senegal, Mali, Guinea, Côte d’Ivoire, Cameroon, DRC, Congo-Brazzaville, francophone Rwanda/Burundi, and others; France, Belgium, Quebec. Minnesota is a present. No Compass map for this umbrella.
chapters.practitioner: Do not assume Minneapolis. Do not assume they have been to Paris. Name the country they name.
chapters.title: The Geography of French as a Door

chapters.body:
Haiti: 1804 is peoplehood. The U.S. occupied Haiti from 1915 to 1934. The January 12, 2010 earthquake killed on a scale this building should not turn into a speech. Temporary Protected Status for Haiti was first designated after that earthquake and has been extended, terminated, and redesignated in later years — including after the 2021 assassination of President Jovenel Moïse and another earthquake. Date the designation you mean. Do not invent this person’s status. Do not collect status you do not need.

### Foundational events

West and Central African migration into Minnesota includes students, skilled workers, family, and people displaced by conflict. French is often the language a school left them, not the language of the kitchen. Colonial borders and later wars are literacy. They are not a news-clip briefing you give the family.

### Who you meet

Euro-French, Belgian, and Quebec streams arrive as professionals, students, and family. Smaller in the service lobby, real. Do not run a refugee script on a Lyon household. Do not run a Paris script on a Cap-Haïtien household.

If you only know “French,” you will miss Kreyòl, miss Lingala, and mash a people.
chapters.evidence: Haiti: revolution 1804, U.S. occupation 1915–1934, 2010 earthquake, TPS. West and Central Africa: colonial school language plus later displacement and skilled migration. Euro-French and Quebec streams are smaller in MN services, real.
chapters.practitioner: If you only know “French,” you will book the wrong interpreter and the wrong CI. TPS climate is current structure. Do not collect status you do not need.
chapters.title: 1804, Occupation, Earthquake, Colonies, and TPS — Foundational Events

chapters.body:
Extended household is common in many Haitian and West/Central African streams. Godparents, church sisters, mosque kin, and cousins who are “auntie” on Tuesday may not match the waiver checkbox. Ask who should be in the room.

### Who is in the household

Euro-French nuclear grammar is not the default for this door. Do not import it.

### Who speaks

Who cares for the child, who holds the lease, and who can sign may not be the same adult. Mixed-status households exist in Haitian and some African streams. Do not collect status you do not need.

Minnesota law still stands. Do not skip mandated reporting and call it culture. Do not turn a family argument into a national personality.
chapters.evidence: Extended households in many Haitian and West/Central African streams. Godparent and church or mosque kin. Euro-French nuclear forms are not the default for this door.
chapters.practitioner: Ask who should be in the room. A nuclear English form already has a who. Do not assume a Paris family grammar in a Port-au-Prince or Dakar household.
chapters.title: Family

chapters.body:
This department will meet these households on waivers, child welfare, health care, cash, food, aging, TPS-adjacent fear, and employment. Twin Cities and Greater Minnesota. Rural is not an afterthought when the plant or the college is the draw.

### Places

Churches (Catholic and Protestant) and mosques are often the actual information channel. Parish and mosque are not “the community.” They are a door if this family names them.

### Partners

Alliance Française and campus French clubs are Euro-French civic and student doors. They are not the service partner for a Haitian or Senegalese household unless that household names them. Do not BCC a conversation group and call it consultation.

Do not make Haitian, Senegalese, Congolese, or Cameroonian staff the interpreter pool or “the African voice.”
chapters.evidence: Twin Cities and Greater Minnesota both. Churches, mosques, and community associations are often the information channel. Alliance Française is a Euro-French civic door — not the service door for a Haitian or Senegalese household unless they name it.
chapters.practitioner: Pay the door this person names. Staff are colleagues, not the curriculum. Do not treat  Haitian or African staff. A festival is not consultation.
chapters.title: Minnesota and This Language Door

chapters.body:
To be filed under French in Minnesota is often to be asked whether you are from France, or from Africa, as if those were two rooms and Haiti were in one of them.

### In this state

Anti-Blackness in this state hits Haitian and African francophone people in the lobby, the clinic, and the traffic stop. That is not a reason to open historic African American CI and stop. Open African American for a Great Migration household. Open this for a Haitian or Senegalese household. Open Somali for Somali. Shared race in the United States is not shared culture. Shared French class in a colonial school is not shared culture.

Colorism sits inside some Haitian and West African families and inside Minnesota’s racial order. You do not lecture it. You do not pretend it is absent.

This guide is a working orientation. Individual variation always supersedes group generalization.
chapters.evidence: A shared colonial language is not a people. Anti-Blackness in Minnesota hits Haitian and African francophone people and is not the same file as historic African American CI.
chapters.practitioner: Open African American for a Great Migration household. Open this for a Haitian or Senegalese household. Open Somali for Somali. Never one Black module.
chapters.title: A language door, not a people mash

chapters.body:
Home language is the first grammar. French may be school. Kreyòl, Lingala, Wolof, Bambara, or Kinyarwanda may be home. Book home.

### One Francophone client is a mash

Haiti is not Senegal. DRC is not Cameroon. Quebec is not Port-au-Prince.

### Colorism and anti-Blackness

Both can be in the room. Neither is a personality.

### Church or mosque as channel

Not the case plan unless they asked.

### TPS and enforcement climate

People skip clinic and waiver meetings when a relative can be moved. That is not noncompliance.

### Respect and titles in many streams

Do not force first-name familiarity on an elder.
chapters.evidence: Which language is home. Kreyòl vs French. Lingala, Wolof, Bambara, Kinyarwanda vs French. Colorism. Church or mosque as channel. TPS and enforcement as climate.
chapters.practitioner: You work with these. You do not perform them. Book the home language. Do not use “Francophone Africa” as a personality.
chapters.title: Core Concepts

chapters.body:
Catholic Christianity is large in Haiti and in parts of West and Central Africa and in Euro-French streams. Protestant and evangelical churches are ordinary too. Islam is ordinary in much of West Africa and present in some Haitian households. None is real.

### Streams

Vodou is a Haitian religious fact in some households. Do not sensationalize it. Do not treat it as horror-film content, as witchcraft for the file, or as the “real” Haiti. Do not make a Vodou priest the case plan unless this family asked. The same rule for a Catholic priest or an imam.

### Practice

Do not assume a mosque because the passport is West African. Do not assume a cathedral because the language is French.
chapters.evidence: Catholic, Muslim (West Africa, some Haiti), Protestant, Vodou in some Haitian households (do not sensationalize), none.
chapters.practitioner: Do not make a priest, an imam, or a Vodou priest the case plan unless this family asked. Do not treat Vodou as horror-film content.
chapters.title: Religion

chapters.body:
French vous vs tu is a formality system some Euro-French and African school-French speakers use. Kreyòl greetings are not that system. Wolof and Lingala greetings are not that system. Follow this room.

### Titles

Elders and titles in many Haitian and African streams. Handshake in many professional rooms. Do not force a hug.

### This room

Do not import a Paris rule onto a Haitian elder. Do not import a Port-au-Prince manner onto a Lille professional. Do not import the Black nod or Somali right-hand rules unless this person is on those pages.

Physical contact: ask the room. Cross-gender touch with elders is not a default.
chapters.evidence: French vous/tu, Kreyòl greetings, Wolof and Lingala greetings — not one script. Elders and titles in many streams. Handshake in many professional rooms.
chapters.practitioner: Follow this room. Do not force familiarity. Do not import a Paris rule onto a Haitian elder or a Bamako mother.
chapters.title: Greetings

chapters.body:
French-style given name plus family name appears in some streams. Haitian naming may not match first-middle-last. West African naming may include a day name, a Muslim name, a family name, or a French school name that is not what the grandmother uses. Ask how to say it. Ask how to file it.

### How to file

Do not invent a last name. Do not “correct” Kreyòl or Wolof spelling to Paris French. Do not treat unmatched last names in a household as fraud by default.

A child may have a different school name than the name on the birth record. Ask. Do not humiliate.
chapters.evidence: French-style given name plus family name in some streams; Haitian and West African naming that does not match first-middle-last; Muslim names in some West African and some Haitian households.
chapters.practitioner: Ask how to say it and how to file it. Do not invent a last name. Do not “correct” spelling to Paris French.
chapters.title: Naming Conventions

chapters.body:
January 1 — Haitian Independence Day, 1804. Literacy. Not a day off the work unless this family names it. Not Bastille Day.

### Calendar

January 12, 2010 — Haiti earthquake. TPS history starts here for many families. Literacy. Not a speech.

West African independence dates vary by country (1960 is a cluster, not a single day). Catholic calendars, Ramadan and Eid in Muslim households, and national days this family names — ask. Do not put Bastille Day (July 14) on a Haitian or Senegalese case note.

A calendar click is not community engagement.
chapters.evidence: Haitian Independence Day January 1, 1804. 2010 earthquake. West African independence dates vary by country. Catholic and Muslim calendars. Bastille Day is not this household’s day unless they say so.
chapters.practitioner: A calendar click is literacy. It is not community engagement. Do not put Bastille Day on a Haitian case note.
chapters.title: Dates of Significance

chapters.body:
French as a school or official language does not mean French is the home language, and does not mean the parent can run an English IEP. Literacy in any language of the form is not guaranteed. Interrupted schooling in Haiti after 2010, or in a conflict region, is structure.

### School and language

A parent who speaks fluent Kreyòl, Wolof, or Lingala and limited English is not illiterate. The English-only form is the gate. So is a French form when the home language is Kreyòl.

Second-generation English is common. CLAS still says do not use minors as interpreters. Book the home language.

Do not invent a Minnesota Francophone attainment rate. Compass has no such row.
chapters.evidence: French as school/official language does not mean French is home, and does not mean the parent can run an English IEP. Literacy in the form language is not guaranteed.
chapters.practitioner: A parent who speaks fluent Kreyòl or Wolof and limited English is not illiterate. Book the home language. The English-only packet is the gate.
chapters.title: Education

chapters.body:
Titles and elders in many Haitian and African streams. Hospitality is a virtue in many rooms. You still keep medical and legal time.

### In the home

Do not assume a French-restaurant manner — wine, first names after one meeting, cheek kisses — is the rule in this living room. Do not assume the absence of that manner is “less educated.”

### Time

Shoes, food, and Sunday church or Friday mosque will vary. Ask. On-time for appointments is a professional default for some and a bus-and-shift problem for others.

Courtesy-yes then no-show happens when the plan was never agreed. Ask whether they agree. Confirm in the language they use.
chapters.evidence: Titles, elders, hospitality, church and mosque time. Variation across Haiti, West Africa, Central Africa, and Europe is the point.
chapters.practitioner: Accept a little food. Keep medical and legal time. Do not assume a French-restaurant manner is the rule in this living room.
chapters.title: Etiquette

chapters.body:
Ask which language is actually home. Book that language.

### Language

Kreyòl is not French. A French interpreter for a Kreyòl household is a closed door. Lingala is not French. Wolof is not French. Bambara is not French. Kinyarwanda is not French. An interpreter billed as “African French” can still be the wrong country, the wrong register, and the wrong language.

French itself is not one French. Haitian school French, Dakar French, Kinshasa French, and Paris French differ in accent and vocabulary. Mutual understanding is often possible and not guaranteed. Ask.

Star Tribune (July 31, 2025): French is about 2 percent of the non-English-at-home group in Minnesota, listed with German, Chinese, Russian, and Arabic. Date it. That share does not tell you which French, or whether French is home.

A short English yes may be exhaustion or courtesy. Do not take a smile as consent. Do not make a Francophone coworker the interpreter.
chapters.evidence: Ask which language is actually home. Kreyòl vs French. Lingala vs French. Wolof, Bambara, Kinyarwanda. An “African French” interpreter can still be the wrong door. Star Tribune 2025: French ~2% of non-English-at-home.
chapters.practitioner: Put the home language on the line. Do not take a smile as consent. Staff are colleagues, not the curriculum. Do not treat  a Francophone coworker.
chapters.title: Language and Communication

chapters.body:
Unvarnished, because Minnesota Nice is how a room that treats everyone the same deletes facts.

### Named harms

Anti-Blackness in Minnesota hits Haitian and African francophone people. Traffic stops, clinic dismissal, and “where are you really from” are structure. Do not fold this household into historic African American CI because both are Black — and do not pretend anti-Blackness is absent because the passport is Haitian or Senegalese.

Colorism inside families and in the U.S. racial order is real. You do not lecture it. You do not skip it when it is the harm in the room.

LGBTQ Haitian and African francophone Minnesotans exist. Enforcement and TPS climate is current structure. People skip clinic, school, and waiver meetings. That is not noncompliance. Do not collect status you do not need.

One Francophone client is how treating everyone the same hides difference. Haiti is not Africa. Africa is not France. France is not Haiti.

Staff who share this community may add facts. They do not get to delete a fact because it is hard to say.
chapters.evidence: Anti-Blackness in Minnesota; do not fold into historic African American CI; colorism; LGBTQ exist; enforcement and TPS climate; one Francophone client is a mash.
chapters.practitioner: Do not collect status you do not need. Do not skip mandated reporting and call it humility. Do not out anyone. Open the right CI.
chapters.title: Other Considerations

chapters.body:
Language is the first health gate. A French consent form for a Kreyòl speaker is not consent. A smile is not consent.

### Access

Trauma and displacement in some Haitian and African streams are real. Do not invent a Minnesota Francophone PTSD rate. Do not skip screening. Do not make earthquake or war a personality.

Believe reported pain. Anti-Blackness in U.S. medicine is documented. Do not mash Tuskegee onto a Port-au-Prince or Dakar history; do not pretend the clinic is neutral.

Gender match may be requested in maternal and intimate care. Offer it. If they name a healer, a priest, or an imam, listen. Do not make that person the case plan unless they asked.
chapters.evidence: Language is the first health gate. Trauma and displacement in some Haitian and African streams. Do not invent a Minnesota Francophone rate.
chapters.practitioner: Book the home language. Offer gender match. Believe reported pain. Do not mash Tuskegee onto a Port-au-Prince or Dakar history.
chapters.title: Health

chapters.body:
Queer and trans Haitian, African francophone, and Euro-French Minnesotans exist. Conservative church, mosque, and family climates can mean silence or exile. Some people live a public English life and a private home-language life. You use the name they use. You do not out them to an elder as cultural humility.

### This person

Minnesota’s Human Rights Act still applies. So does the duty not to treat Haiti or “Africa” as a family-values exhibit.

Do not assume a Paris household is affirming. Do not assume a Port-au-Prince household is not. Ask this person.
chapters.evidence: Queer and trans Haitian, African francophone, and Euro-French Minnesotans exist. Conservative church, mosque, and family climates can mean silence.
chapters.practitioner: Use the name. Do not out someone to family as culture.
chapters.title: LGBTQ

chapters.body:
Hair is political for many Black francophone people in this state. Natural hair, braids, locs, wraps, wigs — follow this person. Minnesota’s CROWN Act still applies. Do not touch. Do not ask to “see it out.” Do not treat a headwrap as a costume.

### Dress

Euro-French dress codes are not the rule on this door. Do not police “professional” hair on Haitian or African staff.

Festival dress is public on some dates and not a daily uniform. Do not ask if they “still wear traditional clothes.”
chapters.evidence: Hair is political for many Black francophone people in Minnesota. Natural hair, braids, wraps, wigs — follow this person. CROWN Act still applies.
chapters.practitioner: Do not touch. Do not ask to “see it out.” Do not treat a headwrap as a costume.
chapters.title: Hair, Dress, and Body

chapters.body:
Kompa and rara in Haitian public life; mbalax in Senegalese streams; Congolese rumba and ndombolo; church music; French pop. Not one soundtrack. Not a festival booth.

### Variation

A playlist is not engagement. Do not ask a client or a staff person to perform.

Sunday choir is operations for some Baptist and Catholic households. It is not consultation.
chapters.evidence: Kompa, rara, mbalax, Congolese rumba, church music, French pop — not one soundtrack. Not a festival booth.
chapters.practitioner: A playlist is not engagement. Do not ask someone to perform.
chapters.title: Music

chapters.body:
Soccer is public in many Haitian and African francophone communities. Ordinary school sport is ordinary for the second generation. Neither is language access.

### Not the whole person

Do not use a national-team jersey as a case plan. Sport clubs are not a substitute for an interpreter or a notice.

A Saturday league in a southern town is not consultation. Book the home language for the parent who is in the stands and cannot run the IEP.
chapters.evidence: Soccer is public in many Haitian and African streams. Ordinary school sport in the second generation. Not language access.
chapters.practitioner: Sport clubs are not a case plan.

chapters.body:
Haitian literature in Kreyòl and French, Senegalese and Congolese and Cameroonian writing, and the French canon are not one shelf. Kreyòl literature is literature. Oral tradition is not the absence of letters.

### Literacy in the lobby

You do not need to quote Césaire, Chauvet, or a Paris syllabus. You need to know this door is not a people without letters, and not one people.

Do not put a proverb on a brochure and call it CLAS.
chapters.evidence: Haitian, Senegalese, Congolese, and French literary traditions exist. Kreyòl literature is literature. Oral and written both.
chapters.practitioner: You do not need to quote Césaire. You need to know this is not a people without letters, and not one people.
chapters.title: Literature

chapters.body:
Haitian painting, sequined flags, West and Central African cloth and carving, Euro-French museum culture — not interchangeable. Do not mash them onto a generic “African art” Heritage Month table.

### Guest

Guest. Public festivals are not consultation. Do not extract a staff person’s child as entertainment.

Alliance Française gallery nights are a Euro-French civic door. They are not the service partner for a Haitian or Senegalese household unless that household names them.

1804 is Haitian peoplehood. U.S. occupation, dictatorship, 2010, and TPS are U.S. and Haitian state history in the same file. Colonial borders and wars in West and Central Africa produced displacement and a school language. You do not invent a briefing from a news clip.

### The badge

Enforcement climate now — TPS uncertainty, raids in the news, a relative who can be moved — changes who opens the door. A DHS badge is not automatically help. Do not collect status you do not need. Do not treat fear as noncompliance.

Do not use 1804 or 2010 as a personality. Do not ask a person to narrate an earthquake or a war for your professional development.

Service, care work, plants in Greater Minnesota, professional class, students, small business. Do not invent a Minnesota Francophone occupational census. Compass has no such row. Pattern: people work here.

### Work

Haitian, Senegalese, Congolese, Cameroonian, and other African staff inside the department are not unpaid interpreters and not “the African community.” Identity is not a staffing plan.

### Staff

Relationship may precede a signature. That is not permission to skip a notice.

### Language

Not historic African American. Not Somali. Not Oromo. Not Liberian. Not Nigerian. Not one Africa. Not France as default. Open those CIs for those households.

### Adjacent doors

Haitian, Senegalese, Malian, Guinean, Ivorian, Cameroonian, Congolese, Rwandan, Burundian, and Québécois households are not interchangeable. Some Somali households have French from Djibouti or camps — not the default. Ask this household.

chapters.title: Adjacent Peoples — Do Not Mash

chapters.body:
There is no Minnesota Compass cultural-community row for French, Haitian, Senegalese, or “Francophone.” Do not invent a census. Do not borrow Compass African American, Somali, or Kenyan counts and file them here.

### Counts

Star Tribune, July 31, 2025, on languages spoken at home in Minnesota: among people who speak a language other than English at home, German, French, Chinese, Russian, and Arabic each represent about 2 percent of that group. Date it. That is a language share. It does not tell you home language vs school language. It does not disaggregate Kreyòl. Kreyòl may be coded elsewhere or missed. Name the gap.

### What the count is not

School-language and interpreter-request data in a county are a pattern when you have them. Date them. A rate you do not have is not a rate you may put on this page.
chapters.evidence: No Compass Francophone row. Do not invent a census. Star Tribune July 31, 2025: French ~2% of Minnesotans who speak a language other than English at home (with German, Chinese, Russian, Arabic). Date that language share.
chapters.practitioner: A language share is not a people. A rate you do not have is not a rate you may invent.
chapters.title: Counts, Dated — and what you may not invent

chapters.body:
Star Tribune, July 31, 2025, languages spoken at home. CLAS fifteen: French. Book Kreyòl when Kreyòl is home. Book Lingala, Wolof, Bambara, or Kinyarwanda when that is home. A French interpreter can still be the wrong door.

### Public doors

Haitian, West African, and Central African associations this person names. Churches and mosques this person names. Alliance Française is a Euro-French civic door — use it if they name it, not as the default partner.

### Learn on your own time

CECLC is a door, not the whole. Learn on your own time. Do not make a Haitian or Senegalese colleague your unpaid tutor. Pay partners. Report back.

chapters.title: Doors and Sources

chapters.body:
Workplace culture and service delivery are both candidates.

Language: a French interpreter for a Kreyòl household is a closed door. A French interpreter for a Lingala or Wolof household can be a closed door. “African French” is not a dialect you may invent. Gender match may be requested in maternal and intimate care.

Names: the database that invents a last name or “corrects” Kreyòl spelling to Paris French is a gate.

sections.heading: A Note on This Guide
paragraphs: Burmese Minnesota: Compass ACS 2019–2023 17,123 is an administrative umbrella. Bamar, and possibly Chin, Kachin, Rohingya, Mon, Karen overlapping. Census recodes some Karen as Burmese. Not “Asian.” CLAS fifteen: Burmese.

There is no single Burmese client. Defer to this family. If Karen, open Karen Minnesota and put S’gaw or Pwo on the line. If Chin, book Chin (Hakha, Falam, etc.). If Rohingya, Rohingya / Bengali may be the language — not Burmese by default.

This brief is about Burmese Minnesota as a people-page and as a warning about an umbrella. CLAS fifteen interpreter cards say Burmese. Minnesota Compass (ACS 2019–2023) says Burmese 17,123. Both are operations and a U.S. administrative name. They are not a people.

### Who this is

Not Karen as a synonym. Not Chin as a synonym. Not Kachin, not Mon, not Rohingya, not “Asian.” Compass Burmese can include Bamar — the majority people of Myanmar, often called Burman — and may overlap or sit beside Chin, Kachin, Rohingya, Mon, Karen. Compass methodology: the Census recodes some people who write Karen into Burmese, with nothing left to show the original response. Ask the people. If the household is Karen, open Karen Minnesota and put S’gaw or Pwo on the line. If Chin, book Chin — Hakha, Falam, or the variety they name. If Rohingya, Rohingya or Bengali may be the language. Burmese is not the default.

### Who this is not

Compass, dated: Twin Cities 79.9 percent, Greater Minnesota 20.1 percent. Age 17 or younger 41.5 percent; 65+ 4.2 percent. Foreign-born 67.1 percent. Language other than English (age 5+) 89.6 percent. English less than “very well” 67.0 percent — a severe language gate. High school or higher among 25+ 32.8 percent; bachelor’s or higher 11.8 percent. Median household about $75,513. Poverty 29.6 percent. Owner-occupied 59.0 percent. Average household size 4.99. Disability 12.9 percent. Date Compass. A rate is not the person.

The diversity inside the umbrella is the point. A Bamar Buddhist elder who reads Myanmar script, a Hakha Chin Christian plant worker in Worthington, a S’gaw Karen household that should have opened the Karen page, a Rohingya family who should not have been booked Burmese, a U.S.-born teenager who uses English with friends and still translates a 67-percent-LEP parent — share a country checkbox and do not share a Tuesday.

### How to read this

Always defer to the person in front of you. This page is a hypothesis you still test on this family.

sections.heading: Origins and the Founding of a People
paragraphs: Bamar majority in Myanmar; many other peoples. British colonial; independence 1948; military rule. Burmese (Myanmar language) is tonal with its own script. Not one people inside the country checkbox.
History is literacy for the desk. It is not a speech you give the family. Do not start with a golden-pagoda souvenir.

Bamar peoplehood on the Irrawaddy is older than the British and older than the junta. Theravada Buddhism, Burmese as a tonal language with its own script, wet-rice agriculture, and a sequence of kingdoms organized a majority that is not the whole country. Chin, Kachin, Karen, Karenni, Mon, Rakhine, Rohingya, Shan, and others are peoples, not dialects. The country checkbox that says Burma or Myanmar is already a mash.

### History for the meeting

British colonial rule, independence in 1948, and decades of military government produced the file this desk meets. 1988. 2007. 2017 in Rakhine. 2021 coup — current structure. Camps in Thailand and Bangladesh are not a personality. They are years of interrupted school, interrupted care, and a kinship the form cannot see.

### What people brought

What people brought: language (maybe Burmese, maybe not), church or monastery or mosque, large household, farming and plant skill, a memory of being hunted by a state. What they met in Minnesota: an English form, one “Asian” checkbox, and often one interpreter labeled Burmese for a household that is Chin or Karen.

sections.heading: The Geography of the Burmese World
paragraphs: Myanmar; camps in Thailand and Bangladesh. Compass Burmese: 79.9% Twin Cities, 20.1% Greater Minnesota. Worthington, Albert Lea, Austin, Marshall, Willmar are a Karen/Burmese pattern. Do not assume St. Paul.
Name the town. Rural is not an afterthought. Do not assume they have been to Yangon.

Homeland is Myanmar — Yangon, Mandalay, the Delta, the hills, Chin State, Kachin State, Kayin, Rakhine. Do not draw one pagoda on a case note. Camps in Thailand (Mae La and others) and in Bangladesh (Cox’s Bazar and others) are origin-of-arrival for many Minnesota families. Years. Not a layover.

### Homeland

The U.S. map is not only Minnesota: Indiana, New York, Texas, California, and others hold Burma-origin communities. Minnesota is a real resettlement and secondary-migration state, including Greater Minnesota.

### Minnesota

In Minnesota: Compass Burmese 79.9 percent Twin Cities, 20.1 percent Greater Minnesota. Name the town. Worthington, Albert Lea, Austin, Marshall, and Willmar are a Karen/Burmese pattern in public telling (MSP Magazine on Minnesota’s refugee history names those towns for Karen). Do not assume St. Paul. Do not assume the person in front of you has been to Yangon. A Worthington household is not a Minneapolis default.

sections.heading: Military Rule, Camps, 2017, 2021 — Foundational Events
paragraphs: Military rule; 1988; 2007; 2017 Rohingya atrocities; 2021 coup as current structure. Camps. U.S. resettlement including Greater Minnesota. MSP Mag: Burma-origin refugees from 1993, most named as Karen in that telling.
If you only know “refugee,” you will miss the U.S.-born child and still fail the 67% LEP gate for the parent. Do not ask a Rohingya survivor to narrate the village for your chart.

If 1975 is Hmong Minnesota and 1991 is Somali Minnesota, military rule, the camps, and the later coups are the foundational events of Burma-origin Minnesota. They are not one event and not one people.

### Foundational events

MSP Magazine’s state refugee timeline: refugees from Burma arrive in Minnesota in 1993, most of them named as Karen in that telling. Later waves include Chin, Bamar, and others. 2017 Rohingya atrocities — mass killing, rape, and expulsion, named as genocide by the United States in 2022 — produced a specific flight. 2021 military coup is current structure: kin still there, remittance, silence, status anxiety here.

### Who you meet

Camps in Thailand and Bangladesh shaped literacy, time, and who counts as family. U.S. resettlement scattered people; secondary migration and church networks pulled some to Minnesota, including plant towns.

The desk in 2026 meets U.S.-born children and a parent facing a 67 percent LEP gate. If you only know “refugee,” you will miss the 18-year-old and still fail the form for the elder. Do not ask a Rohingya survivor to narrate the village for your chart.

### Who is in the household

### Who speaks

Women’s labor — plant, care, second-generation school — sits next to a household in which an elder may still be named as head. Both can be true.

Do not skip mandated reporting and call it culture. Minnesota law still stands. A nuclear two-parent English form already has a who. It was built for a different household.

### Places

Places, not a blob: Twin Cities; Roseville as a Karen Organization of Minnesota address (a Karen door); Greater Minnesota plant towns — Worthington, Albert Lea, Austin, Marshall, Willmar among those named in public Karen/Burmese telling. There is not one heart under this umbrella. Bamar Theravada life, Chin Christian hill life, Karen Baptist or Buddhist life, Rohingya Muslim life — these are peoples. The U.S. file that recodes Karen as Burmese is how a census becomes a closed door.

### In this state

In Minnesota it sits inside another fact: Asian in a checkbox that also holds Hmong, Chinese, Indian, and Korean histories they do not share; camp years; Greater Minnesota isolation for some; a language gate at 67 percent LEP.

This guide is a working orientation. Individual variation always supersedes group generalization. Ask who is actually in the room.

Burmese is tonal with Myanmar script. Hakha, Falam, S’gaw, Pwo, Rohingya/Bengali are not Burmese. 67 percent LEP is the gate. Literacy in any script is not guaranteed.

Information channel for some. Not the case plan unless they asked. Sunday and moon days are operations.

Muslim Rohingya. Mosque, Ramadan, halal. Do not copy Somali Islam blindly; do not assume Burmese is the language. Ask.

sections.heading: Greetings
paragraphs: Elders first. Mingalaba in Burmese. A slight bow or nod with elders. Handshake in many English rooms — ask.
Do not force a handshake. Do not import Somali or Hmong greeting rules. Follow this room. Say the name.

Elders first. A slight bow or nod with an older person is safer than a hard handshake you assume is universal. Mingalaba is a common Burmese greeting. English hello is ordinary in many rooms and in the second generation. Chin and Karen greetings are not Burmese. Follow this room.

### Titles

Say the name. Ask how to say it. Do not force a hand. Cross-gender touch with elders is not a default. Do not import Somali right-hand rules or Hmong nyob zoo onto this page unless this person uses them.

### This room

Do not open with the junta. Do not open with “I have a Karen friend” if this household is not Karen.

sections.heading: Naming Conventions
paragraphs: Myanmar naming often has no family surname as the database wants. Honorifics (U, Daw) in some Bamar rooms. Chin and Karen naming differ. Ask.
Ask how to say it. Do not invent a last name because the screen requires one. Do not treat unmatched names as fraud by default.

Myanmar Bamar naming often has no family surname as the database wants. Personal names may be one, two, or more syllables. Honorifics U (for a man) and Daw (for a woman) in some rooms — titles, not first names. Do not invent a last name because the screen requires one. That invented name becomes a gate.

### How to file

Chin and Karen naming differ — clan, baptismal, and English names exist in those streams. Rohingya naming may follow a different Muslim pattern. Ask how to file. Ask how to say it.

Do not “correct” a mother and child who do not share a last name as a fraud signal until you have a reason. The form that demands first-middle-last and a hyphen will invent a person.

Buddhist moon days are operations for some. Sunday is operations for many Chin and Karen churches. Karen New Year is a Karen page — do not steal it as a Burmese holiday. Christmas and Easter for Christian streams. Lunar Islamic dates if this family is Rohingya or otherwise Muslim.

Compass Burmese, age 25+: high school or higher 32.8 percent; bachelor’s or higher 11.8 percent; less than high school 67.2 percent. Date it. Camp years and interrupted schooling are structure, not a personality and not a refusal to value school.

### School and language

A parent who speaks fluent Burmese, Hakha, or S’gaw and limited English is not illiterate. Literacy in Burmese script is not guaranteed even when Burmese is the spoken language. The English-only IEP is the gate. So is an interpreter in the wrong language.

Second-generation children are in English-dominant schools, including Greater Minnesota. The form still has to reach the parent. 41.5 percent of the Compass umbrella is 17 or younger. That is a school-and-waiver fact, not a vibe.

Hospitality is a virtue. Accept a little food if offered. You still keep medical and legal time.

Quiet endurance can be misread as agreement. A smile is not consent to the plan. Ask whether they agree. Confirm in the language they use.

A “Burmese interpreter” for a Hakha Chin household is a closed door. Same for Falam, S’gaw, Pwo, Rohingya, Bengali. Put the language on the request. Literacy of the spoken language is not literacy of the form. Many camp-schooled adults do not read the script you assumed.
