chapters.title: Core Concepts

chapters.body:
Hindu, Muslim, Sikh, Christian, Jain, Buddhist, and none all live in Indian Minnesota. Do not assume a temple. A large Hindu public life exists. So does a large Muslim, Sikh, and Christian public life. Kerala and Goa Christian streams, Punjabi Sikh streams, Gujarati Jain streams, Hyderabadi and other Muslim streams are literacy, not a piety ranking. Ask.

### Streams

A home shrine in a professional household can be true. A secular household that still shows up at Diwali can be true. Do not treat that as contradiction you need to fix. Do not treat Hindu practice as “more Indian” than the masjid, the gurdwara, or the parish.

### Practice

The temple, masjid, gurdwara, and church are centers of ritual, mutual aid, and information. They are not “the community.” Do not BCC one priest and call it consultation. Do not make clergy the case plan unless this family asked.

Dietary practice is an ask, not a file. Vegetarian, halal, no beef, no restriction — follow this household. Do not write “Indian diet” on a tray.
chapters.evidence: Hindu, Muslim, Sikh, Christian, Jain, Buddhist, none. Not one temple. A secular professional household and a gurdwara household share a Compass row.
chapters.practitioner: Do not make a priest, imam, granthi, or monk the case plan unless this family asked. Ask. Do not treat a home shrine as folklore.
chapters.title: Religion

chapters.body:
Elders first. Namaste or namaskar in some Hindu rooms. Salaam in some Muslim rooms. A handshake is ordinary in many professional rooms and in much of the second generation. Follow this room. Do not force a namaste you saw in a video. Do not force a hug.

### Titles

English “hello” plus the name is ordinary. Say the name. Ask how to say it.

### This room

Do not import Somali right-hand rules, the Black nod, or a Hmong greeting onto this page. This is not those grammars.

Physical contact: ask the room. Cross-gender touch with elders is not a default. A hug from staff is not warmth if the household did not offer it.
chapters.evidence: Namaste / namaskar in some Hindu rooms; salaam in some Muslim rooms; handshake in many professional rooms. Elders first. Follow this room.
chapters.practitioner: Do not force a namaste you saw in a video. Do not force a hug. Do not import Somali or Hmong greeting rules. Say the name.
chapters.title: Greetings

chapters.body:
There is no single Indian name order. North Indian family names often sit last on a U.S. form and first in some Indian documents. South Indian systems in Tamil, Malayalam, Telugu, and Kannada households may use a patronymic — the father’s given name as the “last name” — with no family surname as the form expects. That is not fraud. Ask how to file. Ask how to say it.

### How to file

Patel, Singh, Reddy, Sharma, Kumar, Shah, Rao, Nair, Das are regional and religious markers, not a joke. Do not joke about “too many Patels” or “too many Singhs.” Sikh men may use Singh; Sikh women may use Kaur; both can sit with a family name or as the name. Muslim names may not match a Hindu naming script you memorized.

Women may or may not take a husband’s family name in U.S. records. Mother and child may not match. Unmatched last names are a system problem until you have a reason they are not.

The form that guesses will invent a person, and that invented name follows them through MHCP, school, and child welfare.
chapters.evidence: Patel, Singh, Reddy, Sharma, Kumar, Shah are regional, not a joke. South Indian patronymics: father’s given name as last name. Sikh Singh / Kaur. U.S. forms reverse and invent.
chapters.practitioner: Ask how to file. Ask how to say it. Do not “correct.” Do not treat unmatched last names as fraud. Do not joke about Patels or Singhs.
chapters.title: Naming Conventions

chapters.body:
Diwali is the large public date in many Hindu (and some Jain, Sikh) rooms. Holi, Pongal, Onam, Navaratri, Vaisakhi, Eid al-Fitr, Eid al-Adha, Christmas — this household’s calendar. Do not put “Asian holiday” or “Indian holiday” on a case note. Schedule around a named date when you can. A calendar click is not community engagement.

### Calendar

15 August — Independence Day. 26 January — Republic Day. Literacy for the desk. Not a party on a case note. 15 August 1947 is Partition as well as independence. Grief and politics sit in some rooms. You do not referee.

Regional new years and death-anniversary household dates will not be on your state calendar. Ask.

Do not mash Diwali with Chinese Lunar New Year, Hmong New Year, Tết, or Seollal.
chapters.evidence: Diwali, Holi, Eid, Vaisakhi, Christmas, Pongal, Onam — this household’s calendar, not “Asian holiday.” 15 August (Independence); 26 January (Republic). 1947 is literacy, not a party.
chapters.practitioner: A calendar click is literacy. It is not community engagement. Do not put “Indian holiday” on a case note.
chapters.title: Dates of Significance

chapters.body:
Compass (ACS 2019–2023), among Indian Minnesotans 25 and older: about 95.9 percent high school or higher; about 80.3 percent bachelor’s or higher. Date Compass. Foreign-born about 66.1 percent. LEP about 12.3 percent among those 5 and older. The average is not the elder in front of you.

### School and language

80.3 percent bachelor’s will be used to skip language access. That skip is the gate. An English IEP, an English waiver exception, and an English comment PDF still close the door for the parent who reads Gujarati and limited English. That parent is not illiterate.

Education pressure in some streams is a hypothesis in research and in some households. It is not this teenager. It is not an excuse to skip mental-health screening. A U.S.-born college student is not proof the waiver household needs no interpreter.
chapters.evidence: Compass (25+): HS+ 95.9%; bachelor+ 80.3%. Foreign-born 66.1%. LEP 12.3%. Model-minority hides the elder who does not read the IEP.
chapters.practitioner: Do not skip the interpreter because attainment numbers are high. A parent who reads Telugu and limited English is not illiterate. The English-only packet is the gate.
chapters.title: Education

chapters.body:
Elders first. Shoes off in many homes. Accept a little food if offered. Hospitality is a virtue. You still keep medical and legal time.

### In the home

A home shrine, a Guru Granth Sahib room, a prayer rug — not a museum and not a case plan. Do not photograph. Do not touch ritual objects. Do not ask an elder to explain Hinduism or Islam as entertainment.

### Time

Right-hand practice for food and greeting exists in some rooms. Follow this room. Do not perform a drama of respect you saw online.

Courtesy-yes then no-show happens when the plan was never agreed. Ask whether they agree. Confirm in the language they use. Do not use a child as the go-between and call it family values.
chapters.evidence: Elders first. Shoes in some homes. Hospitality. Right hand for food in some rooms. A shrine is not a museum.
chapters.practitioner: Accept a little food. Keep medical and legal time. Do not photograph a shrine. Do not use a child as the go-between. Follow this room.
chapters.title: Etiquette

chapters.body:
Not one language. Hindi is not the default. Telugu, Tamil, Gujarati, Malayalam, Punjabi, Urdu, Kannada, Bengali, Marathi, English, and others live in this Compass row. An interpreter labeled Indian or Hindi who does not speak this household’s language is a closed door. Book THIS language. Still book a qualified interpreter.

### Language

Compass: among those 5 and older, about 70.2 percent speak a language other than English; about 12.3 percent speak English less than “very well.” Date the number. 12.3 percent is low compared with Vietnamese or Hmong on Compass. It is not “no language gate.” New arrivals and elders are inside it. English-dominant second generation is inside the 29.8 percent English-only and still on this page.

A short English yes may be exhaustion, courtesy, or indirectness. Do not take a smile as consent. Ask whether they agree with the plan.

Do not use a child as the interpreter. Do not make an Indian coworker the interpreter. Do not treat them as “the Indian community.”
chapters.evidence: Not one language. Hindi, Telugu, Tamil, Gujarati, Malayalam, Punjabi, Urdu, Kannada, Bengali, Marathi, English, others. Compass: ~70.2% language other than English (5+); ~12.3% LEP.
chapters.practitioner: Book THIS language. An interpreter labeled Indian or Hindi can still be a closed door. Do not use a child. Do not take a smile as consent.
chapters.title: Language and Communication

chapters.body:
Unvarnished, because Minnesota Nice is how a room that treats everyone the same deletes facts.

### Named harms

Model-minority is a weapon. 80.3 percent bachelor’s and a median near $124,931 will be used to skip LEP elders, 5.4 percent poverty, disability, caste, and youth who are not thriving. That skip is the policy. 12.3 percent LEP is a gate.

Caste is a named harm in some rooms and a word some families will never say to you. You do not icebreak with it. You do not pretend it is over because the person is a software engineer. You do not collect it on a form you do not need. Colorism is a named harm in some rooms. Same rule.

Hindu-Muslim-Sikh politics, Hindutva, and 1947 memory still split some rooms. You do not referee. You do not put it on a case note as color.

H-1B, visa, and green-card climate changes who opens the door. Do not collect status you do not need. Do not treat fear as noncompliance.

LGBTQ Indian Minnesotans exist. You use the name. You do not out someone to kin and call it culture. Do not skip mandated reporting and call it humility. Staff who share this community may add facts. They do not get to delete a fact because it is hard to say.
chapters.evidence: Model-minority as a weapon; caste as a named harm in some rooms not an icebreaker; Hindu-Muslim-Sikh politics you do not referee; H-1B and status anxiety you do not collect; LGBTQ exist; colorism as a named harm in some rooms.
chapters.practitioner: Do not collect caste or status you do not need. Do not skip mandated reporting and call it humility. Do not out anyone. Do not skip screening because the median is high.
chapters.title: Other Considerations — unvarnished, not Minnesota Nice

chapters.body:
Believe reported pain. Do not invent “Asian stoicism.” Do not fold this history into a generic Asian slide. This is not the Chinese page and not the Hmong page.

### Access

Do not invent a Minnesota diabetes, heart, or suicide rate. U.S. public-health patterns for South Asian cardiovascular risk exist in the literature — date the CDC or AHA page you cite. chapters.body:
This brief is about Japanese Minnesota as a people with a country, a long literature, and a U.S. history that includes labor on the West Coast, Exclusion, internment, a Minnesota language school at Camp Savage and Fort Snelling, later-generation families, mixed households, company transferees, and newcomers. They share a Compass row and do not share a Tuesday. This is not Chinese. It is not Korean. It is not interchangeable with either. Shared continent is not shared culture. A full mosaic is not a stereotype. A stereotype is when this page becomes the person in the lobby.

### Who this is

Internment is U.S. literacy for the desk. Executive Order 9066, 19 February 1942. It is not a speech you give the family. It is not an icebreaker in a waiver meeting. Do not skip it because a room that treats everyone the same is uncomfortable. Do not open with it.

### Who this is not

Minnesota Compass (ACS 2019–2023): about 13,391; Twin Cities 76.8 percent; Greater Minnesota 23.2 percent; age 17 or younger 31.8 percent; 65+ about 8.6 percent; foreign-born about 17.3 percent; among those 5 and older, English only about 71.3 percent, language other than English about 28.7 percent, English less than “very well” about 8.6 percent; high school or higher (25+) about 97.0 percent; bachelor’s or higher about 51.0 percent; median household income about $67,817 in 2022 dollars; poverty 5.1 percent; owner-occupied 60.3 percent; average household size about 2.13; individuals living alone about 37.9 percent; cost-burdened households about 36.3 percent. Date the number you use. A rate is not the person.

The diversity inside this Compass row is the point. A Nisei elder who remembers a camp, a Sansei who does not speak Japanese, a company-transfer family in a suburb, a student, a mixed-race child who is asked “what are you,” a newcomer who needs Japanese in the lobby — share a checkbox and do not share a language, a church, or a war memory.

### How to read this

Always defer to the person in front of you. This page is a hypothesis you still test on this family.

chapters.title: A Note on This Guide

chapters.body:
Japanese peoplehood is older than Meiji (1868), older than the empire, and older than the internment file. An archipelago, a language with honorific speech, three scripts in ordinary public literacy — hiragana, katakana, kanji — and successive states. That is literacy for the desk. It is not a lecture you give a parent who came in for a waiver.

### History for the meeting

1868 Meiji transformation, empire, 1945 defeat, the postwar constitution, and a U.S. occupation are the modern political stack. Most Minnesota immigrant and transfer households name Japan as a sending country. Do not test them. Do not ask a later-generation person to narrate a war they were not asked to remember.

### What people brought

What people brought: language, Buddhist or Shinto or Christian or none, education as mobility, foodways, a memory of war and of a state. What they met in this country: Exclusion, a camp, a Minnesota language school that trained Nisei soldiers while families were incarcerated, an English form, and one “Asian” checkbox. What they meet now: an assumption that 17.3 percent foreign-born means you can skip Japanese.

Issei, Nisei, Sansei, Yonsei are generation literacy — like Vietnamese waves, not a personality ranking. Mixed households and company transferees sit in the same Compass row. Ask which Tuesday this is. Do not lecture a parent about a generation word they did not use.

### Homeland

Global diaspora: West Coast United States historically, Hawaii, Brazil, Peru, and a Minnesota present that is unusual in part because of the Military Intelligence Service Language School at Camp Savage (1942) and Fort Snelling. ### Minnesota

Do not assume Minneapolis. Do not assume they have been to Tokyo. A later-generation household in a Greater Minnesota town is still this people. A company-transfer family on a three-year assignment is still this people. A mixed household is still this people.

chapters.body:
Meiji-era labor moved Japanese people to Hawaii and the West Coast. The Gentlemen’s Agreement (1907–08) and the Immigration Act of 1924 closed the door. That is literacy. It is not a speech.

### Foundational events

Executive Order 9066, signed 19 February 1942: the United States incarcerated Japanese Americans on the West Coast. Camps. Loss of homes and businesses. The 442nd Regimental Combat Team. The Military Intelligence Service Language School trained Nisei linguists at Camp Savage, Minnesota, in 1942, then at Fort Snelling. That is this state’s history. It is not a Heritage Month panel unless they asked. It is not an icebreaker.

### Who you meet

Hart-Celler (1965) reopened skilled and family immigration. Later: company transferees, students, marriage, mixed families. Redress: Civil Liberties Act of 1988 (10 August). Date the law. Do not invent this person’s family file. Do not ask them to narrate a camp for your professional development.

This brief is about Kenyan Minnesota as a state-name community of many peoples. Kikuyu (Gikuyu / Agĩkũyũ), Luo, Luhya, Kamba, Kalenjin, Kisii, Meru, Maasai, coastal Mijikenda, Kenyan Somali, and others are not one file. Book the language this household names. English and Kiswahili are official in Kenya. They are not the home language until this family says so. A “Kenyan interpreter” is not a language.

### Who this is

This is not Somali. If the household is Kenyan Somali and names Somali, open Somali Minnesota. Shared Horn and shared border are not shared culture. This is not Ethiopian. This is not Oromo as a synonym — Oromo people live in Kenya; if this household is Oromo, open Oromo Minnesota. This is not historic African American. Shared race in the United States is not shared culture.

### Who this is not

Minnesota Compass (ACS 2019–2023) puts Kenyan Minnesota near 20,967. About 77.3 percent Twin Cities, about 22.7 percent Greater Minnesota. About 44.1 percent age 17 or younger; about 4.6 percent 65+. About 66.6 percent foreign-born. Language other than English (age 5+) 65.8 percent; English less than “very well” 24.4 percent. Date the number. A rate is not the person.

The diversity inside this state name is the point. A Kikuyu Pentecostal nurse in the suburbs, a Luo Catholic household, a Luhya factory family in Greater Minnesota, a Kenyan Somali household that should have been booked Somali, a U.S.-born student who uses English with friends and Gikuyu with an elder, a Muslim coastal family — share a Compass row and do not share a Tuesday.

Always defer to the person in front of you. This page is a hypothesis you still test on this family.

sections.heading: Origins and the Founding of a People
paragraphs: Kenya is a state of many nations. Kikuyu (Gikuyu), Luo, Luhya, Kamba, Kalenjin, Kisii, Meru, Maasai, coastal peoples, Kenyan Somali, and others. English and Kiswahili as official languages. Independence 1963. Not a camp origin myth.

Kenya is a state of many nations. Kikuyu highland peoplehood around Mount Kenya, Luo peoplehood on Lake Victoria, Luhya, Kamba, Kalenjin, Kisii, Meru, Maasai pastoral peoplehood, coastal Swahili and Mijikenda worlds, Kenyan Somali in the northeast — and others. There is no single Kenyan ethnicity. Ask which people they are. Do not lecture taxonomy they did not ask for.

### History for the meeting

English and Kiswahili as official languages are colonial and national history. They are literacy for the desk. They are not permission to skip the home language. Independence in 1963 ended British colony. Mau Mau is literacy, not a speech you give the family, and not every household’s story.

### What people brought

What people brought: ethnic language, English, Kiswahili, church and mosque, harambee as a named mutual-aid ethic in some rooms, kin obligation, a memory of colony and of a state that followed. What they met in Minnesota: an English form, one “East African” checkbox, and often Somali because the building already has that page.

Do not start with a safari sentence. Do not assume Nairobi as identity. Many people name a district, a people, a village.

community.title: Kenyan Minnesota

chapters.body:
This brief is about Kenyan Minnesota as a state-name community of many peoples. Kikuyu (Gikuyu / Agĩkũyũ), Luo, Luhya, Kamba, Kalenjin, Kisii, Meru, Maasai, coastal Mijikenda, Kenyan Somali, and others are not one file. Book the language this household names. English and Kiswahili are official in Kenya. They are not the home language until this family says so. A “Kenyan interpreter” is not a language.

### Who this is

This is not Somali. If the household is Kenyan Somali and names Somali, open Somali Minnesota. Shared Horn and shared border are not shared culture. This is not Ethiopian. This is not Oromo as a synonym — Oromo people live in Kenya; if this household is Oromo, open Oromo Minnesota. This is not historic African American. Shared race in the United States is not shared culture.

### Who this is not

Minnesota Compass (ACS 2019–2023) puts Kenyan Minnesota near 20,967. About 77.3 percent Twin Cities, about 22.7 percent Greater Minnesota. About 44.1 percent age 17 or younger; about 4.6 percent 65+. About 66.6 percent foreign-born. Language other than English (age 5+) 65.8 percent; English less than “very well” 24.4 percent. Date the number. A rate is not the person.

The diversity inside this state name is the point. A Kikuyu Pentecostal nurse in the suburbs, a Luo Catholic household, a Luhya factory family in Greater Minnesota, a Kenyan Somali household that should have been booked Somali, a U.S.-born student who uses English with friends and Gikuyu with an elder, a Muslim coastal family — share a Compass row and do not share a Tuesday.

### How to read this

Always defer to the person in front of you. This page is a hypothesis you still test on this family.

chapters.title: A Note on This Guide

chapters.body:
Kenya is a state of many nations. Kikuyu highland peoplehood around Mount Kenya, Luo peoplehood on Lake Victoria, Luhya, Kamba, Kalenjin, Kisii, Meru, Maasai pastoral peoplehood, coastal Swahili and Mijikenda worlds, Kenyan Somali in the northeast — and others. There is no single Kenyan ethnicity. Ask which people they are. Do not lecture taxonomy they did not ask for.

### History for the meeting

English and Kiswahili as official languages are colonial and national history. They are literacy for the desk. They are not permission to skip the home language. Independence in 1963 ended British colony. Mau Mau is literacy, not a speech you give the family, and not every household’s story.

### What people brought

What people brought: ethnic language, English, Kiswahili, church and mosque, harambee as a named mutual-aid ethic in some rooms, kin obligation, a memory of colony and of a state that followed. What they met in Minnesota: an English form, one “East African” checkbox, and often Somali because the building already has that page.

Do not start with a safari sentence. Do not assume Nairobi as identity. Many people name a district, a people, a village.

chapters.title: Origins and the Founding of a People

chapters.body:
Homeland is not one map. Central highlands, Nyanza, Western, Rift Valley, the coast, the north. Nairobi is not the whole. A person may name Kiambu, Kisumu, Kakamega, Machakos, Eldoret, Mombasa — not the capital. Do not referee regional politics in a waiver meeting. Listen if they name a place.

### Homeland

The diaspora is global: Texas, Minnesota, Washington State, Maryland and D.C., Georgia, the Gulf, the UK. Minnesota is a real community, not the U.S. capital of it. Secondary migration, church networks, and healthcare work pulled people here.

### Minnesota

In Minnesota: Compass 77.3 percent Twin Cities, 22.7 percent Greater Minnesota. That Greater Minnesota share is larger than Ethiopian Compass and larger than Liberian Compass. Do not assume Minneapolis. Do not assume Cedar-Riverside — that hub is Somali unless this family lives there. Do not assume the person in front of you has been to Kenya.

chapters.title: The Geography of the Kenyan World

chapters.body:
There is no single 1975 or 1991 on this page. Independence in 1963 is the political founding of the state. Later Minnesota streams are mixed: students, family, diversity visas, skilled work including healthcare, and displacement after 2007–08 post-election violence for some households. Do not file every Kenyan household as refugee. Do not file every Kenyan household as a nurse.

### Foundational events

2007–08 is named memory for some: killing, camps, flight. It is not a personality. It is not a reason to skip screening. It is literacy. You do not referee Kikuyu/Luo or other ethnic politics in a waiver meeting. You do not pick a side as DHS.

### Who you meet

Healthcare recruitment is a Minnesota labor fact in some rooms — LeadingAge and related pipelines have named Kenya as a nursing source. That is work. It is not a personality and not the whole Compass row.

The desk in 2026 meets first-generation professionals and U.S.-born children — English with peers, still translating, still unable to get Gikuyu or Dholuo in a lobby that offered Somali or “African.” If you only know “East African,” you will miss this household.

Extended households and elder authority sit in many rooms. Harambee — pulling together, fundraising, mutual aid — is a hypothesis in some families, not a personality you assign. Compass average household size about 3.50. Who cares for a disabled adult or a child may be a brother, a cousin, a church mother, not the legally recognized caregiver on the checkbox. Hour caps and “natural supports” can dump unpaid work onto women in that network and call it culture.

### Who is in the household

Naming is already a who: English / Christian given names plus ethnic names; Luo naming is not Kikuyu naming. Do not invent a last name because the screen requires one. Do not assume three Somali names.

### Who speaks

Who speaks in the lobby may be a child with the best English. That child is not the qualified interpreter. CLAS still stands. Ask who should be in the room. Minnesota law still stands. Do not skip mandated reporting and call it humility.

chapters.body:
Minnesota holds a Kenyan Compass community large enough that this department will meet it on waivers, child welfare, health care, cash, food, aging, and employment — and large enough that the building has a habit of hearing East Africa and booking Somali. Compass: about 20,967 (ACS 2019–2023). Greater Minnesota is 22.7 percent. Do not write this people as a Minneapolis anecdote.

### Places

Places, not a blob: Twin Cities suburbs; Minneapolis and St. Paul pockets; Greater Minnesota towns with hospitals, factories, and housing. Churches — ethnic congregations and Kenyan fellowships — are public life. They are not consultation. A food visit does not make you the expert.

### Partners

Partners: churches families name; ethnic associations (Luo, Kikuyu, Luhya, and others as this household names them); professional and nursing networks as doors, not a staffing plan; CECLC as a department door — not the whole. Pay the partner this household actually uses.

Kenyan staff are not unpaid interpreters and not the community. Identity is not a staffing plan. A Jamhuri or harambee visit is optional professional development if you are invited. You are a guest. It does not make you the expert.

chapters.title: Minnesota and Kenyan History

chapters.body:
To be Kenyan in Minnesota is to be a state-name people of many nations, filed under East African, Black, and sometimes Somali by a building that has not studied. Peoplehood after colony and after 1963 is not a safari poster. Kikuyu, Luo, Luhya, and the rest do not share one Tuesday. You do not pick a side.

### In this state

In this building another fact sits on top: many of these households are Black in a U.S. racial order that will file them under Somali or under historic African American and get the language, the church, and the name wrong. Shared race is not shared culture. Shared Horn geography is not shared language.

Face, elder obligation, harambee as hypothesis, and not shaming the name travel into a waiver meeting. Harmony can look like agreement and then a plan nobody follows. Ask whether they agree. Do not take a smile as consent.

This guide is a working orientation. Individual variation always supersedes group generalization. Always defer to the person in front of you.

### Which language

Gikuyu, Dholuo, Luhya languages, Kikamba, Kalenjin languages, Kiswahili, English, others. A “Kenyan interpreter” is not a language. A Somali interpreter is the wrong door unless this household is Somali.

### Harambee as hypothesis

Mutual aid, fundraising, pulling together. Staff do not use it as a guilt tool. If the family names it, you listen.

### Faith is plural

Protestant, Pentecostal, Catholic, AIC, Islam, none. Follow this room.

### Work and school as a family project

chapters.body:
Christianity is the large public stream in Kenyan Minnesota: Protestant, Pentecostal, Catholic, African Independent / AIC churches. Islam lives on the coast, among Kenyan Somali, and in some other families. Traditional practice sits in some rooms and is not a souvenir. None is also a Tuesday. Ask. Do not assume Muslim like Somali.

### Streams

The church is a center of ritual, mutual aid, information, and often the first Minnesota network. It is not “the community.” Do not BCC one pastor and call it consultation. Do not make clergy the case plan unless this family asked.

### Practice

Funerals gather family and can run long. You still keep medical and legal time. You name the conflict instead of punishing it.

Arabic may be religion, not the interview, in Muslim rooms. Kiswahili may be church or market language, not the home language. Book the interview language.

Elders first. English “hello” is ordinary in many professional rooms. Kiswahili habari and related forms live in some rooms. Do not perform tourism “jambo” as icebreaker. Ethnic greetings exist — ask, do not perform one you learned from a video.

### Titles

A hard handshake you assume is universal is already a closed door for some women and some elders. Many second-generation people will shake hands in English-language rooms. If a hand is not offered, nod. Do not force it.

### This room

Do not import Somali right-hand rules onto this page as default. In a Muslim Kenyan room they may apply. Follow this room. Do not assume the Black nod is this grammar.

English and Christian given names are common — after mission schools and colonial record. Ethnic names sit beside them or instead of them. Kikuyu names are not Luo names. Luo names (Ochieng, Achieng, Odhiambo, and others) are not a joke and not a clan icebreaker you pulled from a coworker. Luhya, Kamba, Kalenjin naming each have their own grammar. Ask.

### How to file

U.S. forms want first-middle-last. Kenyan naming may not match. Do not invent a last name because the screen requires one. That invented name becomes a gate. Do not assume three Somali names.

Ask how to say it. Ask how to file it. Pronounce it. Women may or may not take a husband’s name in U.S. records. Mother and child may not match. That is not fraud until you have a reason.

A parent who speaks fluent Gikuyu or Dholuo and limited English is not illiterate. Many Kenyans were schooled in English. Some elders were not. The English-only form is still a gate. Book THIS language. The child is not the interpreter.

### Named harms

Intra-Kenyan ethnic politics are real — Kikuyu, Luo, and others, including 2007–08 memory. Do not pick a side as DHS. Do not referee in a waiver meeting. Do not file politics as a risk score.

FGC exists in some Kenyan communities, including some Kenyan Somali and some other groups. Minnesota law stands. This is not the Somali page. Do not invent a Kenyan rate. Do not mash Somali prevalence onto this household. Follow mandated reporting. Still see a family.

sections.heading: A Note on This Guide
paragraphs: Korean Minnesota: immigrant streams and a historically large adoptee population. Compass ACS 2019–2023: 27,204. LEP 7.9% is not “no language gate.” Census Asian mixes this with Chinese, Hmong, Vietnamese. Date the number you cite.

There is no single Korean client. Defer to this family. Book Korean when the person needs it. Do not ask an adoptee to represent “the Korean community.” Do not open a Chinese or Japanese case with this page.

This brief is about Korean Minnesota as two households that share a Compass row and do not share a Tuesday: immigrant Korean families — including elders who need Korean in the lobby — and Korean adoptees, a population that is Minnesota history. Adoptee households are often white Minnesota families and Korean-born adults. That is not the same as an immigrant Korean household and not “no culture.” Do not skip this page because the person is English-dominant. Do not ask an adoptee to represent “the Korean community.”

### Who this is

This is not a Census “Asian” mash. It is not Chinese. It is not Japanese. It is not Hmong. It is not Vietnamese. Shared continent is not shared culture. Seollal is not Chinese New Year as a file and not Hmong New Year. A full mosaic is not a stereotype. A stereotype is when this page becomes the person in the lobby.

### Who this is not

Minnesota Compass (ACS 2019–2023) puts Korean ancestry near 27,204. About 74.6 percent Twin Cities, 25.4 percent Greater Minnesota. About 37.1 percent age 17 or younger; 65 and older only about 2.7 percent. Foreign-born about 43.7 percent. Among those 5 and older: English only about 82.4 percent; language other than English about 17.6 percent; English less than “very well” about 7.9 percent. High school or higher (25+) about 95.7 percent; bachelor’s or higher about 59.2 percent. Median household income about $79,524 in 2022 dollars. Poverty 4.4 percent. Owner-occupied about 64.2 percent. Average household size about 2.29. Individuals living alone about 37.4 percent. Date the number you use.

CAAL and community sources have estimated Minnesota among the highest concentrations of Korean adoptees of any state — often cited near 15,000 historically, sometimes 15,000–20,000 in later community reporting. Date it as community/CAAL. Compass does not split adoptee vs immigrant. AKConnection has said Minnesota holds on the order of 10 percent of Korean adoptees worldwide. Pattern: this state is a hub. A count is not the person.

### How to read this

Always defer to the person in front of you. This page is a hypothesis you still test on this family.

sections.heading: Origins and the Founding of a People
paragraphs: Korean peoplehood older than 1945. Japanese occupation 1910–1945; 1950–53 Korean War; division of the peninsula. Hangul. Honorific speech.
History is literacy for the desk. It is not a speech you give the family. Do not start with kimchi tourism.

Korean peoplehood is older than 1945, older than the war, and older than the adoption file. Kingdoms on the peninsula, Hangul (promulgated in the fifteenth century; suppressed and revived), honorific speech, and clan surnames are literacy for the desk. They are not a lecture you give a parent who came in for a waiver.

### History for the meeting

Japanese occupation (1910–1945) and the Korean War (1950–1953) are the modern political break. The peninsula divided. The Republic of Korea and the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea are not a mash you referee in a lobby. Most Minnesota immigrant households name the South. Do not test them. Do not ask an adoptee to narrate a war they were not asked to remember.

### What people brought

What people brought: language, church or temple or neither, education as mobility and as pressure, foodways, a memory of occupation and war. What adoptees met: a Minnesota family, often Lutheran or Catholic, a file, and a country that later argued about whether the passport was real. What they met in this department: an English form, one “Asian” checkbox, and often an assumption that LEP at 7.9 percent means you can skip Korean.

sections.heading: The Geography of the Korean World
paragraphs: Korean peninsula (ROK and DPRK). Global diaspora. Minnesota is a present. Compass: 74.6% Twin Cities, 25.4% Greater Minnesota.
Do not assume Minneapolis. Do not referee North/South in a waiver meeting. Do not assume they have been to Seoul.

Homeland is the peninsula — not a Seoul tourism map, and not Pyongyang as a personality. The Republic of Korea is the sending country for most Minnesota immigrant and adoptee files. The North is a political fact in the news and in some families. You do not referee it.

### Homeland

Global diaspora: Los Angeles, New York, China, Central Asia, and a Minnesota concentration that is unusual because of adoption. Compass: about 74.6 percent Twin Cities, 25.4 percent Greater Minnesota. Suburbs, university areas, and Greater Minnesota church-and-farm towns that received adoptees are all on this page.

### Minnesota

Do not assume Minneapolis. Do not assume they have been to Seoul. An adoptee raised in a western Minnesota town is still this people. An immigrant elder in a first-ring suburb is still this people.

sections.heading: War, Church, 1965, and the Adoption Pipeline — Foundational Events
paragraphs: Japanese occupation; Korean War 1950–53; military and missionary adoption pipeline to Minnesota (Lutheran and other); 1965+ immigration; 1980s–90s adoptee peak; later skilled immigration.
If you only know “adoptee” or only know “immigrant,” you will miss the other household. Compass does not split them. Ask.

Japanese occupation, then the Korean War (1950–1953), broke families and filled GI and missionary channels. Minnesota’s Lutheran and other churches sat on those channels. Adoption of Korean children into Minnesota homes is this state’s history, not a side note. MNopedia documents the pipeline. Peaks in the 1980s–1990s sit in today’s adult population. Compass does not split them.

### Foundational events

Hart-Celler (1965) opened skilled and family immigration. Later waves brought students, professionals, and church-sponsored families. Immigrant Korean Minnesota built congregations — Presbyterian especially — that are civic hubs. That hub is not the adoptee’s church unless they say so.

### Who you meet

The Child Citizenship Act of 2000 (signed October 30, 2000; effective February 27, 2001) granted automatic citizenship to certain foreign-born children, including adoptees, who were under 18 on the effective date. It was not retroactive for people already 18. Adoptee Citizenship Act bills (introduced from 2015, reintroduced 2018, 2019, 2021, 2024; 2025 Protect Adoptees and American Families Act in the same line) have tried to close the gap. Date the law that exists. Date the advocacy. Do not invent this person’s status. Do not collect status you do not need.

sections.heading: Family
paragraphs: Patrilineal naming in many immigrant streams; generation names. Adoptee households are often white Minnesota parents + Korean-born adults. Compass avg HH 2.29; 37.4% live alone.
Ask who should be in the room. Do not assume an adoptee has Korean kin in the state. Do not assume an immigrant household is nuclear-English.

Immigrant streams: family-name-first, generation names, obligation to elders as a hypothesis. Households can be multi-generation or Compass-small (average size about 2.29). About 37.4 percent live alone. Ask who should be in the room.

### Who is in the household

Adoptee households: often white Minnesota parents, siblings who may not be Korean, and an adult who is Korean-born. Kin search may point to Korea, to a closed file, or to no one. Do not assume Korean relatives in the metro. Do not assume the adoptive family is the barrier or the solution. Ask this person.

### Who speaks

Marriage, in-law duty, and who holds the child’s medical decision may not match the English form. Minnesota law still stands. Do not skip mandated reporting and call it culture.

Do not use an adoptee’s family as a lesson about “good Minnesota parents.” Do not use an immigrant family as a lesson about “strict Asians.”

This department will meet this community on waivers, child welfare, health care, aging, adoption-adjacent adult services, student households, and employment. Compass: about 74.6 percent Twin Cities, 25.4 percent Greater Minnesota. Greater Minnesota is not an afterthought — the adoption pipeline placed children in towns that still hold adults.

### Places

Korean churches — Presbyterian especially, also Methodist, Catholic, and others — are civic hubs for some immigrant families: language, jobs, information. They are not “the community.” Adoptees may be Minnesota Lutheran or Catholic with no Korean congregation. Do not send them to a Korean church as programming.

### Partners

AKConnection, established in 2000, has been a Minnesota networking organization for adult Korean adoptees. Peer adoptee-led groups exist. Korean Association groups exist. Pay the door this person names. Korean staff are not unpaid interpreters and not the community. Identity is not a staffing plan. Do not use an adoptee coworker as the culture unit.

paragraphs: Two households in one Compass row: immigrant Korean Minnesota and Korean adoptee Minnesota. Asian in a U.S. checkbox that also holds Chinese and Hmong histories they do not share.
Do not fold this household into “Asian Pacific.” Do not ask an adoptee to speak for an immigrant elder, or an immigrant elder to explain an adoptee.

To be Korean in Minnesota is often to be asked whether you were adopted, or whether you “speak it,” as if those were the only two rooms — and to be filed under a checkbox that also holds Chinese, Hmong, and Japanese histories this household does not share.

### In this state

Immigrant Korean Minnesota and Korean adoptee Minnesota share a war and a peninsula and do not share a kitchen, a church, or a language on Tuesday. Do not ask an adoptee to represent “the Korean community.” Do not ask an immigrant elder to explain an adoptee’s grief. Do not skip this page because the person in front of you sounds like Minnesota.

Face, education pressure, and family reputation travel into some immigrant meetings. Adoptee grief, citizenship anxiety, and a body that does not match the family photograph travel into others. Harmony can look like agreement. Ask whether they agree. Do not take a smile as consent.

This guide is a working orientation. Individual variation always supersedes group generalization.

### Name

Family name first. Kim, Lee/Yi, Park/Pak, Choi, Jung. Do not “correct” Lee. Adoptee American names are names.

Minnesota Lutheran/Catholic — some adoptees. Neither is the case plan unless they asked.

### Model-minority

A weapon that hides LEP elders, 4.4 percent poverty, disability, and adoptee grief.

Protestant Christianity, especially Presbyterian, is large in the immigrant stream. Catholic, Buddhist, and none also live here. Church can be the civic hub: Korean language, jobs, a ride, a funeral. It is not “the community.” Do not make a pastor the case plan unless this family asked.

### Streams

Adoptees may be Minnesota Lutheran, Catholic, evangelical, or none, with no Korean congregation. Do not assign a Korean church as cultural programming. Do not assume no faith.

sections.heading: Greetings

Family name first in Korean: Kim, Lee (Yi / Rhee), Park (Pak), Choi, Jung (Jeong). Generation names may sit in a two-syllable given name. U.S. forms reverse the order. The same person can appear as Kim Min-jun and Minjun Kim. That is a system failure, not a fraud signal until you have a reason.

Lee is not a misspelling. Do not “correct” it to Li or to a Chinese romanization. Do not mash with Chinese Chen or Japanese names.

Adoptees often carry an American given name and family name from the adoptive household. They may or may not use a Korean name. Ask. Do not demand the “real” name. Do not announce a Korean name in a waiting room as cultural humility.

Pronounce it. Ask. Do not joke that there are “too many Kims.”

chapters.body:
This brief is about Korean Minnesota as two households that share a Compass row and do not share a Tuesday: immigrant Korean families — including elders who need Korean in the lobby — and Korean adoptees, a population that is Minnesota history. Adoptee households are often white Minnesota families and Korean-born adults. That is not the same as an immigrant Korean household and not “no culture.” Do not skip this page because the person is English-dominant. Do not ask an adoptee to represent “the Korean community.”

### Who this is

This is not a Census “Asian” mash. It is not Chinese. It is not Japanese. It is not Hmong. It is not Vietnamese. Shared continent is not shared culture. Seollal is not Chinese New Year as a file and not Hmong New Year. A full mosaic is not a stereotype. A stereotype is when this page becomes the person in the lobby.

### Who this is not

Minnesota Compass (ACS 2019–2023) puts Korean ancestry near 27,204. About 74.6 percent Twin Cities, 25.4 percent Greater Minnesota. About 37.1 percent age 17 or younger; 65 and older only about 2.7 percent. Foreign-born about 43.7 percent. Among those 5 and older: English only about 82.4 percent; language other than English about 17.6 percent; English less than “very well” about 7.9 percent. High school or higher (25+) about 95.7 percent; bachelor’s or higher about 59.2 percent. Median household income about $79,524 in 2022 dollars. Poverty 4.4 percent. Owner-occupied about 64.2 percent. Average household size about 2.29. Individuals living alone about 37.4 percent. Date the number you use.

CAAL and community sources have estimated Minnesota among the highest concentrations of Korean adoptees of any state — often cited near 15,000 historically, sometimes 15,000–20,000 in later community reporting. Date it as community/CAAL. Compass does not split adoptee vs immigrant. AKConnection has said Minnesota holds on the order of 10 percent of Korean adoptees worldwide. Pattern: this state is a hub. A count is not the person.

### How to read this

Always defer to the person in front of you. This page is a hypothesis you still test on this family.

chapters.title: A Note on This Guide

chapters.body:
Korean peoplehood is older than 1945, older than the war, and older than the adoption file. Kingdoms on the peninsula, Hangul (promulgated in the fifteenth century; suppressed and revived), honorific speech, and clan surnames are literacy for the desk. They are not a lecture you give a parent who came in for a waiver.

### History for the meeting

Japanese occupation (1910–1945) and the Korean War (1950–1953) are the modern political break. The peninsula divided. The Republic of Korea and the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea are not a mash you referee in a lobby. Most Minnesota immigrant households name the South. Do not test them. Do not ask an adoptee to narrate a war they were not asked to remember.

### What people brought

What people brought: language, church or temple or neither, education as mobility and as pressure, foodways, a memory of occupation and war. What adoptees met: a Minnesota family, often Lutheran or Catholic, a file, and a country that later argued about whether the passport was real. What they met in this department: an English form, one “Asian” checkbox, and often an assumption that LEP at 7.9 percent means you can skip Korean.

chapters.title: Origins and the Founding of a People

chapters.body:
Homeland is the peninsula — not a Seoul tourism map, and not Pyongyang as a personality. The Republic of Korea is the sending country for most Minnesota immigrant and adoptee files. The North is a political fact in the news and in some families. You do not referee it.

### Homeland

Global diaspora: Los Angeles, New York, China, Central Asia, and a Minnesota concentration that is unusual because of adoption. Compass: about 74.6 percent Twin Cities, 25.4 percent Greater Minnesota. Suburbs, university areas, and Greater Minnesota church-and-farm towns that received adoptees are all on this page.

### Minnesota

Do not assume Minneapolis. Do not assume they have been to Seoul. An adoptee raised in a western Minnesota town is still this people. An immigrant elder in a first-ring suburb is still this people.
chapters.evidence: Korean peninsula (ROK and DPRK). Global diaspora. Minnesota is a present. Compass: 74.6% Twin Cities, 25.4% Greater Minnesota.

chapters.title: The Geography of the Korean World

chapters.body:
Japanese occupation, then the Korean War (1950–1953), broke families and filled GI and missionary channels. Minnesota’s Lutheran and other churches sat on those channels. Adoption of Korean children into Minnesota homes is this state’s history, not a side note. MNopedia documents the pipeline. Peaks in the 1980s–1990s sit in today’s adult population. Compass does not split them.

### Foundational events

Hart-Celler (1965) opened skilled and family immigration. Later waves brought students, professionals, and church-sponsored families. Immigrant Korean Minnesota built congregations — Presbyterian especially — that are civic hubs. That hub is not the adoptee’s church unless they say so.

### Who you meet

The Child Citizenship Act of 2000 (signed October 30, 2000; effective February 27, 2001) granted automatic citizenship to certain foreign-born children, including adoptees, who were under 18 on the effective date. It was not retroactive for people already 18. Adoptee Citizenship Act bills (introduced from 2015, reintroduced 2018, 2019, 2021, 2024; 2025 Protect Adoptees and American Families Act in the same line) have tried to close the gap. Date the law that exists. Date the advocacy. Do not invent this person’s status. Do not collect status you do not need.

chapters.title: War, Church, 1965, and the Adoption Pipeline — Foundational Events

chapters.body:
Immigrant streams: family-name-first, generation names, obligation to elders as a hypothesis. Households can be multi-generation or Compass-small (average size about 2.29). About 37.4 percent live alone. Ask who should be in the room.

### Who is in the household

Adoptee households: often white Minnesota parents, siblings who may not be Korean, and an adult who is Korean-born. Kin search may point to Korea, to a closed file, or to no one. Do not assume Korean relatives in the metro. Do not assume the adoptive family is the barrier or the solution. Ask this person.

### Who speaks

Marriage, in-law duty, and who holds the child’s medical decision may not match the English form. Minnesota law still stands. Do not skip mandated reporting and call it culture.

Do not use an adoptee’s family as a lesson about “good Minnesota parents.” Do not use an immigrant family as a lesson about “strict Asians.”

chapters.title: Family

chapters.body:
This department will meet this community on waivers, child welfare, health care, aging, adoption-adjacent adult services, student households, and employment. Compass: about 74.6 percent Twin Cities, 25.4 percent Greater Minnesota. Greater Minnesota is not an afterthought — the adoption pipeline placed children in towns that still hold adults.

### Places

They are not “the community.” Adoptees may be Minnesota Lutheran or Catholic with no Korean congregation. Do not send them to a Korean church as programming.

### Partners

AKConnection, established in 2000, has been a Minnesota networking organization for adult Korean adoptees. Peer adoptee-led groups exist. Korean Association groups exist. Pay the door this person names. Korean staff are not unpaid interpreters and not the community. Identity is not a staffing plan. Do not use an adoptee coworker as the culture unit.

chapters.title: Minnesota and Korean History

chapters.body:
To be Korean in Minnesota is often to be asked whether you were adopted, or whether you “speak it,” as if those were the only two rooms — and to be filed under a checkbox that also holds Chinese, Hmong, and Japanese histories this household does not share.

### In this state

Immigrant Korean Minnesota and Korean adoptee Minnesota share a war and a peninsula and do not share a kitchen, a church, or a language on Tuesday. Do not ask an adoptee to represent “the Korean community.” Do not ask an immigrant elder to explain an adoptee’s grief. Do not skip this page because the person in front of you sounds like Minnesota.

Face, education pressure, and family reputation travel into some immigrant meetings. Adoptee grief, citizenship anxiety, and a body that does not match the family photograph travel into others. Harmony can look like agreement. Ask whether they agree. Do not take a smile as consent.

This guide is a working orientation. Individual variation always supersedes group generalization.

Adoptees often carry an American given name and family name from the adoptive household. They may or may not use a Korean name. Ask. Do not demand the “real” name. Do not announce a Korean name in a waiting room as cultural humility.

### Named harms

Adoptee citizenship gaps were a real U.S. legal harm. The Child Citizenship Act of 2000 covered qualifying children under 18 on February 27, 2001, and was not retroactive for those already 18. This brief is about Lao people as a people of Laos — the lowland Lao state history, the Mekong, Theravada wats — and as a Minnesota community counted by Compass as Lao (non-Hmong). This is not Hmong. ### Who this is

This is not a Census “Asian” mash. It is not Thai. It is not Khmer. It is not Vietnamese. Shared continent is not shared culture. The Secret War sits next door. chapters.body:
This brief is about Lao people as a people of Laos — the lowland Lao state history, the Mekong, Theravada wats — and as a Minnesota community counted by Compass as Lao (non-Hmong). This is not Hmong. If the household is Hmong, open Hmong Minnesota and put White Hmong or Mong Leng on the interpreter line. If Lao, book Lao. Do not guess from the war.

### Who this is

This is not a Census “Asian” mash. It is not Thai. It is not Khmer. It is not Vietnamese. Shared continent is not shared culture. The Secret War sits next door. The Hmong alliance with the CIA is a neighboring story, not this people as a footnote. A full mosaic is not a stereotype. A stereotype is when this page becomes the person in the lobby.

### Who this is not

Minnesota Compass (ACS 2019–2023) puts Lao (non-Hmong) near 15,191. About 71.6 percent Twin Cities, 28.4 percent Greater Minnesota. About 21.9 percent age 17 or younger; 13.0 percent 65+. About 49.1 percent foreign-born. Language other than English (age 5+) 71.8 percent; English less than “very well” 36.1 percent. Date the number you use. A rate is not the person.

The diversity inside this people is the point. A person who came through the camps after 1975, a Christian family, a wat household that keeps phi, a U.S.-born nurse, a Greater Minnesota worker the building forgot, a college student who uses English with friends and Lao with an elder — share a people and do not share a Tuesday.

French colonial rule made a border and a school. Independence, the American war in Laos, and 1975 are the modern political sequence. They are not the origin of the people.

### History for the meeting

Lao is related to Thai. Related is not interchangeable. A Thai interpreter is not the default. Isan (northeastern Thai) is a neighboring variety some families will name. Ask. Do not guess.

### What people brought

Hmong people in Laos are a different people. Highland life, clan, and the CIA alliance are the Hmong page. Do not file Lao as the leftover of that war.

What people brought: Lao language, Theravada and phi, kinship, farming, and a memory of a state that changed hands. What they met in Minnesota: an English form, one “Asian” checkbox, and often a Hmong interpreter because the building already has that page.

community.title: Lebanese Minnesota

chapters.body:
This brief is about Lebanese people as a people with a country in the Levant and a Minnesota community that is historic and recent. This is not the Arabic language door. That door is /ci/arabic — a CLAS ten- and fifteen-language line onto many peoples. Do not open it as a synonym for this people-page. This is not Somali. Shared Arabic and shared Islam are not shared culture. Arab Minnesota is not one file.

### Who this is

A full mosaic is not a stereotype. A stereotype is when this page becomes the person in the lobby. Paternalism is one “Arabic interpreter” written for an English-dominant Maronite household, a mosque default, a Somali default because Arabic is on a card, and a 1975 speech you give a third-generation family.

### Who this is not

Minnesota Compass (ACS 2019–2023) puts Lebanese ancestry near 6,959. About 81.0 percent Twin Cities, about 19.0 percent Greater Minnesota. About 20.3 percent age 17 or younger; about 16.4 percent 65+. About 8.5 percent foreign-born — which means a large historic, U.S.-born share. Language other than English (age 5+) 11.8 percent. English less than “very well” is suppressed on that profile. Do not invent a LEP rate. High school or higher 97.9 percent; bachelor’s or higher 50.5 percent. Poverty 12.0 percent. Date the number you use. A rate is not the person.

Christian and Muslim Lebanese both live here. Maronite, Orthodox, Catholic, Protestant; Sunni and Shiʿa. Druze: no dated Minnesota count — do not invent one. If this family is Druze, defer. Do not assume mosque. Do not assume hijab.

### How to read this

Always defer to the person in front of you. This page is a hypothesis you still test on this family.

chapters.title: A Note on This Guide

chapters.body:
Lebanese peoplehood is older than the 1943 independence, older than the 1975–1990 civil war, and older than this department. A Levantine country on the eastern Mediterranean; mountains and coast; Maronite, Orthodox, Sunni, Shiʿa, Druze as named streams. This is literacy for the desk. It is not a speech you give the family. Do not found “the Arabs” in a waiver meeting. Do not lecture a Maronite household about the Hijaz.

### History for the meeting

What people brought: Levantine Arabic for some, French and English for others, a church or a mosque or neither, kinship, and a memory of a state that broke and a diaspora that is old in the Americas. What they met in Minnesota: an English form, a racial order that has often filed Levantine Christians as White and skipped CI, one “Arabic interpreter,” and often a Somali default because the building already has that page.

### What people brought

Do not start with hummus, a cedar, or a Phoenician tourism sentence. Shared language family is not shared culture with Iraq, Egypt, or Somalia.

chapters.title: Origins and the Founding of a People

chapters.body:
Homeland is not one neighborhood in Beirut. Mountains, coast, Bekaa, south — church, mosque, and some speech shift. Confirm the place if they name it. Do not referee in a waiver meeting. Listen.

### Homeland

The diaspora is old in the Americas: Brazil, Argentina, the United States. Dearborn and the Detroit metro hold a large Arab American community. Minnesota is not Dearborn. Do not import a Michigan picture onto a Ramsey County lobby.

### Minnesota

In Minnesota: Twin Cities 81.0 percent; Greater Minnesota 19.0 percent. There is no Cedar-Riverside of Lebanese Minnesota. Do not assume Minneapolis. Do not assume the person in front of you has been to Lebanon.
chapters.evidence: Mountains, coast, Bekaa, south. Diaspora in the Americas is old. Dearborn is not this map. Compass: 81.0% Twin Cities, 19.0% Greater Minnesota.
chapters.practitioner: Do not assume a Little Arabia. Do not assume they have been to Beirut. Greater Minnesota 19.0% is real. Do not import Michigan onto this lobby.
chapters.title: The Geography of Lebanon and Lebanese Minnesota

chapters.body:
If 1975 is Hmong Minnesota and 1991 is Somali Minnesota, Lebanese Minnesota does not get one foundational year that covers the lobby. Late-Ottoman and early-twentieth-century Christian streams built part of U.S. Lebanese life — including families with deep Minnesota roots. Compass foreign-born 8.5 percent (ACS 2019–2023) is the dated share. That is historic. It is not “no immigrant.”

### Foundational events

1975–1990 civil war moved some. 2006. Later economic collapse and the 4 August 2020 Beirut port explosion sit in some later rooms. Secondary migration from other states. U.S.-born children in every stream.

### Who you meet

The desk in 2026 meets an English-dominant third-generation parish household, an elder who needs Levantine Arabic, and a recent arrival. If you only know “refugee” or only know “Muslim,” you will miss this room. Distrust of government has sources that are not one source: 9/11-era surveillance, Gaza-era harassment, and ordinary ICE for some later arrivals. A DHS badge is not automatically help.
chapters.evidence: Late-Ottoman and early-20th-century Christian streams built part of U.S. Lebanese life; 1975–1990 civil war; 2006; later economic collapse and 2020 port explosion as later displacement. Compass foreign-born 8.5% — historic share is the dated fact. Not one refugee poster.
chapters.practitioner: If you only know “Arab immigrant,” you will miss the English-dominant third-generation Maronite household and the recent arrival who still cannot get Levantine in the lobby.

chapters.body:
Who is in the household varies by stream, class, and generation. Compass average household size about 2.14 (ACS 2019–2023) — often smaller, older, more English-dominant than neighboring Arabic-speaking streams. Do not copy it onto a recently arrived household, and do not copy a Sudanese or Iraqi waiver household onto this page.

### Who is in the household

Ask who should be in the room. A nuclear English form already has a who. Elders and adult children may sit in the same week.

### Who speaks

Do not invent a last name because the database wants one. Do not treat unmatched last names as fraud by default. Women’s labor and men’s labor both live here. Gender norms are this family’s, not “Arab.” Ask.

Minnesota law still stands. Domestic violence is not culture. You follow mandated reporting. Do not use a child as interpreter.

chapters.body:
Minnesota holds a Lebanese community large enough for a Compass profile — about 6,959 (ACS 2019–2023) — and large enough that this department will meet it. Greater Minnesota is 19.0 percent. Do not write this people as a Minneapolis anecdote. There is no Cedar-Riverside of Lebanese Minnesota.

### Places

Places, not a blob: Twin Cities; inner-ring suburbs; Greater Minnesota. Named churches — Maronite, Antiochian and other Orthodox, other Catholic and Protestant — and named mosques if this family names them. Partners, not a list to extract from. CECLC is a department door, not the community. Pay the partner this household actually uses.

### Partners

Lebanese staff are not unpaid interpreters and not the community. Identity is not a staffing plan. A Heritage Month table is not consultation. You are a guest. It does not make you the expert.

Do not BCC one priest or one imam and call it consultation.

chapters.title: Minnesota and Lebanese History

chapters.body:
To be Lebanese in Minnesota is to be a people with a country, often filed White, sometimes filed “Arab,” sometimes filed “Muslim” by a building that did not ask. Christian and Muslim both live here. For some, Arabic is the language of the grandmother and the church. For some, it is the language of the Qurʾan and the kitchen. For some U.S.-born adults it is a class they do not speak. Compass LOTE 11.8 percent is dated. It is not “no language gate.”

### In this state

Do not fold this household into Somali Minnesota because both might be Muslim. Do not fold it into /ci/arabic as if a language list were a people. Do not fold it into “MENA” as a file.

Race in the U.S. file has often marked Levantine Christians White. That skip is the gate when the elder needs Levantine. Islamophobia and anti-Arab racism still hit Christian Lebanese when the mash is “Arab.”

This guide is a working orientation. Individual variation always supersedes group generalization. Always defer to this family.

### Christian and Muslim both

Do not assume the mosque. Do not assume the priest. Do not assume hijab.

### Confirm whether Arabic is home language

Levantine if it is. Maghrebi, Egyptian, or MSA can still be a closed door. English-dominant historic share is real. Ask.

### Historic versus later stream

Compass foreign-born 8.5 percent. A third-generation parish household and a 2020 arrival do not share a Tuesday.

### Hospitality as hypothesis

A yes that is courtesy is not a signature. Ask whether they agree.

Do not collect political speech as a risk score.

chapters.title: Core Concepts

chapters.body:
Islam is not Lebanese. Lebanese is not Islam. Maronite, Orthodox, Catholic, Protestant, Sunni, Shiʿa, and none all live in this state. Druze: no dated Minnesota count. Do not invent a community. If this family names Druze, listen. Defer.

### Streams

Do not assume Muslim. Do not assume hijab. Do not rank covering as piety or oppression. Do not make a priest or an imam the case plan unless this family asked.

### Practice

The parish and the mosque are centers of ritual, mutual aid, and information. They are not “the community.” Do not BCC one clergy and call it consultation.

Ramadan, Eid, Christmas, Easter, Maronite and Orthodox calendars — ask. A calendar click is not engagement.
chapters.evidence: Maronite, Orthodox, Catholic, Protestant; Sunni and Shiʿa; Druze: no dated Minnesota count — do not invent one; none. Streams do not share a sanctuary. Ask.

chapters.title: Religion — not the people

chapters.body:
Follow this room. As-salāmu ʿalaykum is ordinary in many Muslim rooms; the reply is wa-ʿalaykumu s-salām. It is not default in a Maronite or Orthodox room. Marḥaban, ahlan, and English hello are ordinary. Say the name.

### Titles

Elders first. Handshake is common in many rooms, including many Christian professional rooms. A hard handshake you assume is universal is already a closed door for some women and some elders. If a hand is not offered, nod. Do not force it.

### This room

Do not import the Black nod onto this page. Do not import Somali greeting rules as if Lebanese were Somali.

Physical contact: ask the room. Cross-gender touch is not a default in some families. It is ordinary in others.
chapters.evidence: Handshake common in many rooms, including many Christian rooms. As-salāmu ʿalaykum in many Muslim rooms — not default in a Maronite room. Marḥaban, ahlan, English hello. Elders first.
chapters.practitioner: Do not force a handshake. Do not use the Islamic greeting as default in a Christian Lebanese room. Follow this room. Say the name.
chapters.title: Greetings

chapters.body:
Naming patterns vary. Some families use given name + father’s name + family name. Some three-part names look like Somali names and are not. Some Lebanese Christian streams use French or English given names and a family surname the database can already see. Some people have Westernized on U.S. forms. Ask.

### How to file

Do not invent a last name because the screen requires one. That invented name becomes a gate.

Pronounce it. Ask. Do not joke about long names. Do not assume three Somali names. Do not assume a hyphen.

Women may or may not take a husband’s family name in U.S. records. Ask how to file. Do not “correct” a mother and child who do not share a last name as a fraud signal until you have a reason.
chapters.evidence: Family surname. Lebanese Christian streams often carry French or English given names. Some three-part. Some Westernized first-middle-last. Ask.
chapters.practitioner: Ask how to say it and how to file it. Do not invent a last name because the screen requires one. Do not assume three Somali names.
chapters.title: Naming Conventions

chapters.body:
Ask this family. Christmas and Easter — Western, Maronite, Orthodox — in Christian rooms. Muslim lunar dates — Ramadan, Eid al-Fitr, Eid al-Adha — in Muslim rooms. Independence 22 November. 1975 is literacy, not a holiday. 4 August 2020 is memory for some later rooms.

### Calendar

11 September 2001 is structure in this country, not a holiday and not a personality. Gaza-era harassment is current structure. Neither is a calendar click that makes you engaged.

Do not put “Arab holiday” or “Muslim holiday” on a case note without asking. A calendar click is literacy. It is not community engagement.
chapters.evidence: Christmas and Easter (Western, Maronite, Orthodox) in Christian rooms; Ramadan and Eid in Muslim rooms; Independence 22 November; 1975 is literacy not a holiday; 4 August 2020 port explosion memory for some.
chapters.practitioner: A calendar click is literacy. It is not community engagement. Ask this family. Do not put “Muslim holiday” on a Christian household.
chapters.title: Dates of Significance

chapters.body:
Compass (ACS 2019–2023): among Lebanese Minnesotans 25 and older, about 97.9 percent high school or higher; about 50.5 percent bachelor’s or higher. Date Compass. About 8.5 percent of the community is foreign-born. High attainment and a large U.S.-born share are not “no language gate” for the household that needs Levantine Arabic.

### School and language

A parent who speaks fluent Arabic and limited English is not illiterate. Literacy in Modern Standard Arabic is not guaranteed for every dialect speaker. The English-only IEP is the gate when Arabic is home.

The child is not the interpreter. Do not skip the interpreter because Compass LOTE is 11.8 percent. Do not copy this attainment onto an Iraqi or Sudanese parent, and do not copy those pages onto this one.

chapters.body:
Hospitality is a virtue in many rooms. Accept a little tea if offered. You still keep medical and legal time.

### In the home

Shoes off in some homes. Right hand for food in some Muslim rooms. Do not import a rule you learned on the Somali page as automatic.

### Time

Do not assume a woman will or will not cover. Do not photograph a family and call it rapport. Do not enter a prayer space as a tour.

On-time for appointments. Multi-household logistics are real. Courtesy-yes then no-show happens when the plan was never agreed. Ask whether they agree. Confirm in the language they use.

Levantine Arabic if Arabic is the home language. Confirm whether it is. Compass: among those 5 and older, about 11.8 percent speak a language other than English. English less than “very well” is suppressed on the Compass Lebanese profile. Do not invent a LEP rate. A large historic share is English-dominant. The elder who is not still needs the line.

### Language

An interpreter labeled Arabic who speaks Maghrebi, or who tests the elder in fuṣḥā, can still be a closed door. Confirm dialect. Do not open Somali Minnesota by default because Arabic is on a card. On a Somali household, Arabic may be recitation — that is the other door.

A short English yes may be exhaustion or courtesy. Do not take a smile as consent. Do not make a coworker the interpreter. The child is not the interpreter.

chapters.title: Language and Communication

chapters.body:
Unvarnished, because Minnesota Nice is how a room that treats everyone the same deletes facts.

### Named harms

Islamophobia and anti-Arab racism after 11 September 2001 and after Gaza are structure in this country and in this state. They hit Muslim Lebanese and they hit Christian Lebanese when the mash is “Arab.” They change who opens the door. That is not noncompliance.

Do not collect political speech as a risk score. Do not file a protest, a flag, or an opinion about Gaza or Hezbollah as a safety note. Enforcement climate is real for some later arrivals. Do not collect status you do not need.

Queer and trans Lebanese exist. You use the name. You do not out someone to kin and call it culture.

Do not assume hijab. Do not assume Muslim. Do not skip mandated reporting and call it humility.

Staff who share this community may add facts. They do not get to delete a fact because it is hard to say.

chapters.practitioner: Follow law. Still see a family. Do not out anyone. Do not collect status you do not need. Do not collect political speech as a risk score. Do not skip mandated reporting and call it humility.
chapters.title: Other Considerations — unvarnished, not Minnesota Nice

chapters.body:
No dated Minnesota-wide Lebanese autism, diabetes, or PTSD rate belongs on this page beyond Compass poverty 12.0 percent (ACS 2019–2023). Do not invent one. War trauma sits in some later streams. It is not a personality and not every household.

### Access

Gender match may be requested in maternal and intimate care. Offer it. Believe reported pain. Do not fold this page into Tuskegee or into a generic “stoicism” slide. Do not skip screening because Compass looks English-dominant.

Mental-health stigma exists in some families. So does a fierce wish for services. You can hold both. Confirm the language. Identification is not a community personality.

chapters.title: Health

chapters.body:
Queer and trans Lebanese Minnesotans exist. Conservative church, mosque, and family climates can mean silence or exile. Some people live a public English life and a private home life. You use the name they use. You do not out them to an elder as cultural humility.

### This person

Minnesota’s Human Rights Act still applies. So does the duty not to treat a whole people as a family-values exhibit.

Do not use this chapter to raid a household. Do not pretend the tension is not there.
chapters.evidence: Queer and trans Lebanese Minnesotans exist. Conservative family, church, and mosque climates can mean silence.
chapters.practitioner: Use the name. Do not out someone to family as culture.
chapters.title: LGBTQ

chapters.body:
Hijab, niqab, and modest dress are ordinary for some Muslim women and not for others. Christian Lebanese dress is Minnesota dress plus, for some, church clothes. Do not assume covering. Do not rank covering as piety or oppression. Second generation looks like Minnesota. Do not ask whether they “still dress Lebanese.”

### Dress

This is not the CROWN Act chapter. Do not mash.

Do not touch. Do not police covering. Do not assume a covered woman cannot speak for herself — ask her, with a gender-matched interpreter if she wants one.
chapters.evidence: Hijab and modest dress for some Muslim women; not all. Christian Lebanese dress is not a costume. Second generation looks like Minnesota. This is not the CROWN Act chapter.

chapters.title: Hair, Dress, and Body

chapters.body:
Lebanese musical life is not one playlist. Levantine pop, dabke, Fairuz as public memory in some rooms, Maronite and Orthodox hymnody, and religious caution about some music in some families all exist.

### Variation

A playlist is not engagement. Do not request a dabke as icebreaker in a waiver meeting.

A liturgy is not staff entertainment.
chapters.evidence: Levantine pop, dabke, Fairuz as public memory in some rooms, Maronite and Orthodox hymnody. Named variation. Religious caution about some music in some families.

chapters.title: Music

chapters.body:
Soccer is a common public sport in many streams. Basketball shows up in the second generation. Do not assume the kid plays. Do not make sport the only excellence you can see.

### Not the whole person

Sport clubs are social infrastructure. They are not language access and not a case plan.

World Cup loyalties are not a risk score.
chapters.evidence: Soccer is common public sport in many streams; basketball in the second generation. Not a people-trait.
chapters.practitioner: Do not assume the kid plays. Sport clubs are not language access.
chapters.title: Sports

chapters.body:
Arabic is one of the world’s major literary languages. French and English letters sit in Lebanese streams as well. This is not a people without letters. Poetry is prestige in some rooms. The Qurʾan is recitation and scripture in Muslim rooms — not a literacy test you give a dialect-speaking elder in the lobby.

### Literacy in the lobby

MSA and dialect are not the same skill. A person who does not read fuṣḥā is not a person without letters. A U.S.-born adult who does not read Arabic is still this people-page.

You do not need to quote a poet. You need the language this person reads.
chapters.evidence: Arabic is a major literary language; French and English letters in Lebanese streams. This is not a people without letters. Literacy in Arabic is not guaranteed for the U.S.-born.

chapters.title: Literature

chapters.body:
Calligraphy in some rooms, church iconography in Christian streams, Levantine visual work, contemporary diaspora artists. Guest, not researcher.

### Guest

A museum visit is optional professional development. It is not consultation.

Do not put a camel or a keffiyeh on a Heritage Month table and call it this people. Do not mash with a Somali table because both might be Muslim.

chapters.body:
1975–1990 civil war, 2006, 2019–present economic collapse, 4 August 2020 port explosion, 11 September 2001 and what the United States did in its name, Gaza-era harassment, enforcement against some later arrivals — that is the political stack. Anti-Arab racism and Islamophobia are structure. They hit Christian Lebanese when the mash is “Arab.” They are not a personality.

### The badge

Do not collect political speech as a risk score. A flag, a protest, a sermon, an opinion about Gaza or Hezbollah is not a safety note.

paragraphs: Liberian Minnesota. Not historic African American. English and Liberian English / Kolokwa. Compass ACS 2019–2023 near 20,720. Compass AA profile includes some Liberian ancestry other counts exclude — this page is not that mash. Date the number you cite.
