community.title: Mexican Minnesota

chapters.body:
This brief is about Mexican Minnesota — mexicano, mexicana. It is the largest Latino origin in this state. Mexico is many peoples. Mixtec (Ñuu Savi) and Zapotec (Benizaa) may be in the home here. A Spanish interpreter can still be a closed door.

### Who this is

Mexican Minnesota. Not the Latino / Hispanic umbrella. Not a synonym for every Spanish-surnamed household in the lobby. Minnesota Compass (ACS 2019–2023) puts the Mexican cultural community at 229,576. Twin Cities 61.1 percent; Greater Minnesota 38.9 percent — nearly 4 in 10 live outside the Twin Cities (Compass Points 2023). About 38.0 percent age 17 or younger; 4.0 percent 65+. Foreign-born 26.7 percent — a majority in that vintage were born here. Language other than English (age 5+) 58.3 percent; English less than “very well” 23.7 percent. Date the number you use. Mixtec and Zapotec may be in the home; Compass does not count speakers. Do not invent that count. A rate is not the person.

### Who this is not

This is not Guatemalan. It is not Salvadoran. It is not Puerto Rican. Shared Spanish is not shared culture. Open the Latino umbrella only as adjacent. That page is the mash and the CLAS Spanish line. This page is Mexican. If you file the household under “Latino” because the checkbox was easier, you have left this door.

### How to read this

Read it as an orientation. A Mixtec dairy worker in a southern county, a U.S.-born professional in a first-ring suburb, a West Side elder whose family has been in St. Paul longer than your unit, a Jalisco restaurant household, a college student who uses English with friends and Spanish with a grandmother, a person who will not open the door because a relative can be moved — share a people and do not share a Tuesday.

Always defer to the person in front of you. The facts that follow are meant to help you meet people well — how family is named, what respect looks like, what a greeting carries, what a form may land on. History is here so the meeting is clearer, not so you deliver a lecture.
chapters.evidence: Mexican Minnesota. Largest Latino origin. Compass ACS 2019–2023: 229,576; Greater MN 38.9% (nearly 4 in 10 — Compass Points 2023). Mixtec/Zapotec may be in the home. Not the Latino umbrella. Not Guatemalan, Salvadoran, or Puerto Rican. Date the number you cite.
chapters.practitioner: There is no single Mexican client. Defer to this family. Do not open the Latino umbrella, a Guatemalan, Salvadoran, or Puerto Rican case with this page. Ask language. Pronounce the name.
chapters.title: A Note on This Guide

chapters.body:
Mexican peoplehood is older than the Bracero program, older than IRCA, and older than the Minnesota plant.

### Many peoples

A country on the land between the United States and Guatemala. Mestizo majority narratives. Mixtec, Zapotec, Purépecha, Maya in the south, and other indigenous nations whose languages may be in a Minnesota home. Ask. Do not lecture a Worthington family about taxonomy they did not ask for.

### History for the meeting

Spanish colonial rule, Catholic mission, independence (the Grito of 16 September 1810; consummation 1821), the Revolution after 1910, and a modern republic that has both claimed and erased indigenous nations — that is literacy for the meeting. It is not a speech you give the family. Do not start with food, a sombrero, or a Heritage Month sentence.

Writing in Spanish is the ordinary public literacy of the Mexican state. Mixtec and Zapotec are languages, not dialects of Spanish. Some elders read Spanish. Some do not. Some U.S.-born adults do not read Spanish either. Oral skill is not print.

### What people brought

Language (Spanish varieties and indigenous languages), kinship, parish and later evangelical church, farm and trade skill, Guadalupe, a memory of a border that used them. What they met in Minnesota: an English form, one “Latino” checkbox, often one interpreter labeled Spanish, and a rural plant town or a St. Paul lobby that had not studied Mixtec.
chapters.evidence: Mexico is many peoples: mestizo majority narratives, and Mixtec, Zapotec, and other indigenous nations. Spanish colonial history, independence, Revolution. Not a Central American file.
chapters.practitioner: History is literacy for the desk. It is not a speech you give the family. Do not start with a taco tourism sentence.
chapters.title: Origins and the Founding of a People

chapters.body:
Mexico is not one climate and not one Spanish.

### Mexico

North, center, south; Oaxaca, Michoacán, Jalisco, Guanajuato, the border states, Mexico City — tones, food, and some vocabulary shift. Confirm the place if they name it. Do not referee Monterrey versus Oaxaca in a waiver meeting. Listen if they name a pueblo.

### United States and Minnesota

The U.S. Mexican map is California, Texas, Illinois, the Southwest, and also the Upper Midwest plant and dairy counties that a Minneapolis default still treats as leftover. Compass: 61.1 percent Twin Cities, 38.9 percent Greater Minnesota. Nearly 4 in 10 (Compass Points 2023). Worthington, Willmar, Austin, Albert Lea, and dairy counties are names you should be able to hold without turning them into a tour.

### Metro

West Side St. Paul / District del Sol is historic Mexican Minnesota, not a museum. Lake Street and Phillips, first-ring suburbs, scattered apartments near plants. Do not assume West Side. Do not assume the person in front of you has been to Mexico. A Greater Minnesota household is still this people.
chapters.evidence: Mexico — north, center, south, Oaxaca, Michoacán, Jalisco, the border. U.S. Mexican America is California, Texas, Illinois, and Minnesota. Compass: 61.1% Twin Cities, 38.9% Greater Minnesota.
chapters.practitioner: Do not assume West Side St. Paul. Do not assume they have been to Mexico. A Worthington, Willmar, or dairy-county household is not an afterthought.
chapters.title: The Geography of the Mexican World

chapters.body:
If 1975 is the foundational event of Vietnamese Minnesota, Mexican Minnesota is stacked.

### Labor and settlement

Labor recruitment into sugar beet, cannery, and later plants and dairy. The Bracero program (1942–1964) as U.S. policy literacy. IRCA-era settlement after 1986. Later family and work streams. Enforcement waves that reorganize who will open the door. This is not a Guatemalan war file and not a Salvadoran TPS file.

Mexican migrant farm labor in Minnesota is older than the current plant map. Settlement followed work, church, and IRCA. Secondary migration pulled kin.

### Who you meet

The desk in 2026 does not only meet a first wave. It meets U.S.-born children — Compass foreign-born 26.7 percent — translating for parents, mixed-status households, and a Mixtec household that has been in a dairy county for years and still cannot get Mixtec in the lobby.

### Enforcement

Enforcement is current structure. When raids, rumored raids, or a visible ICE climate spike, people skip clinic, school, and waiver meetings. That is not noncompliance. A notice mailed to a household afraid to open the door is a closed gate. Do not collect status you do not need. The desk that asks “are you legal?” on visit one has already chosen a who.

If you only know “immigrant,” you will miss the majority born here and still treat the English IEP as culturally neutral.
chapters.evidence: Labor recruitment; sugar beet and seasonal harvest; Bracero; IRCA-era settlement; later family and work streams; enforcement waves. Not a 1990s Central American war file.
chapters.practitioner: If you only know “immigrant,” you will miss the U.S.-born majority (foreign-born 26.7%) and the Mixtec dairy worker who still cannot get the right language in the lobby.
chapters.title: Labor, IRCA, and Enforcement — Foundational Events

chapters.body:
Familismo is a hypothesis, not a personality. Elders often speak first.

### Who is in the household

Adult children may be in the same week as a waiver meeting, a plant shift, and a school conference. Compass: average household size about 3.09. Still not always a nuclear English form. Grandparents may be the household. Who cares for a disabled adult or a child may be a son, a daughter-in-law, a sibling, a padrino — not the legally recognized caregiver on the checkbox.

Hour caps and “natural supports” language can dump unpaid work onto women in that network and call it culture.

### Mixed-status

Mixed-status is structure: a U.S.-citizen child, a parent without status, a sibling with DACA, an aunt who works the plant. Do not collect status you do not need. Do not treat unmatched last names, a grandmother as caregiver, or a missing SSN as fraud until you have a reason.

### Who speaks

Who speaks in the lobby may be a child with the best English. That child is not the qualified interpreter. CLAS still stands. Using a child as the go-between is a closed door and a harm: it reverses respeto, it leaks adult business, and it is not language access. Book the interpreter. Ask who should be in the room.

Minnesota law still stands. Domestic violence is not culture. Do not skip mandated reporting and call it humility.
chapters.evidence: Familismo as hypothesis; elders; mixed-status households. Compass average household size about 3.09. Who speaks may be a child — that is a gate. Do not collect status you do not need.
chapters.practitioner: Ask who should be in the room. Do not use a child as interpreter. A nuclear English form already has a who. Mixed-status is structure.
chapters.title: Family

chapters.body:
Minnesota holds the largest Latino-origin community in the state. Compass: 229,576 (ACS 2019–2023). Greater Minnesota is 38.9 percent — nearly 4 in 10 (Compass Points 2023). Do not write this people as a Minneapolis anecdote. Human services will meet it on waivers, child welfare, health care, cash, food, aging, and employment, in a plant town and on the West Side.

### Places

West Side St. Paul / District del Sol — historic Mexican Minnesota, not a museum. Lake Street and Phillips. First-ring suburbs. Worthington, Willmar, Austin, Albert Lea, dairy counties, southern and western towns. Markets and taquerías are public life. They are not consultation. A food-court visit does not make you the expert.

### Partners

CLUES — Comunidades Latinas Unidas En Servicio (https://clues.org/). Centro Tyrone Guzmán. Rural parish and worker centers — name the local one; do not assume Minneapolis. Churches are often the actual safe channel. CECLC is a department door, not the whole community. Pay the partner this household actually uses.

Mexican staff are not unpaid interpreters and not the community. Identity is not a staffing plan. A fiesta or a Guadalupe mass is optional professional development if you are invited. You are a guest. It does not make you the expert.
chapters.evidence: West Side St. Paul / District del Sol; Lake Street; first-ring suburbs; plants and dairy in southern and western towns. Compass Greater MN 38.9%. CLUES; Centro Tyrone Guzmán; rural parish and worker centers.
chapters.practitioner: Partners, not a harvest list. Staff are colleagues, not the curriculum. Do not treat  Mexican staff. Guest at a fiesta if invited. A taco visit does not make you the expert. Name the local partner — do not assume Minneapolis.
chapters.title: Minnesota and Mexican History

chapters.body:
To be Mexican in Minnesota is to be a people with a country, indigenous nations inside that country, and a long memory of labor that built someone else’s harvest, then building a life in a cold state that filed you under Latino.

### Face and kin

Face, kin obligation, and not shaming the name travel into a waiver meeting. Harmony can look like agreement and then a plan nobody follows. Ask whether they agree. Do not take a smile as consent.

Mixtec and Zapotec peoplehood is not a dialect note. A household that names Mixtec is not “Mexican Spanish with an accent.” The mash is the gate.

### Under a Latino checkbox

In the United States another fact sits on the same desk: Mexican Minnesota is the largest origin under a Latino checkbox that also holds Guatemalan, Salvadoran, Puerto Rican, and Andean histories they do not share. The Mexican default in this state is a count fact. It becomes a harm when the building treats this page as the only Latino file.

This brief is a working orientation. Individual variation always supersedes group generalization. Always defer to the person in front of you.
chapters.evidence: Mexicano / Mexican. Peoplehood after labor, border, and a U.S. checkbox that files you under Latino. Face, kin, work as a family project. Mixtec and Zapotec are peoples, not accents.
chapters.practitioner: Do not fold this household into one Latino blob. Do not copy a Guatemalan, Salvadoran, or Puerto Rican sentence onto this page. Open the Latino umbrella only as adjacent.
chapters.title: Mexicano — the heart of a people

chapters.body:
These concepts recur. They are hypotheses you still test on this family.

### Familismo

Kin as the unit of decision and care. Hypothesis, not a rule. The person who talks in the lobby may not be the person who decides. Ask who should be in the room. Not a license to skip mandated reporting. Staff do not use it as a guilt tool.

### Respeto

Titles, elders, usted. A first-name lobby and a joking tone can read as contempt. Follow this room. A courtesy-yes is not a signature. Ask again, plainly, without humiliation.

### Personalismo and confianza

Relationship before a long form. The first visit may be about whether you are safe. That is not delay. The clock still exists for medical and legal time. Enforcement climate, a bad interpreter, a child used as the mouth, an SSN field that feels like a trap — these spend confianza before you have it.

### Two surnames

Apellido paterno then apellido materno. The database that keeps one invents a person.

### Mixtec and Zapotec

Peoples and languages. A Spanish interpreter can still be a closed door. Compass does not count speakers. Ask.

Work, school, Guadalupe, mixed-status. A plant shift and a second-generation degree can sit in the same household. Do not collect status you do not need.
chapters.evidence: Familismo, respeto, personalismo as hypotheses; two surnames; Mixtec/Zapotec in some homes; Guadalupe; work and school as family project; mixed-status as structure.
chapters.practitioner: You work with these. You do not perform them. Do not make a priest the case plan unless this family asked. Do not collect status you do not need.
chapters.title: Core Concepts

chapters.body:
Catholic majority in many Mexican Minnesota streams — not all.

### Parish and church

Our Lady of Guadalupe (12 December) is central in many Catholic lives. The parish may be the trusted channel for information, mutual aid, baptismal records, and a room people will enter when they will not enter yours. Evangelical and Pentecostal churches are large. Indigenous practice lives in some Mixtec and Zapotec homes and is not a souvenir.

Do not make a priest, a pastor, or a curandero the case plan unless this family asked. Do not BCC one parish and call it consultation. Do not treat evangelical growth as the evolved version of Catholic, or indigenous practice as witchcraft.

### Calendar and public history

Día de los Muertos is public history — ofrendas, 1–2 November — not a file and not a personality. Holy Week, quinceañera as religious-family event, Las Posadas, and funeral obligation can collide with your calendar. You still keep medical and legal time. You name the conflict instead of punishing it. Do not photograph an ofrenda or a Guadalupe altar.

Help that looks like a report is not help. Religious framing of disability, mental health, or gender can sit next to a fierce wish for services. You can hold both.
chapters.evidence: Catholic majority in many streams; evangelical and Pentecostal large; indigenous practice in some homes. Our Lady of Guadalupe (Dec 12). Parish may be the trusted channel.
chapters.practitioner: Do not make a priest or a pastor the case plan unless this family asked. Do not treat Mixtec practice as folklore. Día de los Muertos is public history, not a file.
chapters.title: Religion

chapters.body:
Elders first. A handshake is common in many rooms. A slight nod with an older person is safer than a hard first-name hello you assume is warmth.

### Titles

Some streams greet familiars with a cheek kiss — follow this room; do not initiate because a training slide said Latinos are tactile.

Titles until invited: Señor, Señora, Don, Doña. Use the last name you were given — and remember there may be two. Do not use a first name with an elder because the form printed it. Usted versus tú is respect in Spanish; a qualified interpreter matches register. You do not correct it.

### This room

Do not import Somali right-hand rules or the Black nod onto this page. This is not those grammars. Cross-gender touch with elders is not a default. A hug from staff is not warmth if the household did not offer it.
chapters.evidence: Elders first. Handshake common. Titles — Señor, Señora, Don, Doña — until invited. Usted is respect in many Spanish rooms.
chapters.practitioner: Do not force a first name on an elder because the form printed it. Do not import Somali or African American greeting rules. Say the name.
chapters.title: Greetings

chapters.body:
Two surnames is the default in much of Mexican Spanish-language naming: apellido paterno then apellido materno.

### Two surnames

José Luis García Hernández is not “José García” with leftover words. A U.S. database that keeps one surname invents a person. That invented name then follows them through MHCP, child welfare, and school. It is a gate.

Ask how to file. Ask how to say it. Pronounce it. Do not drop accents as a joke. Do not anglicize Jesús, Muñoz, Ñ as a convenience. Given names may be Spanish, Mixtec, Zapotec, English, or both. Some people use a middle given name as the call-name. Ask.

### How to file

Women may or may not take a husband’s surname in U.S. records; some add de plus the husband’s paternal surname; some keep both family surnames. Children may carry two surnames that do not match a parent’s U.S. “last name” field. That is not fraud until you have a reason.

Do not treat unmatched last names in a household as a fraud flag by default. Do not invent a hyphen and then punish the person when the hyphen moves.
chapters.evidence: Two surnames: apellido paterno + apellido materno. U.S. databases that keep one invent a person. Given names may be Spanish, indigenous, English, or both.
chapters.practitioner: Ask how to file. Ask how to say it. Do not drop the second surname as clutter. Unmatched last names in a household are not fraud by default.
chapters.title: Naming Conventions

chapters.body:
A calendar click is literacy for scheduling. It is not community engagement.

### Independence and Guadalupe

16 September — Mexican independence. Literacy for the meeting. Cinco de Mayo is the Battle of Puebla (1862), not independence, and not a party you put on a case note as the national day. Do not file this household under a restaurant calendar.

12 December — Our Lady of Guadalupe. Major for many Mexican Catholic families. Las Posadas in some streams (mid-December). Día de los Reyes / Three Kings — 6 January. Holy Week. Quinceañera is family-religious time, not a case note.

### Día de los Muertos

1–2 November. Public history in Minnesota. Guest if you are in a public ofrenda space. Not a file. Not a costume for staff.

Hispanic Heritage Month (15 September–15 October) is the umbrella calendar. It is not this people’s day and not consultation. Do not put “Latino holiday” on a case note.
chapters.evidence: 16 September (independence — not Cinco de Mayo). 12 December Guadalupe. Día de los Muertos (Nov 1–2). Las Posadas. Literacy, not a holiday sticker.
chapters.practitioner: A calendar click is literacy. It is not community engagement. Do not put “Cinco de Mayo party” on a file as the national day.
chapters.title: Dates of Significance

chapters.body:
Compass (ACS 2019–2023): among Mexican Minnesotans 25 and older, about 71.5 percent high school or higher; about 18.9 percent bachelor’s or higher. Date Compass. About 26.7 percent of the community is foreign-born.

### School and language

A large share of children are U.S.-born and in English-dominant schools. The IEP still has to reach the parent who does not read it.

A parent who speaks fluent Spanish, or fluent Mixtec, and limited English is not illiterate. Some elders read Spanish. Some do not. Mixtec or Zapotec in the home is not a Spanish IEP. The English-only form is the gate. Do not use a child as interpreter.

### Mobility and gap

Second-generation educational mobility is real. So is a gap that a room that treats everyone the same will call “culture” instead of language access plus poverty plus enforcement fear plus a school that never learned the second surname. Do not treat a college student as proof the waiver household needs no interpreter.
chapters.evidence: Compass: ~71.5% high school or higher (25+); ~18.9% bachelor’s or higher. Foreign-born 26.7%. English IEP is still a gate for the parent who does not read it. Mixtec is not a Spanish IEP.
chapters.practitioner: A parent who speaks fluent Spanish or Mixtec and limited English is not illiterate. The English-only packet is the gate. Do not use a child as interpreter.
chapters.title: Education

chapters.body:
Elders first. Titles. Accept a little food if offered. Hospitality is a virtue. You still keep medical and legal time.

### In the home

Do not walk into a living room and photograph an ofrenda or a Guadalupe altar. Do not touch ritual objects. Do not ask an elder to explain “your culture” as entertainment. Shoes: follow the household.

### Time

On-time for appointments. Traffic, plant shifts, and multi-household logistics are real. So is a pattern of courtesy-yes then no-show when the plan was never agreed. Ask whether they agree. Confirm in the language they use. Do not write a “Latino time” joke in a case note.

Do not use a child as the go-between and call it family values. Book the interpreter.
chapters.evidence: Elders first. Hospitality. Titles. Food. Do not photograph an ofrenda or a Guadalupe altar.
chapters.practitioner: Accept a little food. Keep medical and legal time. Do not use a child as the go-between. Relationship before the packet is not delay.
chapters.title: Etiquette

chapters.body:
Mexican Spanish is not Salvadoran Spanish, not Caribbean Spanish, and not one interpreter accent test.

### Spanish

Book a qualified Spanish interpreter AND ask this household. Register matters: usted, not a buddy tú, until the room says otherwise.

### Mixtec and Zapotec

Mixtec and Zapotec may be in the home. Compass notes the language possibility; it is not a count of speakers. Do not invent that count. A Spanish interpreter for those households is still a closed door. Name the language on the request. A scarce interpreter is a gate, not an excuse to proceed in English only without recording the gap.

### What Compass shows

Among those 5 and older, about 58.3 percent speak a language other than English; about 23.7 percent speak English less than “very well.” Date the number. Many U.S.-born people use English with peers and Spanish with an elder. The IEP still has to reach the parent. Literacy in any language is not guaranteed: oral skill is not print.

A long answer may be story. A short English yes may be exhaustion or courtesy. Do not take a smile as consent. Ask whether they agree with the plan. Do not use a child as the interpreter. Do not make a Mexican coworker the interpreter.

Unvarnished, because Minnesota Nice is how a room that treats everyone the same deletes facts.

### Enforcement

ICE and enforcement climate is structure. Mixed-status households skip clinic, school, and waiver meetings when a relative can be moved. That is not noncompliance. Do not collect status you do not need. SSN on the first screen is a gate.

### Named harms

Indigenous erasure under “they all speak Spanish” is a named harm. Mixtec, Zapotec. A Spanish interpreter can still be a closed door. Colorism is real. Intra-Latino hierarchy is real: the Mexican default in this state will talk over a Maya or Caribbean household if you let the umbrella page do this page’s job — and this page will talk over Mixtec if you let mestizo Spanish be the only file.

Machismo is a named harm, not a joke and not “that’s culture.” Who speaks in the meeting, who holds the papers, who is allowed to leave the house — ask, and follow law. Domestic violence is not culture. You follow mandated reporting. You still see a family.

LGBTQ Mexican Minnesotans exist. You use the name. You do not out someone to kin and call it familismo. Staff who share this community may add facts. They do not get to delete a fact because it is hard to say.

Believe reported pain. Do not invent “Latino stoicism” or “they are dramatic.” Do not fold this history into Tuskegee or into a generic immigrant-mistrust slide.

### Patterns to date

U.S. public-health literature has treated Mexican-origin adults as a higher-prevalence group for type 2 diabetes — date the CDC page you cite. Do not invent a Minnesota rate. Do not skip screening because the person looks well. Uninsured and delayed-care patterns sit here. Date Minnesota figures when you have them. Compass poverty (ACS 2019–2023) is 12.8 percent — a poverty figure, not an uninsured rate.

### Access

Fear of the lobby is a health access fact. A badge, a form that asks for SSN, a child called to interpret a diagnosis, an interpreter who does not speak this Spanish or this Mixtec — these are clinical events. When enforcement spikes, people skip clinic. That is not noncompliance.

Traditional medicine, yerberías, and parish prayer can sit next to a fierce wish for biomedicine. Ask. Co-create. Do not mock. Gender match may be requested in maternal and intimate care. Offer it. Do not use a child as interpreter in a health encounter. Mental-health stigma is real in some families. A smile is not a PHQ-9.

### Dress

Mixtec and Zapotec dress is public at fiesta and ceremony, not a daily costume, and not yours to request for a Heritage Month photo. Do not ask a woman in clinic whether she “still wears the costume.”

Colorism and hair texture are real. Mestizo default beauty is a hierarchy. Name it if it is in the room. Do not rank. Do not touch.

### Labor and the badge

U.S. recruitment, Bracero, IRCA 1986 and settlement, and enforcement that reorganizes Tuesday. A DHS badge is not automatically help. That is not paranoia. It is pattern.

sections.heading: A Note on This Guide
paragraphs: Nigerian Minnesota. Not Somali. Yoruba, Igbo, Hausa, Edo, and others. Compass ACS 2019–2023 near 18,141. Census Black mixes this with historic African American and other African immigrant communities. Date the number you cite.
There is no single Nigerian client. Defer to this family. Do not open Somali or historic African American with this page. Book the language they name. Not one “African” interpreter.

This brief is about Nigerian Minnesota as a state-name community of many peoples. Yoruba, Igbo, Hausa, Edo, Ijaw, Tiv, Ibibio, Fulani, and others are not one file. Book the language this household names. English is official. Nigerian Pidgin is a language, not broken English. Yoruba is not Igbo. Hausa is not Yoruba. A “Nigerian interpreter” is not a language. An “African interpreter” is a closed door.

### Who this is

This is not Somali. Shared race in the United States is not shared culture. This is not historic African American. Compass African American is a different mash. This is not Liberian as a synonym — related West African coast, different state, different war, different languages. This is not Ghanaian.

### Who this is not

Minnesota Compass (ACS 2019–2023) puts Nigerian Minnesota near 18,141. About 87.6 percent Twin Cities, about 12.4 percent Greater Minnesota. About 29.9 percent age 17 or younger; about 8.2 percent 65+. About 60.3 percent foreign-born. Language other than English (age 5+) 55.7 percent; English less than “very well” 7.6 percent. Bachelor’s or higher (25+) 54.0 percent. Date the number. A rate is not the person. High attainment is not the interpreter.

The diversity inside this state name is the point. A Yoruba Pentecostal professional, an Igbo Catholic household that still names Biafra, a Hausa Muslim family, an Edo association member, a U.S.-born student who uses English with friends and Igbo with an elder, a Greater Minnesota nurse — share a Compass row and do not share a Tuesday.

### How to read this

Always defer to the person in front of you. This page is a hypothesis you still test on this family.

sections.heading: Origins and the Founding of a People
paragraphs: Nigeria is a state of many nations. Yoruba, Igbo, Hausa-Fulani, Edo, Ijaw, Tiv, Ibibio, and others. English as official language. Independence 1960. Biafra 1967–70 as Igbo literacy, not a speech. Not a camp origin myth.
History is literacy for the desk. It is not a speech you give the family. Do not start with a Nollywood tourism sentence. Ask which people they are.

Nigeria is a state of many nations. Yoruba peoplehood in the southwest, Igbo peoplehood in the southeast, Hausa-Fulani in the north, Edo, Ijaw, Tiv, Ibibio, and hundreds of others. There is no single Nigerian ethnicity. Ask which people they are. Do not lecture taxonomy they did not ask for.

### History for the meeting

English as official language is colonial history. Independence in 1960. Biafra — 1967–1970 — is foundational literacy for many Igbo households. It is not a speech you give the family. It is not every Nigerian’s story. Do not referee it in a waiver meeting.

### What people brought

What people brought: ethnic language, English, Pidgin, church and mosque, titles, kin obligation, a memory of colony and of a civil war some will name and some will not. What they met in Minnesota: an English form, one “African” checkbox, one “Black” mash, and often Somali because the building already has that page.

Do not start with a Nollywood or jollof tourism sentence. Origins did not begin in Minneapolis.

sections.heading: The Geography of the Nigerian World
paragraphs: Nigeria — southwest Yoruba, southeast Igbo, north Hausa-Fulani, Niger Delta, Middle Belt. Diaspora in Texas, New York, Maryland/D.C., Georgia, Minnesota. Compass: 87.6% Twin Cities, 12.4% Greater Minnesota.
Do not assume Minneapolis. Do not assume Lagos. Greater Minnesota share is real. Do not assume they have been to Nigeria.

Homeland is not one map. Lagos and the Yoruba southwest, Igbo southeast, Hausa-Fulani north, Niger Delta, Middle Belt. Abuja is not the whole. A person may name Ibadan, Enugu, Kano, Benin City, Port Harcourt, a village — not the capital. Do not referee regional politics in a waiver meeting. Listen if they name a place.

### Homeland

The diaspora is global and large: Texas, New York, Maryland and D.C., Georgia, the UK, the Gulf. Minnesota is a real community, not the U.S. capital of it. Secondary migration, church networks, school, and professional work pulled people here.

### Minnesota

In Minnesota: Compass 87.6 percent Twin Cities, 12.4 percent Greater Minnesota. Do not assume Minneapolis. Do not assume Cedar-Riverside. Do not assume the person in front of you has been to Nigeria. Inner-ring suburbs and Greater Minnesota towns with hospitals and housing are still this people.

sections.heading: Independence, Biafra, and Later Streams — Foundational Events
paragraphs: Independence 1960; Biafra 1967–70 as a named stream for some Igbo households; later student, skilled, and family streams; diversity visas. U.S.-born children. Not a single refugee file.
If you only know “African,” you will book the wrong language. If you only know “refugee,” you will miss the professional who still cannot get Igbo in the lobby.

There is no single 1975 or 1991 on this page. Independence in 1960 is the political founding of the state. Biafra, 1967–1970, is the foundational political event of much of Igbo Minnesota’s first memory. Dead in the millions by some counts. Famine as a weapon. That sentence is literacy. It is not a speech. It is not every Nigerian household.

### Foundational events

Later Minnesota streams are mixed: students, skilled work including healthcare, family reunification, diversity visas. Do not file every Nigerian household as refugee. Do not file every Nigerian household as a doctor. Both sit in this Compass row.

### Who you meet

The desk in 2026 meets first-generation professionals and U.S.-born children — English with peers, still translating for a grandmother whose Igbo or Yoruba was never booked, still filed under Black or under African.

If you only know “African,” you will miss this household.

sections.heading: Family
paragraphs: Extended households and titles in some rooms; nuclear forms in others. Compass average household size 2.63 — smaller than some neighboring spines, still not always Mary Jones. Who cares for the child may not match the form.
Ask who should be in the room. Do not invent a last name. A nuclear English form already has a who. Do not use a child as interpreter.

Family can be larger than a nuclear English form and can look like one. Compass average household size about 2.63 — smaller than Kenyan, Liberian, and Ethiopian Compass rows, dated, still not always Mary Jones. Elders often speak first. Titles — Chief, Obi, Igwe, Alhaji, Deacon — sit in some rooms. Who cares for a disabled adult or a child may be a sibling, an in-law, a church mother, not the legally recognized caregiver on the checkbox.

### Who is in the household

Hour caps and “natural supports” can dump unpaid work onto women in that network and call it culture. Naming is already a who: Yoruba, Igbo, Hausa, English. Do not invent a last name because the screen requires one.

### Who speaks

Who speaks in the lobby may be a child with Minnesota English. That child is not the qualified interpreter even when Compass LEP is 7.6 percent. CLAS still stands if this elder needs Yoruba, Igbo, Hausa, or Pidgin. Ask who should be in the room. Minnesota law still stands. Do not skip mandated reporting and call it humility.

Minnesota holds a Nigerian Compass community large enough that this department will meet it on waivers, child welfare, health care, cash, food, aging, and employment — and large enough that the building has a habit of hearing African and booking Somali or opening historic African American. Compass: about 18,141 (ACS 2019–2023). Greater Minnesota is 12.4 percent. Do not write this people as a Minneapolis anecdote.

### Places

Places, not a blob: Twin Cities suburbs; Minneapolis and St. Paul pockets; Greater Minnesota towns with hospitals and housing. IgboFest as public life (including North Hennepin / Brooklyn Park in public listings). Churches are public life. They are not consultation. A jollof visit does not make you the expert.

### Partners

Partners: Minnesota Institute for Nigerian Development (MIND) historically as an umbrella; Igbo associations and IgboFest; Yoruba, Edo, and other associations families name; churches and mosques families name; CECLC as a department door — not the whole. Pay the partner this household actually uses.

Nigerian staff are not unpaid interpreters and not the community. Identity is not a staffing plan. IgboFest or Independence Day is optional professional development if you are invited. You are a guest. It does not make you the expert.

sections.heading: Nigerian Minnesota — the heart of a people
paragraphs: A state name is not one ethnicity. Nigerian peoplehood after colony, after Biafra for some, after oil and military rule. Black in a U.S. checkbox that also holds Somali, Liberian, and historic African American.

To be Nigerian in Minnesota is to be a state-name people of many nations, filed under African, Black, and sometimes Somali by a building that has not studied. Peoplehood after colony, after Biafra for some, after oil and military rule, is not a Nollywood poster. Yoruba, Igbo, Hausa, and the rest do not share one Tuesday. You do not pick a side.

### In this state

In this building another fact sits on top: many of these households are Black in a U.S. racial order that will file them under historic African American and get the language, the church, the title, and the name wrong. Shared race is not shared culture.

Face, elder obligation, titles, and not shaming the name travel into a waiver meeting. Harmony can look like agreement and then a plan nobody follows. Ask whether they agree. Do not take a smile as consent.

This guide is a working orientation. Individual variation always supersedes group generalization. Always defer to the person in front of you.

Yoruba names often carry a sentence — Oluwaseun, Adebola, Temitope. Igbo names often carry Chi or Chukwu — Chukwuemeka, Chinwe, Ngozi. Hausa and Muslim names in northern and some Yoruba rooms. chapters.body:
This brief is about Nigerian Minnesota as a state-name community of many peoples. Yoruba, Igbo, Hausa, Edo, Ijaw, Tiv, Ibibio, Fulani, and others are not one file. Book the language this household names. English is official. Nigerian Pidgin is a language, not broken English. Yoruba is not Igbo. Hausa is not Yoruba. A “Nigerian interpreter” is not a language. An “African interpreter” is a closed door.

### Who this is

This is not Somali. Shared race in the United States is not shared culture. This is not historic African American. Compass African American is a different mash. This is not Liberian as a synonym — related West African coast, different state, different war, different languages. This is not Ghanaian.

### Who this is not

Minnesota Compass (ACS 2019–2023) puts Nigerian Minnesota near 18,141. About 87.6 percent Twin Cities, about 12.4 percent Greater Minnesota. About 29.9 percent age 17 or younger; about 8.2 percent 65+. About 60.3 percent foreign-born. Language other than English (age 5+) 55.7 percent; English less than “very well” 7.6 percent. Bachelor’s or higher (25+) 54.0 percent. Date the number. A rate is not the person. High attainment is not the interpreter.

The diversity inside this state name is the point. A Yoruba Pentecostal professional, an Igbo Catholic household that still names Biafra, a Hausa Muslim family, an Edo association member, a U.S.-born student who uses English with friends and Igbo with an elder, a Greater Minnesota nurse — share a Compass row and do not share a Tuesday.

### How to read this

Always defer to the person in front of you. This page is a hypothesis you still test on this family.

chapters.title: A Note on This Guide

chapters.body:
Nigeria is a state of many nations. Yoruba peoplehood in the southwest, Igbo peoplehood in the southeast, Hausa-Fulani in the north, Edo, Ijaw, Tiv, Ibibio, and hundreds of others. There is no single Nigerian ethnicity. Ask which people they are. Do not lecture taxonomy they did not ask for.

### History for the meeting

English as official language is colonial history. Independence in 1960. Biafra — 1967–1970 — is foundational literacy for many Igbo households. It is not a speech you give the family. It is not every Nigerian’s story. Do not referee it in a waiver meeting.

### What people brought

What people brought: ethnic language, English, Pidgin, church and mosque, titles, kin obligation, a memory of colony and of a civil war some will name and some will not. What they met in Minnesota: an English form, one “African” checkbox, one “Black” mash, and often Somali because the building already has that page.

Do not start with a Nollywood or jollof tourism sentence. Origins did not begin in Minneapolis.

chapters.title: Origins and the Founding of a People

chapters.body:
Homeland is not one map. Lagos and the Yoruba southwest, Igbo southeast, Hausa-Fulani north, Niger Delta, Middle Belt. Abuja is not the whole. A person may name Ibadan, Enugu, Kano, Benin City, Port Harcourt, a village — not the capital. Do not referee regional politics in a waiver meeting. Listen if they name a place.

### Homeland

The diaspora is global and large: Texas, New York, Maryland and D.C., Georgia, the UK, the Gulf. Minnesota is a real community, not the U.S. capital of it. Secondary migration, church networks, school, and professional work pulled people here.

### Minnesota

In Minnesota: Compass 87.6 percent Twin Cities, 12.4 percent Greater Minnesota. Do not assume Minneapolis. Do not assume Cedar-Riverside. Do not assume the person in front of you has been to Nigeria. Inner-ring suburbs and Greater Minnesota towns with hospitals and housing are still this people.

chapters.title: The Geography of the Nigerian World

chapters.body:
There is no single 1975 or 1991 on this page. Independence in 1960 is the political founding of the state. Biafra, 1967–1970, is the foundational political event of much of Igbo Minnesota’s first memory. Dead in the millions by some counts. Famine as a weapon. That sentence is literacy. It is not a speech. It is not every Nigerian household.

### Foundational events

Later Minnesota streams are mixed: students, skilled work including healthcare, family reunification, diversity visas. Do not file every Nigerian household as refugee. Do not file every Nigerian household as a doctor. Both sit in this Compass row.

### Who you meet

The desk in 2026 meets first-generation professionals and U.S.-born children — English with peers, still translating for a grandmother whose Igbo or Yoruba was never booked, still filed under Black or under African.

If you only know “African,” you will miss this household.

Minnesota holds a Nigerian Compass community large enough that this department will meet it on waivers, child welfare, health care, cash, food, aging, and employment — and large enough that the building has a habit of hearing African and booking Somali or opening historic African American. Compass: about 18,141 (ACS 2019–2023). Greater Minnesota is 12.4 percent. Do not write this people as a Minneapolis anecdote.

### Places

Places, not a blob: Twin Cities suburbs; Minneapolis and St. Paul pockets; Greater Minnesota towns with hospitals and housing. IgboFest as public life (including North Hennepin / Brooklyn Park in public listings). Churches are public life. They are not consultation. A jollof visit does not make you the expert.

### Partners

Partners: Minnesota Institute for Nigerian Development (MIND) historically as an umbrella; Igbo associations and IgboFest; Yoruba, Edo, and other associations families name; churches and mosques families name; CECLC as a department door — not the whole. Pay the partner this household actually uses.

Nigerian staff are not unpaid interpreters and not the community. Identity is not a staffing plan. IgboFest or Independence Day is optional professional development if you are invited. You are a guest. It does not make you the expert.

chapters.title: Minnesota and Nigerian History

chapters.body:
To be Nigerian in Minnesota is to be a state-name people of many nations, filed under African, Black, and sometimes Somali by a building that has not studied. Peoplehood after colony, after Biafra for some, after oil and military rule, is not a Nollywood poster. Yoruba, Igbo, Hausa, and the rest do not share one Tuesday. You do not pick a side.

### In this state

In this building another fact sits on top: many of these households are Black in a U.S. racial order that will file them under historic African American and get the language, the church, the title, and the name wrong. Shared race is not shared culture.

Face, elder obligation, titles, and not shaming the name travel into a waiver meeting. Harmony can look like agreement and then a plan nobody follows. Ask whether they agree. Do not take a smile as consent.

This guide is a working orientation. Individual variation always supersedes group generalization. Always defer to the person in front of you.

sections.heading: A Note on This Guide
paragraphs: Puerto Rican Minnesota. Compass ACS 2019–2023: 21,802; Greater MN 32.9%. U.S. citizens since 1917. Foreign-born 1.3%. Do not run an immigration script by default. Spanish varieties; English-dominant households exist. Not Mexican. Not the Latino umbrella. Date the number you cite.
There is no single Puerto Rican client. Defer to this family. Do not open a Mexican or Latino-umbrella case with this page. Do not collect status you do not need. Ask language. Pronounce the name.

This brief is about Puerto Rican Minnesota as a people — boricua, puertorriqueño, puertorriqueña — not as a Mexican variant, not as an immigrant file, and not as the Latino / Hispanic umbrella. U.S. citizens since the Jones Act (2 March 1917). Do not run an immigration script by default. Compass foreign-born is 1.3 percent because ACS does not count birth on the island as foreign. Spanish varieties exist. English-dominant households exist. This is not Mexican. It is not Guatemalan. It is not Salvadoran. Shared Spanish is not shared culture. A full mosaic is not a stereotype. A stereotype is when this page becomes the person in the lobby.

### Who this is

Open the Latino umbrella only as adjacent. That page is the mash and the CLAS Spanish line. This page is Puerto Rican. If you leave this door and file the household under “Latino” or under Mexican, or greet them with an ICE speech because the name is Spanish, you have left this door.

### Who this is not

Minnesota Compass (ACS 2019–2023) puts the Puerto Rican cultural community at 21,802. Twin Cities 67.1 percent; Greater Minnesota 32.9 percent — not an afterthought. About 38.2 percent age 17 or younger; 5.5 percent 65+. English only (age 5+) 62.2 percent; language other than English 37.8 percent; English less than “very well” 10.2 percent. Date the number you use. LEP 10.2 percent is not “no language gate.” A rate is not the person.

The diversity inside this people is the point. An island-born elder who uses Spanish, a Minnesota-born English-dominant kid, a Nuyorican household that moved west, a person displaced after Hurricane María, an Afro-Puerto Rican student, a Greater Minnesota worker the building filed as Mexican, a queer second-generation adult who uses English with friends and Spanish with a grandmother — share a people and do not share a Tuesday.

### How to read this

Always defer to the person in front of you. This page is a hypothesis you still test on this family.

sections.heading: Origins and the Founding of a People
paragraphs: Borikén. Taíno, Spanish colonial, African enslavement — literacy for the desk, not a three-root speech. 1898 U.S. colony. Jones Act 1917 citizenship. Not a Mexican origin story.
History is literacy for the desk. It is not a speech you give the family. Do not start with a salsa tourism sentence.

Puerto Rican peoplehood is older than 1917 and older than the Minnesota file. Borikén. Taíno people, Spanish colonial rule, African enslavement in the sugar and later coffee economy — that three-root sentence is literacy for the desk. It is incomplete. It is not a speech you give the family. Do not start with a salsa tourism sentence or a Heritage Month flag.

### History for the meeting

1898: the United States took the island in the war with Spain. Colony. The Jones Act (2 March 1917) made Puerto Ricans U.S. citizens. Citizenship without treating the household as foreign is the first operational fact on this desk. They still cannot vote for president from the island. They can, if they reside in Minnesota. That is colonial status as literacy, not a lecture.

### What people brought

Spanish and English are both official on the island. Writing in both exists. Some elders read Spanish and not English. Some Minnesota-born adults read English and not Spanish. Some read both. Ask. Oral skill is not print.

What people brought: language (Caribbean Spanish and English), kinship, Catholic and later Protestant church, Afro-diasporic practice in some families, baseball, a memory of a colony that claimed them. What they met in Minnesota: an English form, one “Latino” checkbox, often one interpreter labeled Spanish, and a lobby that had already decided they were immigrants.

sections.heading: The Geography of the Puerto Rican World
paragraphs: The island; Vieques; Culebra; Nuyorican and other U.S. diasporas; Minnesota. Compass: 67.1% Twin Cities, 32.9% Greater Minnesota.
Do not assume Minneapolis. Do not assume they have been to the island. Greater Minnesota 32.9% is not an afterthought. Do not assume a Spanish-surnamed plant-town household is Mexican.

Homeland is the island — municipalities people name, San Juan, Ponce, Mayagüez, the mountains, the coast. Vieques and Culebra are not trivia. Confirm the place if they name it. Do not referee San Juan versus the west in a waiver meeting. Listen.

### Homeland

The U.S. Puerto Rican map is New York (Nuyorican as a named diaspora), Chicago, Florida, Pennsylvania, and also Minnesota. Those hubs are not this map. Secondary migration, military, school, and work pulled people here. Hurricane María (2017) moved people again.

### Minnesota

In Minnesota: Twin Cities 67.1 percent, Greater Minnesota 32.9 percent (Compass ACS 2019–2023). Greater Minnesota is not an afterthought. Do not assume Minneapolis. Do not assume the person in front of you has been to the island. Do not assume a Spanish-surnamed household in a plant town is Mexican. A Greater Minnesota household is still this people.

sections.heading: Citizenship, Island, and Internal Migration — Foundational Facts
paragraphs: Internal U.S. migration, not immigration. Operation Bootstrap; Nuyorican and Midwest streams; Hurricane María (2017) displacement. Citizenship since 1917.
If you only know “immigrant,” you will miss this household and run an ICE script on a citizen. Do not collect status you do not need.

This is internal U.S. migration, not immigration. Jones Act, 1917. Operation Bootstrap in the mid-twentieth century pushed industrial policy on the island and labor to the mainland — New York, Chicago, and later other states. Nuyorican is a named diaspora. Minnesota is a later present. Do not run an immigration script by default because the name is Spanish.

### Foundational events

Hurricane María (September 2017) is displacement literacy for the desk. People left a wrecked grid. Some came here. That is not an immigrant wave. It is citizens moving inside the United States after a disaster. PROMESA and the fiscal control board are political literacy. They are not a speech you give the family.

### Who you meet

The desk in 2026 meets island-born elders, U.S.-mainland-born adults, Minnesota-born children, and mixed island–mainland households. Compass foreign-born 1.3 percent is the ACS fact: birth in Puerto Rico is not foreign-born. If you only know “immigrant,” you will miss them and you will harm them.

Enforcement climate in the wider Latino lobby still spills. A Puerto Rican citizen can still be asked for papers because the building mashed the file. That is the gate. Do not collect status you do not need.

Do not treat this household as mixed-status by default. Citizenship is the fact. Do not collect status you do not need. Who speaks in the lobby may be a child. Even in an English-dominant household, a child is not the qualified interpreter for a Spanish-speaking elder — and an English-speaking adult is not a child to be skipped. CLAS still stands when Spanish is needed. Using a child as the go-between is a harm.

To be Puerto Rican in Minnesota is to be a people with an island, a colony, and U.S. citizenship, filed under a checkbox that defaults Mexican and often immigrant. Face, kin, and not shaming the name travel into a waiver meeting. Harmony can look like agreement and then a plan nobody follows. Ask whether they agree. Do not take a smile as consent.

### In this state

Afro-Puerto Rican people exist. Colorism is real. Do not bleach this household into a mestizo Latino story, and do not mash them into historic African American because both are Black. Ask.

The Mexican default in this state is a count fact on another page. It is a harm on this one when staff copy Guadalupe, ICE, and “the interpreter” onto a citizen household that may be English-dominant.

English-style single last names exist in some U.S.-born and some mainland-raised households. Ask how to file. Ask how to say it. Pronounce it. Do not drop accents as a joke. Given names may be Spanish, English, or both. Some people use a middle given name as the call-name.

Women may or may not take a husband’s surname in U.S. records. Children may carry two surnames that do not match a parent’s U.S. “last name” field. That is not fraud until you have a reason.

Do not treat unmatched last names in a household as a fraud flag by default. Do not invent a hyphen and then punish the person when the hyphen moves.

A parent who speaks fluent Caribbean Spanish and limited English is not illiterate. A parent who is English-dominant is not “no culture” and not proof the elder in the household needs no interpreter. Ask. Do not use a child as interpreter.

Second-generation educational mobility is real. So is a gap that a room that treats everyone the same will call “culture” instead of a school that never learned the second surname, or that filed this student as “immigrant.” Puerto Rican students are not immigrant students by default. chapters.body:
This brief is about Puerto Rican Minnesota as a people — boricua, puertorriqueño, puertorriqueña — not as a Mexican variant, not as an immigrant file, and not as the Latino / Hispanic umbrella. U.S. citizens since the Jones Act (2 March 1917). Do not run an immigration script by default. Compass foreign-born is 1.3 percent because ACS does not count birth on the island as foreign. Spanish varieties exist. English-dominant households exist. This is not Mexican. It is not Guatemalan. It is not Salvadoran. Shared Spanish is not shared culture. A full mosaic is not a stereotype. A stereotype is when this page becomes the person in the lobby.

### Who this is

Open the Latino umbrella only as adjacent. That page is the mash and the CLAS Spanish line. This page is Puerto Rican. If you leave this door and file the household under “Latino” or under Mexican, or greet them with an ICE speech because the name is Spanish, you have left this door.

### Who this is not

Minnesota Compass (ACS 2019–2023) puts the Puerto Rican cultural community at 21,802. Twin Cities 67.1 percent; Greater Minnesota 32.9 percent — not an afterthought. About 38.2 percent age 17 or younger; 5.5 percent 65+. English only (age 5+) 62.2 percent; language other than English 37.8 percent; English less than “very well” 10.2 percent. Date the number you use. LEP 10.2 percent is not “no language gate.” A rate is not the person.

The diversity inside this people is the point. An island-born elder who uses Spanish, a Minnesota-born English-dominant kid, a Nuyorican household that moved west, a person displaced after Hurricane María, an Afro-Puerto Rican student, a Greater Minnesota worker the building filed as Mexican, a queer second-generation adult who uses English with friends and Spanish with a grandmother — share a people and do not share a Tuesday.

### How to read this

Always defer to the person in front of you. This page is a hypothesis you still test on this family.

chapters.title: A Note on This Guide

chapters.body:
Puerto Rican peoplehood is older than 1917 and older than the Minnesota file. Borikén. Taíno people, Spanish colonial rule, African enslavement in the sugar and later coffee economy — that three-root sentence is literacy for the desk. It is incomplete. It is not a speech you give the family. Do not start with a salsa tourism sentence or a Heritage Month flag.

### History for the meeting

1898: the United States took the island in the war with Spain. Colony. The Jones Act (2 March 1917) made Puerto Ricans U.S. citizens. Citizenship without treating the household as foreign is the first operational fact on this desk. They still cannot vote for president from the island. They can, if they reside in Minnesota. That is colonial status as literacy, not a lecture.

### What people brought

Spanish and English are both official on the island. Writing in both exists. Some elders read Spanish and not English. Some Minnesota-born adults read English and not Spanish. Some read both. Ask. Oral skill is not print.

What people brought: language (Caribbean Spanish and English), kinship, Catholic and later Protestant church, Afro-diasporic practice in some families, baseball, a memory of a colony that claimed them. What they met in Minnesota: an English form, one “Latino” checkbox, often one interpreter labeled Spanish, and a lobby that had already decided they were immigrants.

### Homeland

The U.S. Puerto Rican map is New York (Nuyorican as a named diaspora), Chicago, Florida, Pennsylvania, and also Minnesota. Those hubs are not this map. Secondary migration, military, school, and work pulled people here. Hurricane María (2017) moved people again.

### Minnesota

In Minnesota: Twin Cities 67.1 percent, Greater Minnesota 32.9 percent (Compass ACS 2019–2023). Greater Minnesota is not an afterthought. Do not assume Minneapolis. Do not assume the person in front of you has been to the island. Do not assume a Spanish-surnamed household in a plant town is Mexican. A Greater Minnesota household is still this people.

This is internal U.S. migration, not immigration. Jones Act, 1917. Operation Bootstrap in the mid-twentieth century pushed industrial policy on the island and labor to the mainland — New York, Chicago, and later other states. Nuyorican is a named diaspora. Minnesota is a later present. Do not run an immigration script by default because the name is Spanish.

### Foundational events

Hurricane María (September 2017) is displacement literacy for the desk. People left a wrecked grid. Some came here. That is not an immigrant wave. It is citizens moving inside the United States after a disaster. PROMESA and the fiscal control board are political literacy. They are not a speech you give the family.

### Who you meet

The desk in 2026 meets island-born elders, U.S.-mainland-born adults, Minnesota-born children, and mixed island–mainland households. Compass foreign-born 1.3 percent is the ACS fact: birth in Puerto Rico is not foreign-born. If you only know “immigrant,” you will miss them and you will harm them.

Enforcement climate in the wider Latino lobby still spills. A Puerto Rican citizen can still be asked for papers because the building mashed the file. That is the gate. Do not collect status you do not need.

Titles — Señor, Señora, Don, Doña — until invited in some Spanish rooms. English “hello” is ordinary in others. Say the name. There may be two surnames. Do not assume a Spanish greeting is required, and do not assume English is a closed door to Spanish.

### This room

Do not import Somali right-hand rules or the Black nod onto this page. This is not those grammars. Cross-gender touch: follow this room. A hug from staff is not warmth if the household did not offer it.

Two surnames remain common: apellido paterno then apellido materno. A U.S. database that keeps one surname invents a person. That invented name then follows them through MHCP, child welfare, and school. It is a gate.

### How to file

English-style single last names exist in some U.S.-born and some mainland-raised households. Ask how to file. Ask how to say it. Pronounce it. Do not drop accents as a joke. Given names may be Spanish, English, or both. Some people use a middle given name as the call-name.

Women may or may not take a husband’s surname in U.S. records. Children may carry two surnames that do not match a parent’s U.S. “last name” field. That is not fraud until you have a reason.

Do not treat unmatched last names in a household as a fraud flag by default. Do not invent a hyphen and then punish the person when the hyphen moves.

A parent who speaks fluent Caribbean Spanish and limited English is not illiterate. A parent who is English-dominant is not “no culture” and not proof the elder in the household needs no interpreter. Ask. Do not use a child as interpreter.

Second-generation educational mobility is real. So is a gap that a room that treats everyone the same will call “culture” instead of a school that never learned the second surname, or that filed this student as “immigrant.” Puerto Rican students are not immigrant students by default. Do not collect status you do not need at enrollment theater.

This brief is about Salvadoran Minnesota as a people — salvadoreño, salvadoreña — not as a Mexican variant and not as the Latino / Hispanic umbrella. Civil war (1980–1992) and Temporary Protected Status are literacy for the desk, not a speech you give the family. Spanish is not one Spanish. Voseo is ordinary in Salvadoran rooms. A Mexican interpreter can still be a closed door. This is not Mexican. It is not Guatemalan. It is not Puerto Rican. Shared Spanish is not shared culture. A full mosaic is not a stereotype. ### Who this is

Open the Latino umbrella only as adjacent. That page is the mash and the CLAS Spanish line. This page is Salvadoran. If you leave this door and file the household under “Latino” or under Mexican because that is the Minnesota default, you have left this door.

Minnesota Compass (ACS 2019–2023) puts the Salvadoran cultural community at 17,571. Twin Cities 76.7 percent; Greater Minnesota 23.3 percent — not an afterthought. The diversity inside this people is the point. A 1980s arrival who came through the war, a TPS holder whose status is a clock, a U.S.-born nurse, a Greater Minnesota factory household, an evangelical grandmother, a college student who uses English with friends and voseo with an uncle, a person who will not open the door because a relative can be moved — share a people and do not share a Tuesday.

Always defer to the person in front of you. This page is a hypothesis you still test on this family.

### History for the meeting

Spanish colonial rule, independence with the other Central American republics (15 September 1821), a coffee oligarchy, and the twentieth-century state that went to war with its own people — that is literacy for the desk. It is not a speech you give the family. Do not start with a pupusa, a volcano, or a Heritage Month sentence.

### What people brought

Writing in Spanish is the ordinary public literacy. Some elders read Spanish. Some do not. Some U.S.-born adults do not read Spanish either. Oral skill is not print. Salvadoran Spanish is not Mexican Spanish.

What people brought: language (including voseo), kinship, Catholic and later evangelical church, work knowledge, remittance as obligation, a memory of a war the United States funded. What they met in Minnesota: an English form, one “Latino” checkbox, often one interpreter labeled Spanish — usually Mexican — and a lobby that had not studied TPS.

sections.heading: Civil War, TPS, and Later Streams — Foundational Event
paragraphs: Civil war 1980–1992; U.S.-backed conflict; Romero 1980; later TPS after disasters; family and work streams. Not IRCA-Mexican as the file. Not Guatemalan Maya flight as the file.

If 1975 is the foundational event of Vietnamese Minnesota, the Salvadoran civil war (1980–1992) is the foundational political event of Salvadoran Minnesota. Archbishop Óscar Romero was assassinated on 24 March 1980. The United States backed the government. People fled. That is literacy for the desk. It is not a speech you give the family. It is not an icebreaker. Do not ask a person to narrate killing for your professional development.

### Foundational events

Peace Accords, 16 January 1992. Later streams carry family reunification, work, disasters, and Temporary Protected Status — including after the 2001 earthquakes — as a clock that reorganizes Tuesday. TPS is structure. It is not a personality. It is not a reason to collect status you do not need, and it is a reason a form that feels like enforcement will empty the lobby.

### Who you meet

The desk in 2026 does not only meet a 1980s arrival. It meets U.S.-born children — Compass foreign-born 43.9 percent — translating for parents, mixed-status households, TPS holders, and a person who has lived here since childhood and still cannot get Salvadoran Spanish in the lobby. If you only know “immigrant,” you will miss them. If you only know “Mexican,” you will mash them.

Enforcement is current structure. When TPS is threatened, or raids are rumored, people skip clinic, school, and waiver meetings. That is not noncompliance.

Language: CLAS Spanish is not one Spanish. Salvadoran Spanish / voseo. A Mexican interpreter can still be a closed door. Still book a qualified interpreter. Do not use a child. Gender match may be requested in maternal and intimate care. LOTE 79.1 percent and LEP 39.0 percent (Compass ACS 2019–2023) are gates. Date them.

Names: two surnames. The database that keeps one invents a person. Unmatched last names are not fraud by default.

Hour caps, exception processes, SSN on the first screen, and life-sharing matches without language are not culturally neutral. TPS and mixed-status households will bounce if the first field feels like enforcement. Do not collect status you do not need.

Child welfare and disability: help-seeking that becomes a report is part of why people wait. Mandated reporting still exists. So does the duty not to treat a whole community as a risk score — or a last name as a gang file. Domestic violence is not culture. You follow law.

Enforcement climate: people skip clinic, school, and waiver meetings when TPS is a clock or a relative can be moved. That is not noncompliance. Do not collect status you do not need.

Notices and comment: an eList and an English PDF is not how this community was reached. Empty follow-up cells are theater. Greater Minnesota is 23.3 percent — a St. Paul meeting is not the whole channel.

Workforce: Salvadoran staff are not the interpreter pool and not the community. Staff are colleagues, not the curriculum. Do not treat  them.

Latino mash: opening Mexican, or the umbrella, because the checkbox says Hispanic is a closed door.

Legislation, funding, rule: you cannot advocate for a channel you will not study. This cultural intelligence exists so the 40% has a household in it — not a paternalistic program designed in a building that never learned that Spanish is not one Spanish.

community.title: Salvadoran Minnesota

chapters.body:
This brief is about Salvadoran Minnesota as a people — salvadoreño, salvadoreña — not as a Mexican variant and not as the Latino / Hispanic umbrella. Civil war (1980–1992) and Temporary Protected Status are literacy for the desk, not a speech you give the family. Spanish is not one Spanish. Voseo is ordinary in Salvadoran rooms. A Mexican interpreter can still be a closed door. This is not Mexican. It is not Guatemalan. It is not Puerto Rican. Shared Spanish is not shared culture. A full mosaic is not a stereotype. A stereotype is when this page becomes the person in the lobby.

### Who this is

Open the Latino umbrella only as adjacent. That page is the mash and the CLAS Spanish line. This page is Salvadoran. If you leave this door and file the household under “Latino” or under Mexican because that is the Minnesota default, you have left this door.

### Who this is not

Minnesota Compass (ACS 2019–2023) puts the Salvadoran cultural community at 17,571. Twin Cities 76.7 percent; Greater Minnesota 23.3 percent — not an afterthought. About 48.5 percent age 17 or younger. Compass suppresses 65+ in this vintage — do not invent it. Foreign-born 43.9 percent. Language other than English (age 5+) 79.1 percent; English less than “very well” 39.0 percent. Date the number you use. Compass does not split an indigenous-language count on this profile. Do not invent one. A rate is not the person.

The diversity inside this people is the point. A 1980s arrival who came through the war, a TPS holder whose status is a clock, a U.S.-born nurse, a Greater Minnesota factory household, an evangelical grandmother, a college student who uses English with friends and voseo with an uncle, a person who will not open the door because a relative can be moved — share a people and do not share a Tuesday.

### How to read this

Always defer to the person in front of you. This page is a hypothesis you still test on this family.
chapters.evidence: Salvadoran Minnesota. Compass ACS 2019–2023: 17,571; Greater MN 23.3%. Not Mexican. Civil war and TPS history. Spanish is not one Spanish. Date the number you cite.
chapters.practitioner: There is no single Salvadoran client. Defer to this family. Do not open a Mexican or Latino-umbrella case with this page. Pronounce the name. Book qualified Spanish AND ask.
chapters.title: A Note on This Guide

chapters.body:
Salvadoran peoplehood is not a Mexican origin story with a different flag. El Salvador is the smallest mainland republic in Central America. Pipil / Nahua history was largely mestizo-ized by the colony and the coffee state; do not invent a Minnesota indigenous-language count Compass does not have, and do not copy K’iche’ from the Guatemalan page onto this one. Ask this household.

### History for the meeting

Spanish colonial rule, independence with the other Central American republics (15 September 1821), a coffee oligarchy, and the twentieth-century state that went to war with its own people — that is literacy for the desk. It is not a speech you give the family. Do not start with a pupusa, a volcano, or a Heritage Month sentence.

### What people brought

Writing in Spanish is the ordinary public literacy. Some elders read Spanish. Some do not. Some U.S.-born adults do not read Spanish either. Oral skill is not print. Salvadoran Spanish is not Mexican Spanish.

What people brought: language (including voseo), kinship, Catholic and later evangelical church, work knowledge, remittance as obligation, a memory of a war the United States funded. What they met in Minnesota: an English form, one “Latino” checkbox, often one interpreter labeled Spanish — usually Mexican — and a lobby that had not studied TPS.
chapters.evidence: El Salvador — smallest mainland Central American republic. Pipil / Nahua history largely mestizo-ized. Independence with the other republics. Not a Mexican origin story and not a Maya file.
chapters.practitioner: History is literacy for the desk. It is not a speech you give the family. Do not start with a pupusa tourism sentence.
chapters.title: Origins and the Founding of a People

chapters.body:
Homeland is El Salvador — departments people name, San Salvador, the coast, the interior. Confirm the place if they name it. Do not referee Santa Ana versus San Miguel in a waiver meeting. Listen.

### Homeland

The U.S. Salvadoran map is California (Los Angeles among the named hubs), the D.C.–Maryland–Virginia corridor, Texas, New York, and also Minnesota. Those hubs are not this map. Secondary migration and family pulled people here.

### Minnesota

In Minnesota: Twin Cities 76.7 percent, Greater Minnesota 23.3 percent (Compass ACS 2019–2023). Greater Minnesota is not an afterthought. Do not assume Minneapolis. Do not assume a plant town is Guatemalan by default. Do not assume the person in front of you has been to El Salvador. A Greater Minnesota household is still this people.
chapters.evidence: El Salvador — departments people name; San Salvador; the coast. U.S. Salvadoran America is California, D.C./Maryland/Virginia, Texas, New York, and Minnesota. Compass: 76.7% Twin Cities, 23.3% Greater Minnesota.
chapters.practitioner: Do not assume Minneapolis. Do not assume they have been to El Salvador. Greater Minnesota 23.3% is not an afterthought. Do not assume a plant town is Guatemalan by default.
chapters.title: The Geography of the Salvadoran World

chapters.body:
If 1975 is the foundational event of Vietnamese Minnesota, the Salvadoran civil war (1980–1992) is the foundational political event of Salvadoran Minnesota. Archbishop Óscar Romero was assassinated on 24 March 1980. The United States backed the government. People fled. That is literacy for the desk. It is not a speech you give the family. It is not an icebreaker. Do not ask a person to narrate killing for your professional development.

### Foundational events

Peace Accords, 16 January 1992. Later streams carry family reunification, work, disasters, and Temporary Protected Status — including after the 2001 earthquakes — as a clock that reorganizes Tuesday. TPS is structure. It is not a personality. It is not a reason to collect status you do not need, and it is a reason a form that feels like enforcement will empty the lobby.

### Who you meet

The desk in 2026 does not only meet a 1980s arrival. It meets U.S.-born children — Compass foreign-born 43.9 percent — translating for parents, mixed-status households, TPS holders, and a person who has lived here since childhood and still cannot get Salvadoran Spanish in the lobby. If you only know “immigrant,” you will miss them. If you only know “Mexican,” you will mash them.

Enforcement is current structure. When TPS is threatened, or raids are rumored, people skip clinic, school, and waiver meetings. That is not noncompliance.
chapters.evidence: Civil war 1980–1992; U.S.-backed conflict; Romero 1980; later TPS after disasters; family and work streams. Not IRCA-Mexican as the file. Not Guatemalan Maya flight as the file.
chapters.practitioner: If you only know “immigrant,” you will miss TPS as structure and the U.S.-born child who still cannot get Salvadoran Spanish in the lobby.
chapters.title: Civil War, TPS, and Later Streams — Foundational Event

chapters.body:
Familismo is a hypothesis, not a personality. Elders often speak first. Adult children may be in the same week as a waiver meeting, a shift, and a school conference. Compass: average household size about 3.79. Still not always a nuclear English form. Who cares for a child may not match the waiver checkbox. Ask who should be in the room.

### Who is in the household

TPS and mixed-status are structure: a U.S.-citizen child, a parent on TPS, a sibling without status, an aunt who works service. Do not collect status you do not need. Do not treat unmatched last names, a grandmother as caregiver, or a missing SSN as fraud until you have a reason. Hour caps and “natural supports” language can dump unpaid work onto women in that network and call it culture.

### Who speaks

Who speaks in the lobby may be a child with the best English. That child is not the qualified interpreter. CLAS still stands. Using a child as the go-between is a closed door and a harm. Book the interpreter. Ask who should be in the room.

Minnesota law still stands. Domestic violence is not culture. Do not skip mandated reporting and call it humility.
chapters.evidence: Extended and mixed-status households. Compass average household size about 3.79. Who speaks may be a child — that is a gate. TPS and mixed-status are structure. Do not collect status you do not need.
chapters.practitioner: Ask who should be in the room. Do not use a child as interpreter. A nuclear English form already has a who.
chapters.title: Family

chapters.body:
Minnesota holds a Salvadoran community large enough that this department will meet it on waivers, child welfare, health care, cash, food, aging, and employment. Compass: 17,571 (ACS 2019–2023). Twin Cities 76.7 percent; Greater Minnesota 23.3 percent — not an afterthought. Do not write this people as a Minneapolis anecdote and do not write them as a Mexican leftover.

### Places

Places, not a blob: Twin Cities corridors and first-ring suburbs; Greater Minnesota towns with work and housing. Pupusa shops and markets are public life. They are not consultation. A food visit does not make you the expert.

### Partners

Partners: parishes and evangelical churches families name; rural parish and worker centers — name the local one; do not assume Minneapolis. CLUES is a Twin Cities door, not the whole community. CECLC is a department door, not the people. Pay the partner this household actually uses.

Salvadoran staff are not unpaid interpreters and not the community. Identity is not a staffing plan. A fiesta or a Romero commemoration is optional professional development if you are invited. You are a guest. It does not make you the expert.
chapters.evidence: Twin Cities majority (76.7%) and a real Greater Minnesota share (23.3%). Parishes, evangelical churches, worker centers. CLUES is metro, not the whole.
chapters.practitioner: Partners, not a harvest list. Staff are colleagues, not the curriculum. Do not treat  Salvadoran staff. Name the local partner — do not assume Minneapolis. A pupusa visit does not make you the expert.
chapters.title: Minnesota and Salvadoran History

chapters.body:
To be Salvadoran in Minnesota is to be a people with a small country and a long memory of a war the United States funded, then building a life in a cold state that filed you under Latino and often under Mexican. Face, kin, remittance, and not shaming the name travel into a waiver meeting. Harmony can look like agreement and then a plan nobody follows. Ask whether they agree. Do not take a smile as consent.

### In this state

Spanish is not one Spanish. Voseo is ordinary. A Mexican interpreter who does not hear this household is a closed door.

The Mexican default in this state is a count fact on another page. It is a harm on this one when staff copy Guadalupe, norteño, and Mexican Spanish onto a Salvadoran household.

This guide is a working orientation. Individual variation always supersedes group generalization. Always defer to the person in front of you.
chapters.evidence: Salvadoreño. Peoplehood after civil war, TPS, and a U.S. checkbox that defaults Mexican. Face, kin, remittance as obligation. Spanish is not one Spanish.
chapters.practitioner: Do not fold this household into one Latino blob or into Mexican. Do not copy a Guadalupe or Maya sentence onto this page. Open the Latino umbrella only as adjacent.
chapters.title: Salvadoreño — the heart of a people

chapters.body:
Civil-war memory. Foundational for the community. Not a personality for the person in the lobby. Not an icebreaker.

### TPS

Temporary Protected Status as a clock. Structure. Not a reason to collect status you do not need. A reason a badge is not automatically help.

### Voseo

Salvadoran Spanish. Not Mexican Spanish. Book qualified Spanish AND ask.

### Familismo and respeto as hypotheses

Titles, elders, kin as the unit of decision. Not a license to skip mandated reporting. A courtesy-yes is not a signature.

### Two surnames

The database that keeps one invents a person.

### Remittance, church, work

Evangelical and Catholic both. A plant shift and a second-generation degree can sit in the same household. Do not make a priest or a pastor the case plan unless they asked.
chapters.evidence: Civil-war memory; TPS as structure; voseo; evangelical and Catholic both; familismo as hypothesis; two surnames; remittance; not Mexican.
